That all 500 records were durably written to the stream
That none of the records were written, since 200 only confirms validation
That the records were written in the exact order they were submitted

cards.prompt: The response's ___ field gives the number of entries that failed, and each failed entry's own result carries an error code — typically a throttling or internal error — rather than a record id.
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Adding data to a stream'
cards.answer: FailedRecordCount

cards.prompt: Why is retrying an entire failed PutRecords batch, rather than just the failed entries, the wrong approach even though it is simpler to code?
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Adding data to a stream'
cards.answer: It needlessly resubmits records that already succeeded, and Kinesis has no built-in deduplication, so each resubmitted record becomes a genuine duplicate in the stream — the correct approach reads FailedRecordCount and each entry's own result, then retries only the entries that actually failed.

cards.prompt: A batch of 500 records is submitted with PutRecords. Ten fail and are retried in a second call. Explain why the ten retried records are not guaranteed to end up in their original relative position among the other 490, even though the whole batch shared the same partition key.
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Adding data to a stream'
cards.answer: Kinesis assigns sequence numbers at the moment a record is actually accepted, not at the moment it was first attempted. The 490 that succeeded on the first call were sequenced immediately; the 10 that failed are only sequenced later, on the retry, after whatever else has been written to that shard in between — so their position in the shard's log reflects when the retry landed, not when the batch was originally submitted.

cards.prompt: Throttling shows up as an explicit ___, thrown when a shard's write limit is exceeded — whether from one producer sending too fast or several producers combining to exceed the shared limit. Backing off immediately and retrying at full speed just recreates the same collision; exponential backoff with jitter is required, not a nice-to-have, because without the random jitter component, multiple throttled producers retry in lockstep and re-collide on the same schedule.
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Adding data to a stream'
cards.answer: ProvisionedThroughputExceededException

cards.prompt: Underneath all of this, Kinesis gives producers an honest but modest guarantee: writes are ___. A `PutRecord` or `PutRecords` call that times out on the client side may well have succeeded on the server side — the client has no way to distinguish "the write never happened" from "the write happened but the acknowledgment was lost" — so a producer that retries on timeout can produce a genuine duplicate.
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Adding data to a stream'
cards.answer: at-least-once

cards.prompt: Does a client-side timeout on a Kinesis PutRecord call mean the write definitely failed?
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Adding data to a stream'
cards.answer: No — the client cannot distinguish a write that truly failed from one that succeeded but whose acknowledgment was lost in transit, so a timed-out call may have already been durably written; retrying it can therefore create a duplicate, which is why consumers must tolerate at-least-once delivery rather than assume every record they see is new.

cards.prompt: On-demand's scaling is ___, not anticipatory — it responds to traffic it has already observed, which means it cannot pre-provision for a step change it has no way to see coming.
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Resharding a stream'
cards.answer: reactive

cards.prompt: A team knows a marketing campaign will drive a 10x traffic spike at a specific hour tomorrow. The stream currently runs in on-demand mode. What is the risk of leaving it on-demand for that event?
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Resharding a stream'

choices.text: On-demand scales reactively after observing increased traffic, so the sudden spike can throttle requests before new capacity is added
On-demand mode cannot scale at all without a support ticket
There is no risk — on-demand always pre-allocates enough headroom for any spike
On-demand mode caps throughput permanently at the account's default limit

cards.prompt: Why is a known, scheduled traffic spike specifically an argument for switching to provisioned capacity rather than trusting on-demand mode?
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Resharding a stream'
cards.answer: Because on-demand only scales in reaction to traffic it has already measured, so a sudden step change can outrun it and throttle briefly before it catches up — a known spike lets you provision the needed shard count in advance, which sidesteps that reaction lag entirely rather than relying on it to catch up in time.

cards.prompt: The fact that matters most about both operations: resharding does ___ move existing data. A split closes the parent shard to further writes and opens two child shards to take over its hash key range, but every record already written to the parent stays exactly where it is until it naturally expires under the stream's retention policy — nothing is copied or migrated into the children.
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Resharding a stream'
cards.answer: not

cards.prompt: A shard is split into two children while a consumer is partway through reading records from the parent. Explain why that consumer must finish reading everything remaining in the parent before it starts reading either child, and what breaks if it doesn't.
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Resharding a stream'
cards.answer: The parent shard still holds records that were written before the split, and those records keep their original relative order only within that parent. If the consumer jumps to a child shard early, it can read records that were written to that child after the split before it has read older records still sitting in the parent — for any partition key whose records happened to be mid-stream at split time, that reorders what the consumer sees relative to write order. Draining the parent fully first preserves the per-key ordering guarantee across the split; skipping ahead breaks exactly the guarantee resharding is supposed to leave intact.

cards.prompt: Does splitting a shard copy or move that shard's existing records into the two new child shards?
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Resharding a stream'
cards.answer: No — a split only closes the parent to new writes and routes future writes for its key range to the two children; every record already in the parent stays in the parent until it expires under the stream's normal retention, with nothing migrated.

cards.prompt: What state is a shard in once it has been split or merged and stopped accepting new writes, while its records remain readable until they expire?
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Resharding a stream'
cards.answer: Closed — a closed shard is no longer written to but stays readable for the remainder of its retention window, and a stream routinely has both open and closed shards present at once during and after resharding.

cards.prompt: A shard's limits are fixed and worth knowing exactly, because they drive almost every design decision downstream. A single shard accepts up to ___ of data per second on write, or 1,000 records per second, whichever limit is hit first.
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Shard'
cards.answer: 1 MB

cards.prompt: A shard's limits are fixed and worth knowing exactly, because they drive almost every design decision downstream. A single shard accepts up to 1 MB of data per second on write, or ___ records per second, whichever limit is hit first.
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Shard'

cards.prompt: On the read side, a shard supports up to 2 MB/s of output, and that capacity is ___ across every standard (non-fan-out) consumer reading it — three consumers polling the same shard split that same 2 MB/s three ways, not 2 MB/s each.
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Shard'
cards.answer: shared

cards.prompt: Why does adding more producers writing to the same shard never raise that shard's throughput ceiling?
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Shard'
cards.answer: The limit is enforced per shard, not per producer or per connection — every producer writing to a given shard shares the same 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s budget, so more producers just divide the existing ceiling rather than raising it.

cards.prompt: A stream has 20 shards. A producer sends every record with the partition key `"US"`, `"CA"`, or `"MX"` — a customer's country. What happens to write throughput as volume grows?
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Shard'

choices.text: Throughput is capped near the limit of a single shard, since only three distinct keys can ever hash to at most three shards, no matter how many shards the stream has
Throughput scales with the stream's full 20-shard capacity, since Kinesis load-balances any key across all shards
Kinesis automatically detects the skew and reassigns extra shards to the hot keys
Throughput is unaffected, because partition keys only affect ordering, not shard placement

cards.prompt: Why can't a stream with many distinct partition-key values ever go fully idle-throttled the way a low-cardinality key can, yet also not guarantee any ordering between two records for the same entity?
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Shard'
cards.answer: High cardinality spreads records across most or all shards, so no single shard absorbs a disproportionate share of traffic — but spreading also means two records sharing a logical entity are no longer guaranteed to hash to the same shard, and ordering only holds within a shard, so records for that entity can arrive out of order relative to each other.

cards.prompt: Explain why a Kinesis record is addressed by the pair (shard id, sequence number) rather than by a single global offset the way you might expect from a simpler log design.
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Shard'
cards.answer: There is no single log — a stream is a collection of independently ordered shards, each with its own sequence-number space starting from its own creation. A sequence number only has meaning relative to the shard that issued it; the same number could exist in two different shards and refer to two unrelated records. A consumer must therefore always know which shard it is reading before a sequence number tells it anything, which is exactly why consumer state is tracked per shard, never per stream.

cards.prompt: Does a Kinesis sequence number identify a record uniquely on its own, without knowing which shard it belongs to?
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Shard'
cards.answer: No — a sequence number is only unique and meaningful within its own shard; the same numeric value has no relationship to a record with that number in a different shard, so a record is only fully addressed by the pair of shard id and sequence number.

cards.prompt: Why might a Kinesis consumer built on the KCL appear to stop processing records even though the stream itself is healthy and well within its throughput limits?
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Developing Consumer Applications with the Kinesis Client Library'
cards.answer: Because the KCL coordinates shard ownership through a DynamoDB lease table, and if that table is under-provisioned or throttled, workers can't acquire, renew, or update leases — stalling consumption in a way that has nothing to do with the stream's own capacity and everything to do with the lease table's.

cards.prompt: Where does the KCL store a worker's checkpoint progress for a shard?
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Developing Consumer Applications with the Kinesis Client Library'

choices.text: In the same DynamoDB lease table used for shard-ownership coordination
In the Kinesis stream itself, as a special marker record
In a separate S3 object per shard
In memory only, recovered by replaying from TRIM_HORIZON on restart

cards.prompt: Why is there no checkpoint frequency that eliminates both reprocessing risk and lease-table load at once?
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Developing Consumer Applications with the Kinesis Client Library'
cards.answer: The two costs move in opposite directions along the same dial — checkpointing more often shrinks how much gets reprocessed after a crash but increases the write volume against the lease table (risking the throttling described above), while checkpointing less often reduces that write load but widens the window of work a crashed worker's successor has to redo; there is no frequency that minimizes both simultaneously, only a point chosen for the workload's tolerance for each.

cards.prompt: Because a worker can crash between finishing a record and recording its checkpoint, the same record can be handed to the next worker and processed again — which is exactly why Kinesis consumption via the KCL is ___ delivery, and why the processing logic itself has to be written to tolerate seeing a record more than once.
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Developing Consumer Applications with the Kinesis Client Library'
cards.answer: at-least-once

cards.prompt: Explain why "the KCL checkpoints for you" does not, by itself, make a consumer's downstream writes safe to run without additional care, given that a crash can occur between processing a record and checkpointing it.
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Developing Consumer Applications with the Kinesis Client Library'
cards.answer: A checkpoint only marks progress after the fact — it can't make the gap between "processed" and "checkpointed" atomic with whatever side effect the record caused. If a worker crashes in that gap, the next owner resumes from the last checkpoint and reprocesses the record, so the record's effect (a write, a message sent) can happen twice. The KCL guarantees the record isn't lost; it does not and cannot guarantee the record's downstream effect only happens once — that has to be built into the processing logic itself, the way idempotency is described for queue consumers.

cards.prompt: A rebalance after a reshard follows one strict rule that would be easy to violate by hand: the KCL always finishes processing a ___ shard completely before it will assign out either of its two children to any worker.
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Developing Consumer Applications with the Kinesis Client Library'
cards.answer: parent

cards.prompt: What ordering guarantee does the KCL enforce across a reshard, and why does it matter?
citations: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Developer Guide — 'Developing Consumer Applications with the Kinesis Client Library'
cards.answer: It fully finishes a parent shard before assigning either of its child shards to a worker, which preserves the sequential ordering a stream promises within a partition key's lineage — without this rule, a worker could start consuming a child shard's records while records still sit unprocessed on the parent, and since the child's records are logically downstream of the parent's, they'd be seen out of order.

cards.prompt: A cold start occurs when a request needs a ___, which happens on a function's very first invocation, after AWS reclaims an idle environment, or when scale-out needs more concurrent environments than currently exist.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'
cards.answer: brand-new execution environment

cards.prompt: The delay a cold start adds comes entirely from work the ___ has to do before invoke can start: provisioning the microVM, initializing the runtime, and running your module-level code — none of which a warm invocation has to repeat.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'
cards.answer: init phase

cards.prompt: Which of these is NOT part of what makes a cold start slower than a warm invocation?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'

choices.text: The handler function's own per-request logic runs slower on a cold start
The execution environment (microVM) has to be provisioned
The runtime has to start up
Module-level initialization code has to run

cards.prompt: Why does a larger deployment package, or a runtime with a heavier startup sequence, tend to make cold starts worse?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'
cards.answer: All of that additional code and any runtime bootstrapping has to be loaded and executed during init before the handler can run for the first time on that environment, so more bytes to fetch and more code to initialize directly lengthens the phase that a cold start puts on the request's critical path.

cards.prompt: Moving expensive setup — parsing large config, opening the first connection to a downstream service — out of the handler and into module-level code doesn't eliminate a cold start's cost; it just makes that cost visible during ___ rather than hidden inside the first invoke, which is still where a cold-started request pays for it.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'
cards.answer: init

cards.prompt: A team notices their function's median latency is fine but their p99 is dominated by occasional multi-second spikes that correlate with traffic bursts rather than with any particular time of day. Explain the mechanism connecting bursty traffic to cold starts, given that Lambda scales out by adding new execution environments.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'

cards.prompt: What lever, provided by the platform rather than by trimming your own code, keeps environments pre-initialized so an invocation skips init entirely?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'
cards.answer: Provisioned concurrency, which keeps a chosen number of execution environments already initialized and idle, ready to serve an invoke immediately rather than going through init on the request's own critical path.

cards.prompt: A cold start is bounded to the environments that are actually being created; once a burst of traffic has enough warm environments to absorb it, every additional request lands on ___ instead of paying init again, which is why cold starts show up disproportionately at the start of a traffic spike rather than throughout it.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'
cards.answer: reuse

cards.prompt: When concurrent invocations exceed the number of existing execution environments, Lambda responds by creating ___ in parallel, rather than queuing requests behind the ones already running — this is what "scaling out" means for Lambda specifically.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Managing Lambda reserved concurrency', 'Configuring provisioned concurrency'
cards.answer: additional environments

cards.prompt: Because each environment serves one invocation at a time, a function's concurrency is fundamentally an ___, not a property of the code itself; the same handler running on ten environments handles ten concurrent requests, and on one environment it handles one.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Managing Lambda reserved concurrency', 'Configuring provisioned concurrency'
cards.answer: environment count

cards.prompt: Reserved concurrency is a ___, not a target: it guarantees a function never gets starved of capacity by other functions sharing the account, but it also means that same function can never scale past the number reserved for it, no matter how much traffic arrives.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Managing Lambda reserved concurrency', 'Configuring provisioned concurrency'
cards.answer: cap

cards.prompt: What is the main functional difference between reserved and provisioned concurrency?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Managing Lambda reserved concurrency', 'Configuring provisioned concurrency'

choices.text: Reserved concurrency caps how many environments a function may use; provisioned concurrency keeps a number of environments pre-initialized and warm
Reserved concurrency pre-warms environments; provisioned concurrency caps them
They are two names for the same mechanism
Reserved concurrency only applies to asynchronous invocations

cards.prompt: Why doesn't provisioned concurrency prevent a function from ever cold-starting?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Managing Lambda reserved concurrency', 'Configuring provisioned concurrency'
cards.answer: Provisioned concurrency only pre-warms a fixed number of environments; traffic beyond that number still has to scale out onto newly created environments the normal way, and those new environments still pay the init phase on their first invocation.

cards.prompt: What happens to a request when a function is already running at its reserved concurrency limit and a new invocation arrives?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Managing Lambda reserved concurrency', 'Configuring provisioned concurrency'
cards.answer: It is throttled — Lambda rejects the invocation rather than creating another environment beyond the cap, and what the caller experiences next depends entirely on the invocation mode (an immediate error for a synchronous caller, an automatic retry for an asynchronous or poll-based one).

cards.prompt: A function shares an account-level concurrency pool with several other functions and has no reserved concurrency configured. Explain the risk this creates for that function's availability during a traffic spike on an unrelated function in the same account, and how reserved concurrency addresses it.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Managing Lambda reserved concurrency', 'Configuring provisioned concurrency'

cards.prompt: For a ___ invocation, Lambda does not retry a function error on the caller's behalf at all — the caller receives the error directly and any retry has to be code the caller itself writes.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Error handling and automatic retries in AWS Lambda', 'Configuring destinations for asynchronous invocation'
cards.answer: synchronous

cards.prompt: Why does it make sense that Lambda leaves retries to the caller for a synchronous invocation, rather than retrying internally the way it does for async?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Error handling and automatic retries in AWS Lambda', 'Configuring destinations for asynchronous invocation'
cards.answer: The caller is already there, waiting on the result, and is in the best position to decide whether retrying is safe or useful for that specific request (e.g. it may already have its own backoff and circuit-breaker logic) — Lambda retrying silently underneath a caller that is also blocked and waiting would just add latency the caller didn't ask for.

cards.prompt: For an ___ invocation, Lambda's internal event queue does retry a failed invocation automatically, without any caller involvement, before giving up and routing the event to whatever failure handling has been configured for it.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Error handling and automatic retries in AWS Lambda', 'Configuring destinations for asynchronous invocation'
cards.answer: asynchronous

cards.prompt: A function invoked asynchronously (e.g. by S3) throws an unhandled exception on every attempt. What happens to that event?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Error handling and automatic retries in AWS Lambda', 'Configuring destinations for asynchronous invocation'

choices.text: Lambda retries it automatically a limited number of times, then sends it to a configured destination or dead-letter queue if one exists
The event is dropped immediately with no retry, because S3 doesn't wait for a response
S3 itself detects the failure and re-sends the event
The function is throttled to prevent further invocations

cards.prompt: **Destinations** are the newer mechanism that supersede the DLQ pattern: they can route an event on ___ as well as on failure, to a wider set of targets (SQS, SNS, another Lambda function, or EventBridge), and they carry richer context — the invocation's response payload or error details — that a bare DLQ message does not.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Error handling and automatic retries in AWS Lambda', 'Configuring destinations for asynchronous invocation'
cards.answer: success

cards.prompt: Why can a single event's underlying operation end up applied more than once even though the platform "handled" retries correctly?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Error handling and automatic retries in AWS Lambda', 'Configuring destinations for asynchronous invocation'
cards.answer: A retry — whether Lambda's internal async retry or an SQS redelivery after a visibility timeout — re-delivers the same event to a new invocation with no knowledge of whether the previous attempt's side effects (a write, a charge, a message sent) actually completed before it failed; the platform's job is only to make sure the event isn't silently lost, not to guarantee it is processed exactly once.

cards.prompt: Explain why idempotency has to be built into the function's own logic (e.g. by checking a stored idempotency key before applying a write) rather than something Lambda's retry machinery can provide, given that retries by design re-deliver events whose prior outcome is unknown.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Error handling and automatic retries in AWS Lambda', 'Configuring destinations for asynchronous invocation'

cards.prompt: For a poll-based SQS trigger specifically, which mechanism controls whether a failed message gets redelivered, and how does that differ from an async invocation's retry behavior?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Error handling and automatic retries in AWS Lambda', 'Configuring destinations for asynchronous invocation'
cards.answer: The queue's own visibility timeout and redrive policy control redelivery — a message becomes visible again for another poll once its visibility timeout expires, and after enough failed receives (per the redrive policy) it moves to an SQS dead-letter queue; this is entirely SQS's own retry mechanism, distinct from the internal retry queue Lambda uses for asynchronous invocations.

cards.prompt: In a ___ invocation, the caller (an API Gateway request, another service calling the Invoke API directly) blocks and waits for the function to run and return a response, so the caller sees success or failure immediately and is responsible for deciding what to do next.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda invocation types', 'Using AWS Lambda with event source mappings'
cards.answer: synchronous

cards.prompt: In an ___ invocation, the caller hands the event to Lambda's internal event queue and gets an immediate acknowledgment that the event was accepted — not that it succeeded — while Lambda itself runs the function and handles retries in the background, decoupled from the caller.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda invocation types', 'Using AWS Lambda with event source mappings'
cards.answer: asynchronous

cards.prompt: Services like S3 and SNS invoke a function ___ by default; the caller (S3, SNS) never sees whether the function eventually succeeded, because it already moved on after Lambda accepted the event.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda invocation types', 'Using AWS Lambda with event source mappings'
cards.answer: asynchronously

cards.prompt: An API Gateway endpoint backed by a Lambda function times out and returns a 504 to the client. Which invocation mode is API Gateway using?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda invocation types', 'Using AWS Lambda with event source mappings'

choices.text: Synchronous — the caller is blocked waiting on the function and directly experiences the failure
Asynchronous — the caller would have already received an acknowledgment and moved on
Poll-based via an event source mapping — there is no caller to time out
It depends on the function's own configured invocation type

cards.prompt: The third mode, used for stream- and queue-based sources like Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams, and SQS, is **poll-based**: Lambda itself runs a separate component called an ___ that polls the source, batches records, and invokes the function on the service's behalf — there is no external caller at all, synchronous or otherwise.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda invocation types', 'Using AWS Lambda with event source mappings'
cards.answer: event source mapping

cards.prompt: What role does the event source mapping play for a poll-based source like SQS, and why does that make "who invoked the function" a different question than it is for API Gateway?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda invocation types', 'Using AWS Lambda with event source mappings'
cards.answer: The event source mapping is a Lambda-managed poller that reads batches of records off the queue or stream and calls Invoke on the function itself; there is no external client waiting on a response the way there is with API Gateway, so retry behavior and failure handling are governed entirely by the mapping's own configuration rather than by anything a caller does.

cards.prompt: Why can't you look at a trigger's name alone (e.g. "SNS", "SQS") and assume you already know how errors propagate?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda invocation types', 'Using AWS Lambda with event source mappings'
cards.answer: The invocation mode, not the service name, determines error propagation — SNS invokes asynchronously and Lambda's internal queue owns retries, while SQS is polled by an event source mapping whose batching and retry configuration is entirely separate machinery, so two different services can behave alike or two triggers on the same service can behave differently depending on how the mapping or invocation is configured.

cards.prompt: A function is triggered by SQS. Explain, at the level of who is doing the calling, why treating this the same as an API-Gateway-triggered function — assuming the caller sees and reacts to a failed invocation — would lead you to design its error handling incorrectly.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda invocation types', 'Using AWS Lambda with event source mappings'

cards.prompt: Which invocation mode leaves error handling and retries entirely to whatever code called Invoke directly, with no built-in queue or poller involved?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda invocation types', 'Using AWS Lambda with event source mappings'
cards.answer: Synchronous invocation — the caller gets the failure directly and must itself decide whether to retry, so there is no separate retry mechanism to inspect the way there is for the other two modes.

cards.prompt: Every execution environment goes through an ___ before it can handle any invocation, during which the runtime starts, your handler's module-level code runs, and any SDK clients you construct outside the handler function are created.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'
cards.answer: init phase

cards.prompt: The ___ runs your handler function itself, once per request, against an execution environment that has already completed init.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'
cards.answer: invoke phase

cards.prompt: Code written at module scope, outside the handler function, runs during which phase?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'

choices.text: Init — once, when the execution environment is created
Invoke — once per request
Only during a cold start, never during a warm one
It runs concurrently with every invocation on that environment

cards.prompt: Because the runtime may route the ___ to the same warm environment, anything expensive to create — a database connection, an HTTP client, a parsed configuration file — is worth building once at module scope and reusing, instead of rebuilding it inside the handler on every call.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'
cards.answer: next invocation

cards.prompt: Reused environment state is a double-edged tool: it saves setup cost, but a warm environment is never ___ on any given invocation, because AWS can, without warning, route a request to a brand-new environment instead of an existing warm one.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'
cards.answer: guaranteed

cards.prompt: What follows from that guarantee not holding?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'
cards.answer: A function must be correct whether or not any prior state survives — never assume a counter, cache entry, or connection set up on a previous call is present, and never rely on side effects from one invocation being visible to another beyond opportunistic reuse.

cards.prompt: Why is it a mistake to open a new database connection inside the handler body on every invocation, rather than at module scope?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'
cards.answer: A connection opened inside the handler is created and torn down on every single call, paying the connection-setup cost every time; a connection opened at module scope is created once per execution environment and then reused across every invocation that lands on that same warm environment, amortizing the cost across many requests.

cards.prompt: A function stores a mutable in-memory cache in a module-level variable to avoid a repeated downstream lookup. Explain both why this works most of the time, and the concrete way it can produce stale or inconsistent results across invocations.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda execution environment'

cards.prompt: Attaching a function to a VPC gives it a network interface inside one or more of that VPC's ___, so it can reach private resources — an RDS instance on a private subnet, an internal load balancer — that aren't reachable from the public internet at all.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Configuring a Lambda function to access resources in a VPC'
cards.answer: subnets

cards.prompt: Why can't a Lambda function reach a database sitting on a private RDS subnet unless the function is attached to that VPC?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Configuring a Lambda function to access resources in a VPC'
cards.answer: A private subnet has no route from the public internet by definition, and a function's default execution environment sits outside the VPC entirely on AWS-managed networking; without an elastic network interface placed inside that VPC's subnet, the function has no network path into it, no matter what credentials or SDK calls it has.

cards.prompt: A VPC-attached function's outbound traffic follows the same rules as any other resource inside that VPC: a private subnet has no direct route to the internet, so a function placed there needs a ___ in a public subnet to reach the public internet or any AWS service endpoint that isn't accessed through a VPC endpoint.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Configuring a Lambda function to access resources in a VPC'
cards.answer: NAT gateway

cards.prompt: A Lambda function is attached to a VPC's private subnets with no NAT gateway configured. What happens when its code tries to call a public API over the internet?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Configuring a Lambda function to access resources in a VPC'

choices.text: The call fails — a private subnet has no route to the internet without a NAT gateway
The call succeeds normally, because Lambda always has internet access regardless of VPC configuration
The call is automatically routed through AWS's managed non-VPC network path instead
The call succeeds, but only for HTTPS traffic

cards.prompt: What must be added to a function's VPC configuration for it to reach a downstream AWS service like DynamoDB or S3 without traversing a NAT gateway at all?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Configuring a Lambda function to access resources in a VPC'
cards.answer: A VPC endpoint for that service — either a gateway or interface endpoint — routes the traffic privately within AWS's network instead of sending it out through a NAT gateway to the public internet, which also avoids NAT gateway data-processing cost and keeps the traffic off the public internet entirely.

cards.prompt: A function that calls a third-party HTTPS API and also needs to query an RDS instance on a private subnet is moved into that VPC. Explain both why the VPC attachment is necessary for the RDS access, and what additional piece of infrastructure it now needs purely to keep the third-party API call working, and why.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Configuring a Lambda function to access resources in a VPC'

cards.prompt: Only attach a function to a VPC when it actually needs to reach a resource that lives inside one; a function that only talks to public AWS service endpoints gains ___ from VPC attachment and only inherits its extra networking surface to maintain.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Configuring a Lambda function to access resources in a VPC'
cards.answer: nothing

cards.prompt: Anything a function writes to standard output or standard error during invocation is captured and shipped to ___, grouped into a log group per function, without the function needing to configure a logging destination itself.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Monitoring and troubleshooting Lambda applications', 'AWS Lambda pricing'
cards.answer: CloudWatch Logs

cards.prompt: Log output alone tells you what happened inside one invocation but not how that invocation's latency was spent across the services it called — that gap is what distributed ___ closes, by instrumenting a request as it crosses service boundaries (API Gateway, the function, a downstream DynamoDB call) and stitching those spans into one timeline.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Monitoring and troubleshooting Lambda applications', 'AWS Lambda pricing'
cards.answer: tracing

cards.prompt: A function's total latency looks high, but its own CloudWatch logs show the handler code finishing quickly. What's the most direct way to find where the remaining time went?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Monitoring and troubleshooting Lambda applications', 'AWS Lambda pricing'

choices.text: Enable tracing to see a timeline of the invocation's spans across every service it called, including time spent outside the function's own code
Increase the function's memory allocation, which always reduces latency regardless of cause
Add more log statements inside the handler
Switch the function from zip packaging to a container image

cards.prompt: Why can CloudWatch Logs alone be insufficient to diagnose latency that isn't the function's own code running slowly?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Monitoring and troubleshooting Lambda applications', 'AWS Lambda pricing'
cards.answer: Logs only capture what the function itself chose to print during its own invocation; time spent in cold start, in the platform's own invocation overhead, or inside a downstream service the function called doesn't show up as a log line, so a trace spanning those boundaries is needed to see where the time actually went.

cards.prompt: Lambda's cost model is built around actual consumption rather than provisioned capacity: what you're billed for is a function of the ___ and the amount of compute time each invocation consumes (duration multiplied by allocated memory), not a fixed hourly rate for a server sitting idle.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Monitoring and troubleshooting Lambda applications', 'AWS Lambda pricing'
cards.answer: number of invocations

cards.prompt: What does it mean, conceptually, that Lambda charges per invocation and per duration-times-memory rather than a flat rate for having the function deployed?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Monitoring and troubleshooting Lambda applications', 'AWS Lambda pricing'
cards.answer: A function that is deployed but never invoked costs nothing to run (aside from any provisioned concurrency kept warm), and a function that runs efficiently — finishing quickly, using less allocated memory — costs less per call than one that runs the same workload slowly or over-provisioned; cost tracks actual usage rather than the mere existence of the function.

cards.prompt: Explain why provisioned concurrency changes Lambda's usual "pay only for what you use" story — what are you now paying for that you wouldn't be paying for with on-demand scaling alone, and why does that tradeoff exist?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Monitoring and troubleshooting Lambda applications', 'AWS Lambda pricing'

cards.prompt: Memory allocation in Lambda's cost model is not purely a cost lever: it also determines the proportional share of ___ a function's execution environment receives.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Monitoring and troubleshooting Lambda applications', 'AWS Lambda pricing'
cards.answer: CPU

cards.prompt: A **container image** deployment package is instead a full ___, built from a base image implementing the Lambda runtime API, giving you control over the entire dependency tree and OS-level libraries rather than just the application code.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda deployment packages', 'Lambda layers', 'Building custom Lambda runtimes'
cards.answer: OCI image

cards.prompt: What is the main practical reason a team would choose a container image over a zip package for a Lambda function?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda deployment packages', 'Lambda layers', 'Building custom Lambda runtimes'

choices.text: They need OS-level dependencies or a dependency tree too complex to fit AWS's managed runtime environment cleanly
Container images start up faster than zip packages in every case
Only container images support environment variables
Zip packages cannot be versioned

cards.prompt: Why might a team with a heavy native-library dependency (e.g. a machine-learning framework with compiled binaries) prefer packaging as a container image?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda deployment packages', 'Lambda layers', 'Building custom Lambda runtimes'
cards.answer: A container image lets them control the exact base OS and every system library the dependency needs, rather than being constrained to whatever a managed runtime's execution environment already provides, which matters when a native dependency needs libraries or versions outside that managed environment.

cards.prompt: Lambda merges a function's configured layers into the execution environment's filesystem alongside its own package, which is what lets several unrelated functions reference the same ___ instead of each bundling its own private copy of it.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda deployment packages', 'Lambda layers', 'Building custom Lambda runtimes'
cards.answer: shared dependency

cards.prompt: What is a limitation of layers that a container image's dependency model doesn't share?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda deployment packages', 'Lambda layers', 'Building custom Lambda runtimes'
cards.answer: A layer is still just a zip archive merged into a managed runtime's filesystem, so it inherits that runtime's constraints (the same base OS, the same set of system libraries) — it can share code across functions but it can't give a function a fundamentally different base OS or system library set the way packaging as a container image can.

cards.prompt: The **Lambda Runtime API** is the HTTP-based interface a runtime uses to fetch the next invocation event and return its response; AWS's managed runtimes implement it for you, but a ___ implements it directly, which is how languages and versions AWS doesn't natively support still get to run on Lambda.
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda deployment packages', 'Lambda layers', 'Building custom Lambda runtimes'
cards.answer: custom runtime

cards.prompt: Explain what "custom runtime" actually means at the mechanism level — it is not a new execution model, but an implementation of something specific. What is that something, and what does the custom runtime's code have to do in a loop to keep the function serving invocations?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda deployment packages', 'Lambda layers', 'Building custom Lambda runtimes'

cards.prompt: Why does packaging as a container image not change anything about the execution environment's init-and-invoke lifecycle?
citations: AWS Lambda Developer Guide — 'Lambda deployment packages', 'Lambda layers', 'Building custom Lambda runtimes'
cards.answer: Container image is only a packaging format for getting code and its dependencies into the execution environment; the environment still goes through the same init and invoke phases, still gets reused across invocations the same way, and still cold-starts the same way — packaging choice affects what's inside the environment, not how the environment itself behaves.

cards.prompt: Reach for **SNS** when one event needs to reach several independent subscribers that each do something different with it, and you control (or at least enumerate) that ___ — the fan-out model. Message filtering narrows what each subscriber receives, but the routing primitive underneath is still "this topic's current subscriptions," decided by who subscribed, not by the event's content.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon EventBridge, 'Choosing between Amazon EventBridge, Amazon SNS, and Amazon SQS'
cards.answer: subscriber list

cards.prompt: A team is building a system where a checkout event should trigger billing, inventory, and analytics, and they expect to add more unrelated consumers over time without touching the checkout service or existing consumers. Which service's routing model most directly matches what they want to add consumers into?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon EventBridge, 'Choosing between Amazon EventBridge, Amazon SNS, and Amazon SQS'

choices.text: EventBridge, because a new consumer is just a new rule matched against the event's existing content, not a change anyone upstream or downstream has to make
SQS, because a shared queue is the simplest way to add more consumers
A single SNS topic with no filter policies, since every subscriber already gets every message
None of these; a static subscriber list can't be extended without code changes in any of the three

cards.prompt: Why would a team put an SQS queue behind each SNS subscription instead of subscribing each consumer's compute (Lambda, HTTP endpoint) directly to the topic?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon EventBridge, 'Choosing between Amazon EventBridge, Amazon SNS, and Amazon SQS'
cards.answer: Because a queue in front of a consumer absorbs load spikes and survives that consumer being temporarily down — the message waits in the queue rather than depending on SNS's own retry policy for a directly-subscribed endpoint, matching the durability point already made about SNS-to-SQS fan-out.

cards.prompt: What single assumption should hold across an SQS consumer, an SNS-via-SQS consumer, and most EventBridge targets, regardless of which of the three routed the message?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon EventBridge, 'Choosing between Amazon EventBridge, Amazon SNS, and Amazon SQS'
cards.answer: The consumer may receive the same logical message more than once and must be written to handle that safely (idempotently), since none of the three provides an unconditional exactly-once delivery guarantee.

cards.prompt: A colleague proposes using EventBridge for everything, arguing it can subsume both SQS and SNS since it can target a queue or invoke many rules. Explain what capability they would be giving up by replacing a plain SQS-backed worker pool with an EventBridge rule targeting that same queue, referring to what visibility timeouts and dead-letter-queue redrive actually depend on.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon EventBridge, 'Choosing between Amazon EventBridge, Amazon SNS, and Amazon SQS'

cards.prompt: Between SNS and EventBridge, which one's routing decision depends on who has subscribed, and which one's depends on what the event itself contains?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon EventBridge, 'Choosing between Amazon EventBridge, Amazon SNS, and Amazon SQS'
cards.answer: SNS's fan-out depends on the current subscription list attached to the topic; EventBridge's rule matching depends on the event's own fields (source, type, nested detail), independent of any fixed subscriber list.

cards.prompt: SQS tracks this with a per-message ___: the number of times a given message has been delivered (received) without being deleted. A redrive policy compares that count against a configured maximum and, once it is exceeded, moves the message to a separate dead-letter queue instead of returning it to the source queue for another attempt.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS dead-letter queues'
cards.answer: receive count

cards.prompt: Redriving messages back from a dead-letter queue to their source queue — after the underlying bug is fixed or the downstream dependency is back — is a distinct, ___ action (`StartMessageMoveTask`), not something the DLQ does automatically. This is deliberate: if a message that was moved to a DLQ because it crashed a consumer got redelivered automatically the moment it arrived, the same crash would just recur, and the DLQ would provide no isolation at all.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS dead-letter queues'
cards.answer: manual

cards.prompt: Why is redriving messages from a dead-letter queue back to the source queue a manual, operator-initiated action rather than automatic?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS dead-letter queues'

choices.text: Automatic redrive would immediately reintroduce whatever caused the failure in the first place, defeating the DLQ's purpose of isolating problem messages until the underlying cause is actually fixed
SQS has no API for moving messages between queues
Dead-letter queues cannot hold more than one message at a time
Redrive would violate the FIFO deduplication window

cards.prompt: What determines whether a message is moved to a dead-letter queue?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS dead-letter queues'
cards.answer: Its receive count — the number of times it has been delivered without being deleted — exceeding the maxReceiveCount configured in the source queue's redrive policy.

cards.prompt: Is a dead-letter queue a retry mechanism?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS dead-letter queues'
cards.answer: No — it is the opposite: a holding area for messages a redrive policy has already given up retrying on the source queue, kept around for inspection rather than automatic reprocessing.

cards.prompt: A team configures a redrive policy with maxReceiveCount set to 1. Explain the operational risk of setting this threshold too low, given that a message can fail its first attempt for reasons that have nothing to do with the message itself (e.g. a transient downstream outage).
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS dead-letter queues'

cards.prompt: Why does an unbounded retry loop on a permanently failing message cost more than just wasted consumer time on a FIFO queue specifically?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS dead-letter queues'
cards.answer: Because FIFO enforces per-group ordering, a poison message stuck at the front of its group blocks every message behind it in that same group from being processed at all, not just the poison message itself.

cards.prompt: An ___ is where events land — a default bus that many AWS services publish to automatically, custom buses an application defines for its own events, and partner buses fed by third-party SaaS integrations.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon EventBridge, 'What is Amazon EventBridge?'
cards.answer: event bus

cards.prompt: A ___ attached to a bus defines an event pattern — a structural match against an event's fields (source, type, nested detail fields) — and a list of targets to invoke for any event that matches it.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon EventBridge, 'What is Amazon EventBridge?'
cards.answer: rule

cards.prompt: An EventBridge rule's event pattern matches on `source: "aws.ec2"` and `detail.state: "terminated"`. An EC2 state-change event arrives with `source: "aws.ec2"` and `detail.state: "running"`. What happens?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon EventBridge, 'What is Amazon EventBridge?'

choices.text: The event does not match this rule (the detail.state field differs), so this rule does not invoke its targets for that event — though the event could still match a different rule
The event matches because the source matches, and detail fields are advisory only
EventBridge raises an error because the event doesn't fully satisfy the pattern
The event is placed in a dead-letter queue automatically

cards.prompt: Why can one EventBridge event end up invoking several completely different targets, in a way plain SNS fan-out cannot replicate without filter policies on every subscription?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon EventBridge, 'What is Amazon EventBridge?'
cards.answer: Because EventBridge evaluates the event's actual structure against each rule's pattern independently, and any number of rules can match the same event — routing is a function of what's inside the event, not of a fixed subscriber list, so adding a new rule that matches existing events doesn't require touching the publisher or any existing subscriber at all.

cards.prompt: SNS fan-out and EventBridge rule-based routing both let a single published message reach multiple different downstream consumers. Explain the difference in intent between the two: what kind of system is SNS fan-out designed for, and what kind of system is EventBridge's pattern-matching model designed for instead?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon EventBridge, 'What is Amazon EventBridge?'

cards.prompt: What two things does an EventBridge rule need to define in order to do anything?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon EventBridge, 'What is Amazon EventBridge?'
cards.answer: An event pattern (the structural match against incoming events) and a list of targets to invoke for any event that matches that pattern.

cards.prompt: Does an event that matches zero rules on an EventBridge bus get delivered anywhere by default?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon EventBridge, 'What is Amazon EventBridge?'
cards.answer: No — with no matching rule, the event is not routed to any target; EventBridge does not have an SNS-style "every subscriber gets a copy" default, since routing there is entirely rule-driven.

cards.prompt: This is why true exactly-once ___ is not achievable for a queue built on an unreliable network.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS FIFO queues'
cards.answer: delivery

cards.prompt: What systems actually offer instead is exactly-once ___: not a promise that a consumer's code only ever runs once per message, but a promise that duplicate deliveries can be detected and neutralized so their *effect* only happens once. FIFO's deduplication window is one version of this, implemented by the queue; consumer-side idempotency is the other version, implemented by the application.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS FIFO queues'
cards.answer: processing

cards.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes "exactly-once delivery" from "exactly-once processing"?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS FIFO queues'

choices.text: Exactly-once delivery would mean a message physically arrives exactly once, which an unreliable network can't guarantee; exactly-once processing means duplicates may still arrive, but their effect is applied only once
They describe the same guarantee; the terms are interchangeable
Exactly-once processing means a consumer is only ever invoked once, full stop
Exactly-once delivery is what FIFO queues provide, and processing-level dedup is unnecessary on them

cards.prompt: The practical way an application achieves exactly-once processing on top of at-least-once (or FIFO) delivery is ___: designing the consumer's write so that applying the same message a second time produces the same end state as applying it once, typically by keying the write on a unique ID carried in the message and either checking that ID before acting or using a natively idempotent operation (e.g. `SET` rather than `INCREMENT`).
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS FIFO queues'
cards.answer: idempotency

cards.prompt: Why is an `INCREMENT balance BY 10` operation dangerous to run from a message consumer that might receive the same message twice, while a `SET balance TO 110` operation is not?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS FIFO queues'
cards.answer: INCREMENT is not idempotent — running it twice applies the change twice (adding 20 instead of 10); SET to an absolute value produces the same end state no matter how many times it's applied, so a duplicate delivery is harmless.

cards.prompt: A consumer processes messages by writing "append this line to a log file" for each one, and receives the same message twice due to a visibility timeout expiry. Explain why this particular operation is naturally NOT idempotent, and describe one concrete change to the consumer's logic that would make it idempotent without changing what the log is used for.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS FIFO queues'

cards.prompt: Besides an idempotent write operation, what information does a consumer typically need in hand to detect that "this message" has already been applied?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS FIFO queues'
cards.answer: A stable, unique identifier for the message or the underlying event (a dedup ID, an idempotency key) that survives redelivery unchanged, plus somewhere durable to record which IDs have already been applied, so a duplicate can be recognized and skipped rather than reapplied.

cards.prompt: Why can a short-poll ReceiveMessage call return zero messages even though the queue is not actually empty?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS short and long polling'

choices.text: Messages are spread across many internal SQS servers, and a short poll only samples a subset of them in one request
Short polling is rate-limited to one call per queue per second
SQS deletes messages that are not received within a few seconds
Short polling only works on FIFO queues

cards.prompt: What does long polling change about how ReceiveMessage checks for messages, compared to short polling?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS short and long polling'
cards.answer: It waits, and checks across more of the queue's internal servers during that wait window, instead of sampling once and returning immediately — trading a longer-held connection for a much lower rate of empty responses.

cards.prompt: Batching lets a single API call carry multiple messages — `SendMessageBatch`, and `ReceiveMessage` requesting up to its batch limit — instead of one call per message. This raises effective throughput mainly by ___ the fixed per-request overhead (network round trip, request processing) across many messages rather than paying it once per message.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS short and long polling'
cards.answer: amortizing

cards.prompt: Batching also changes the shape of failure: a batch call can ___, where some entries in the batch succeed and others fail independently, and the response reports success or failure per entry rather than for the call as a whole.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS short and long polling'
cards.answer: partially succeed

cards.prompt: A `SendMessageBatch` call submits 10 messages. 2 of them fail due to a transient throttling error while the other 8 succeed. What does the API response look like?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS short and long polling'

choices.text: A per-entry result: 8 successful entries with message IDs, and 2 failed entries identifying which ones failed and why
The entire batch is reported as failed, since not all entries succeeded
The entire batch is reported as successful, since most entries succeeded
SQS automatically retries the 2 failed entries before returning a response

cards.prompt: Why must a caller using batched sends or deletes inspect each entry's individual result, rather than just checking whether the overall call returned without an error?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS short and long polling'
cards.answer: Because the call itself succeeding only means SQS accepted and processed the batch request — individual entries within it can still fail independently, and an error-free response at the call level says nothing about whether every message inside it was actually sent, received, or deleted.

cards.prompt: Explain why increasing batch size mostly helps throughput (messages per second) without doing much for the latency of any single message, and under what condition a large batch size could actually start hurting latency.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS short and long polling'

cards.prompt: The alternative — deliver everything and let each subscriber's own code decide what to ___ — looks equivalent from a correctness standpoint but is worse on every other axis: every uninterested subscriber still pays the cost of receiving and deserializing messages it never wanted before throwing them away, and that wasted work scales with total publish volume rather than with how much that particular subscriber actually cares about.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Notification Service, 'Amazon SNS message filtering'
cards.answer: ignore

cards.prompt: A topic publishes 10,000 messages a day, and one Lambda subscriber only needs to act on roughly 50 of them. What does attaching a filter policy to that subscription change, compared to filtering inside the Lambda function's own code?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Notification Service, 'Amazon SNS message filtering'

choices.text: SNS never invokes the Lambda function for the ~9,950 irrelevant messages, instead of invoking it 10,000 times and having it immediately discard most of them
The Lambda function receives all 10,000 messages either way; filter policies only affect SQS subscriptions
Filtering moves from per-message evaluation to a one-time check at subscription creation
The publisher must know about the filter policy and tag each message accordingly at send time

cards.prompt: Why does filtering at the SNS subscription level scale better than filtering identically inside every subscriber's own code?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Notification Service, 'Amazon SNS message filtering'
cards.answer: Because the filtering decision is made once, centrally, at publish time — a message that matches no subscription's filter policy is never delivered anywhere, so the cost of "not caring about this message" for N subscribers doesn't multiply into N separate receive-and-discard operations, and each subscriber's invocation count reflects only the messages it actually needs.

cards.prompt: Does a filter policy change what a publisher sends, or only where a given published message ends up?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Notification Service, 'Amazon SNS message filtering'
cards.answer: Only where it ends up — the publisher still sends one message to the topic exactly as before; the filter policy determines, per subscription, whether that particular subscription receives a copy of it.

cards.prompt: A team considers two designs for a subscriber that only cares about "high priority" events: (a) attach an SNS filter policy matching a `priority: high` message attribute, or (b) subscribe to everything and check `event.priority == "high"` in the handler's first line. Explain a concrete scenario where these two designs behave differently in practice, not just in code cleanliness.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Notification Service, 'Amazon SNS message filtering'

cards.prompt: What must a message carry for an attribute-based SNS filter policy to be able to match against it?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Notification Service, 'Amazon SNS message filtering'
cards.answer: A message attribute (a key set alongside the message body at publish time) whose value the filter policy's condition can be evaluated against — a filter can't match on data that exists only inside an unparsed body unless body filtering is explicitly enabled for that subscription.

cards.prompt: A ___ is the channel a publisher sends messages to; it has no notion of who, if anyone, is listening on the other end.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Notification Service, 'Fanout to Amazon SQS queues'
cards.answer: topic

cards.prompt: A ___ attaches an endpoint — an SQS queue, a Lambda function, an HTTP endpoint, an email address — to that channel, and SNS delivers a copy of every published message to every current one of these independently.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Notification Service, 'Fanout to Amazon SQS queues'
cards.answer: subscription

cards.prompt: A publisher sends one message to an SNS topic with five active subscriptions. How many deliveries does SNS attempt?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Notification Service, 'Fanout to Amazon SQS queues'

choices.text: One delivery attempt to each of the five subscriptions, independently
One delivery total, to whichever subscription is first to respond
The publisher must send five separate messages, one per subscriber
SNS picks one subscription at random per message

cards.prompt: Why is subscribing an SQS queue to an SNS topic (rather than subscribing an HTTP endpoint or Lambda directly) often called the "durable" version of fan-out?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Notification Service, 'Fanout to Amazon SQS queues'
cards.answer: Because a message SNS delivers to a queue sits there until a consumer explicitly processes and deletes it — if that consumer is down when the message arrives, the message waits in the queue rather than being lost; an HTTP endpoint that is unreachable has no such buffer, so SNS's delivery to it can exhaust its retries and the message is effectively gone for that subscriber.

cards.prompt: Explain why fan-out to several SQS queues (one per subscriber) is a better default than fanning out directly to several Lambda functions, in terms of what happens when one downstream consumer is slow or temporarily broken while the others are healthy.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Notification Service, 'Fanout to Amazon SQS queues'

cards.prompt: What must be true for the same message published once to an SNS topic to reach five different downstream systems?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Notification Service, 'Fanout to Amazon SQS queues'
cards.answer: Each of the five systems must have its own subscription attached to that topic — SNS delivers independently to each subscription, so one message becomes as many independent deliveries as there are current subscriptions.

cards.prompt: Can a publisher sending a message to an SNS topic tell how many subscribers will receive it, or who they are?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Notification Service, 'Fanout to Amazon SQS queues'
cards.answer: No — the topic is the only thing the publisher addresses; subscriptions are managed independently of publishing, so the publisher has no visibility into or dependency on who is currently subscribed.

cards.prompt: A message is not removed from the queue just because a consumer read it. ___ hands a copy of a message to a consumer and starts its visibility timeout, but the message still physically remains in the queue.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'How Amazon SQS works'
cards.answer: ReceiveMessage

cards.prompt: A consumer calls ReceiveMessage, then crashes before processing the message or calling DeleteMessage. What happens to the message?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'How Amazon SQS works'

choices.text: It stays in the queue and becomes visible again once its visibility timeout expires, so another consumer can receive it
It is permanently lost, since ReceiveMessage already removed it from the queue
SQS automatically retries delivery to the same consumer only
The message is moved to a dead-letter queue immediately

cards.prompt: Why does SQS split retrieval into a separate receive step and delete step, instead of having one call that reads and removes a message atomically?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'How Amazon SQS works'
cards.answer: So that a consumer's failure between receiving and finishing its work leaves the message recoverable — if delete were implicit in receive, a crash right after receiving would delete a message that was never actually processed, silently losing it. Splitting the steps trades that risk for the opposite one: an unacknowledged message gets redelivered.

cards.prompt: This split is also why SQS's default delivery contract is ___ rather than exactly-once: a message can be delivered to a consumer more than once, either because delete never arrived in time or because SQS's own distributed, redundant storage occasionally delivers a duplicate copy even when the consumer behaved correctly.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'How Amazon SQS works'
cards.answer: at-least-once

cards.prompt: A queue with at-least-once delivery and a queue with at-most-once delivery each fail differently when something goes wrong. Explain what kind of application-level bug each one risks producing if the consumer is written as if the queue guaranteed the OTHER semantics.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'How Amazon SQS works'

cards.prompt: Does receiving a message from an SQS queue remove it from the queue?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'How Amazon SQS works'
cards.answer: No — receiving only starts a visibility timeout that hides the message from other consumers; the message is only removed once the consumer explicitly calls DeleteMessage with the receipt handle from that receive.

cards.prompt: What does a producer's SendMessage call wait for before returning?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'How Amazon SQS works'
cards.answer: Only confirmation that SQS has durably stored the message — it does not wait for any consumer to read or process it, which is what lets producer and consumer scale and fail independently of each other.

cards.prompt: A **FIFO queue** preserves order, but only within a ___ — a set of related messages sharing one `MessageGroupId`. Order is guaranteed within a group, but messages belonging to different groups can still be delivered interleaved with each other, so a FIFO queue's ordering guarantee is per-group, not queue-wide.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'FIFO queues'
cards.answer: message group

cards.prompt: A FIFO queue receives messages from two different `MessageGroupId` values, A and B, interleaved. What ordering guarantee actually applies?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'FIFO queues'

choices.text: Messages within group A arrive in send order, and messages within group B arrive in send order, but A's and B's messages can be interleaved with each other
All messages across both groups arrive in one strict global send order
No ordering guarantee applies once more than one message group is in use
FIFO queues only support a single message group per queue

cards.prompt: FIFO's deduplication uses a ___: SQS treats two sends with the same deduplication ID (explicit, or a content hash) as the same message if the second arrives within that window, and silently discards the duplicate rather than enqueuing it a second time. Outside that window, an identical resend is treated as a brand-new message.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'FIFO queues'
cards.answer: deduplication window

cards.prompt: This is the precise thing to be careful about calling "exactly-once." FIFO's documentation describes ___, not exactly-once delivery: it eliminates duplicates that originate from the producer resending within the dedup window, and a message a consumer receives is not made visible to any other consumer while its visibility timeout is active. It does not mean a consumer can never receive the same message more than once for any reason — a consumer that receives a message, is slow, and lets the visibility timeout lapse before deleting it will still see that message again, exactly as in a Standard queue.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'FIFO queues'
cards.answer: exactly-once processing

cards.prompt: What does FIFO's "exactly-once processing" guarantee actually cover?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'FIFO queues'

choices.text: It suppresses duplicate enqueues from resends within the deduplication window; it does not prevent a consumer from ever receiving the same message twice if its own visibility timeout lapses
A message can never be delivered to a consumer more than once, under any circumstance
The consumer is exempt from needing to call DeleteMessage
Deduplication only suppresses a duplicate within the same message group; a duplicate sent under a different MessageGroupId is delivered as a new message

cards.prompt: Why would an application deliberately give every message the same `MessageGroupId`, even though that serializes all processing to effectively one consumer at a time?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'FIFO queues'
cards.answer: Because ordering is only guaranteed within a group — if the application's correctness depends on strict global order across all its messages, a single group is the only way to get that, accepting the throughput cost as the price of the guarantee.

cards.prompt: What is the practical throughput consequence of FIFO's per-group ordering guarantee, compared to a Standard queue?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'FIFO queues'
cards.answer: Because SQS must deliver each group's messages in order, it can only have one message from a given group in flight (unprocessed) at a time, so fanning work out across many consumers requires many distinct message groups; a Standard queue has no such constraint and can hand out messages to as many consumers as are polling.

cards.prompt: A team picks a FIFO queue "to be safe" for a workload that has no actual ordering or duplicate-sensitivity requirement. Explain what they are giving up, and why Standard would have been the better default absent a specific need for FIFO's guarantees.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'FIFO queues'

cards.prompt: If the timeout is set ___ than the actual processing time, SQS gives up on the first consumer too early: a second consumer receives and starts processing the same message while the first one is still working on it, so the same message is now being handled twice concurrently.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS visibility timeout'
cards.answer: shorter

cards.prompt: A message takes 90 seconds to process, but the queue's visibility timeout is 30 seconds. What is the most direct consequence?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS visibility timeout'

choices.text: A second (and possibly third) consumer receives and processes the same message while the first consumer is still working on it
The message is silently dropped after 30 seconds
SQS automatically extends the timeout to match the actual processing time
The producer is notified that the message needs a longer timeout

cards.prompt: If the timeout is set ___ than necessary, the opposite failure shows up: when a consumer actually crashes partway through, no other consumer can pick the message back up until that whole long window elapses, so a real failure recovers slowly even though the queue holds a perfectly deliverable message the entire time.
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS visibility timeout'
cards.answer: longer

cards.prompt: A consumer crashes immediately after receiving a message, and the queue's visibility timeout is set very long. What is the cost?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS visibility timeout'

choices.text: The message sits invisible and undelivered until the long timeout expires, even though no consumer is actually working on it
The message is processed twice by two different consumers
The message is deleted without being processed
SQS reduces the timeout automatically once it detects the crash

cards.prompt: Why can't a single fixed visibility timeout be "safe" for both a workload with wildly variable processing times and a workload that wants fast failure recovery?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS visibility timeout'
cards.answer: Because the two failure modes pull in opposite directions on the same knob — a timeout short enough to recover quickly from a crash risks being shorter than a slow item's real processing time and causing duplicate work, while a timeout long enough to never cut off a slow item makes every genuine crash recover slowly; the fix is not a better fixed value but extending the timeout dynamically (`ChangeMessageVisibility`) while a specific message is still legitimately being worked on.

cards.prompt: Explain, in terms of what SQS can and cannot observe about a consumer, why visibility timeout has to be a guess (a timer) rather than something SQS can determine directly, such as "is this consumer still alive and still working on this message."
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS visibility timeout'

cards.prompt: What SQS call lets a consumer extend its own visibility timeout mid-processing, for a message whose work is taking longer than expected?
citations: AWS Developer Guide — Amazon Simple Queue Service, 'Amazon SQS visibility timeout'
cards.answer: ChangeMessageVisibility.
