cards.prompt: The coupon collector problem asks the opposite kind of question: given m distinct bins, how many balls must you throw, on average, before *every* bin has been hit at least once? Each new ball is likely to land in an already-hit bin once most bins are full, so the last few empty bins are disproportionately expensive to fill — the expected number of throws needed grows as m times the harmonic sum, which works out to ___, not m.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 4
Mitzenmacher & Upfal, Probability and Computing, Ch. 5
cards.answer: m ln(m)

cards.prompt: Why does filling the last few empty bins dominate the cost in the coupon collector problem, rather than the cost being spread evenly across all m bins?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 4
Mitzenmacher & Upfal, Probability and Computing, Ch. 5
cards.answer: Once k bins have already been hit, a new ball only has probability (m - k)/m of landing in one of the remaining empty bins, so the expected wait for the next new bin is m/(m - k); as k approaches m that wait blows up, meaning the final few empty bins each take, in expectation, a number of throws proportional to m, while the very first bin costs only 1 throw.

cards.prompt: What is the expected number of balls needed to fill all m bins at least once, and how does it compare in growth rate to filling only half of them?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 4
Mitzenmacher & Upfal, Probability and Computing, Ch. 5
cards.answer: The expectation is m times the mth harmonic number, which is roughly m*ln(m); filling only half the bins takes only about m*ln(2) throws by the same harmonic-sum argument restricted to the still-empty half, so the second half of the bins — going from half-full to completely full — costs far more than the first half did, even though both halves have the same number of bins.

cards.prompt: Throwing n balls independently and uniformly into n bins, the maximum load of any single bin is, with high probability, of what order?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 4
Mitzenmacher & Upfal, Probability and Computing, Ch. 5

choices.text: Theta(log n / log log n)
Theta(1) — the same order as the average load
Theta(log n)
Theta(sqrt(n))

cards.prompt: Explain, in one or two sentences, why the maximum load of Theta(log n / log log n) balls in the fullest of n bins is much larger than the average load of 1 ball per bin, without invoking any specific proof technique.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 4
Mitzenmacher & Upfal, Probability and Computing, Ch. 5
cards.answer: The average load only says what happens when the n balls are spread perfectly evenly, but the throws are independent and random rather than coordinated, so by chance some bins receive a run of several balls in a row while others receive none; the maximum-load result quantifies how large that lucky-bin effect gets, and it grows (slowly, like log n / log log n) rather than staying bounded, precisely because with n independent trials there are n chances for some bin to get an unusually long run of hits.

cards.prompt: In inference problems, A is usually a hypothesis and B is observed evidence, and the three pieces of the formula get names: P(A) is the ___ — what you believed about the hypothesis before seeing the evidence — P(B|A) is the likelihood — how probable the evidence is under that hypothesis — and P(A|B) is the posterior, your belief after updating on the evidence. P(B), the overall probability of the evidence regardless of hypothesis, acts as a normalizing constant and is often expanded with the law of total probability, conditioning on whether A holds or not:
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 2
cards.answer: prior

cards.prompt: Why does the denominator P(B) in Bayes' theorem need to be expanded using the law of total probability rather than measured directly, in a typical inference problem?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 2
cards.answer: Because the evidence's overall probability P(B) depends on how likely it is under every hypothesis, weighted by how likely each hypothesis is, and that is exactly what the law of total probability computes; conditioning on whether the hypothesis A holds or not (or on a full partition of hypotheses) turns an otherwise unknown quantity into one built from pieces the problem already supplies — the likelihood and the prior.

cards.prompt: Write Bayes' theorem, and name which of its four quantities is the prior, which is the likelihood, and which is the posterior.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 2
cards.answer: P(A|B) = P(B|A) P(A) / P(B). P(A) is the prior (belief in the hypothesis before seeing evidence), P(B|A) is the likelihood (how probable the evidence is if the hypothesis is true), P(A|B) is the posterior (updated belief after seeing the evidence), and P(B) is the normalizing constant — the overall probability of the evidence across every hypothesis.

cards.prompt: The most common real-world Bayes mistake is the ___ fallacy: judging P(hypothesis|evidence) by the likelihood P(evidence|hypothesis) alone, while ignoring how rare the hypothesis was to begin with. A highly specific piece of evidence can still leave the posterior low if the prior was low enough — the likelihood being large does not override a prior being small, since the posterior is a *product* of both.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 2
cards.answer: base rate

cards.prompt: Why can a "99% accurate" test still leave most positive results false, when the disease is rare?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 2
cards.answer: Because the healthy population vastly outnumbers the sick population, so a small false-positive rate applied to that much larger group produces more false positives in raw count than the true positives coming from the small sick group, even though each individual accuracy number looks high.

cards.prompt: A test with the same 99%/99% accuracy is run for a disease with prevalence 1 in 10 instead of 1 in 1,000. What happens to the posterior P(disease|positive), and why?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 2

choices.text: It rises substantially, because a much higher prior means the sick group is no longer swamped by false positives from the much larger healthy group
It stays at roughly 9%, since the test's accuracy numbers haven't changed
It falls, since a more common disease is intuitively harder to diagnose
It becomes exactly 99%, matching the test's stated accuracy

cards.prompt: A friend says "the test is 99% accurate, so a positive result means I'm 99% likely to have the disease." Using the base-rate idea from this note, explain what's wrong with that reasoning without recomputing the exact number.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 2
cards.answer: They are treating the likelihood P(positive|disease) as if it were the posterior P(disease|positive), skipping the prior entirely. The disease's rarity (a low prior) matters just as much as the test's accuracy: Bayes' theorem multiplies the likelihood by the prior and renormalizes, so a low enough prior can pull the posterior far below the likelihood's own value, however accurate the test looks in isolation.

cards.prompt: The weakest and most universally applicable is Markov's inequality. It needs only two facts: that X is ___, and that you know (or can bound) E[X]. Given just that, it says the probability X exceeds any threshold a is capped by the ratio of the mean to the threshold.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 6, 10
cards.answer: nonnegative

cards.prompt: Which two facts does Markov's inequality require about a random variable X before it can be applied?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 6, 10
cards.answer: That X takes only nonnegative values, and that you know (or have an upper bound on) E[X]; given those two facts alone, no distributional shape or independence assumption is needed.

cards.prompt: Chebyshev's inequality tightens this by spending a second piece of information: a finite ___. Applying Markov to the nonnegative random variable (X - E[X])^2 with threshold a^2 gives a bound on how far X deviates from its own mean in *either* direction, not just above a fixed threshold — Chebyshev is inherently a two-sided, symmetric-deviation statement.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 6, 10
cards.answer: variance

cards.prompt: How is Chebyshev's inequality derived from Markov's inequality?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 6, 10
cards.answer: By applying Markov's inequality to the nonnegative random variable (X - E[X])^2 with threshold a^2, since P(|X - E[X]| >= a) equals P((X - E[X])^2 >= a^2); the mean of that squared quantity is by definition Var(X), so Markov's E[Y]/a form becomes Var(X)/a^2.

cards.prompt: That is what Chernoff bounds (and the closely related Hoeffding bound for bounded variables) deliver, at a steeper price: they require the variable of interest to be a sum of ___ random variables, and typically that each summand is bounded (or, for the classic Chernoff form, that each is an indicator or otherwise has a controllable moment generating function). Given those, the probability of deviating from the sum's mean by even a small fraction of its size falls off exponentially in the number of terms, not polynomially.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 6, 10
cards.answer: independent

cards.prompt: You are told only that a random variable X is nonnegative and you know E[X] — nothing about its variance or independence structure. Which bound can you legally apply?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 6, 10

choices.text: Markov's inequality
Chebyshev's inequality
A Chernoff bound
None of these apply without more assumptions

cards.prompt: You have a sum of n independent, bounded random variables and want a bound that decays exponentially in n rather than polynomially in the deviation. Which tool fits?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 6, 10

choices.text: A Chernoff or Hoeffding bound
Markov's inequality alone
Chebyshev's inequality alone
The union bound alone

cards.prompt: The fourth tool, the ___, is not a concentration inequality at all — it makes no use of means, variances, or independence. It simply says the probability that *any* of several events occurs is at most the sum of their individual probabilities, and it holds unconditionally, even when the events are heavily dependent or negatively correlated.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 6, 10
cards.answer: union bound

cards.prompt: Why does the union bound require no assumption about independence between the events A_1, ..., A_n, unlike a Chernoff bound?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 6, 10
cards.answer: Because it is proved purely from the axiom that probability is countably subadditive over a union of sets, which holds for any events regardless of how they are correlated; a Chernoff bound instead needs independence to control the joint moment generating function of a sum, so it fails outright if that assumption is dropped.

cards.prompt: Rank Markov, Chebyshev, and a Chernoff/Hoeffding bound from loosest to sharpest for bounding the tail of a sum of independent bounded variables, and explain what extra piece of information each step up the ranking requires you to already know about the variable.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 6, 10
cards.answer: Markov is loosest (needs only nonnegativity and a mean); Chebyshev is tighter for large deviations because it additionally uses the variance; Chernoff/Hoeffding is tightest for sums because it additionally uses independence and boundedness of the summands, converting polynomial decay into exponential decay in the number of terms.

cards.prompt: A rare disease test is 99% accurate. A patient tests positive. Which quantity does "99% accurate" most directly describe, and which quantity does the patient actually want to know?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 2

choices.text: It describes something like P(positive|disease) or P(negative|no disease); the patient wants P(disease|positive)
It describes P(disease|positive) directly, which is also what the patient wants
It describes P(disease), the overall prevalence, which is what the patient wants
The two quantities are interchangeable here since the test is highly accurate

cards.prompt: This is the ___, and it is the standard move whenever an event's overall probability is hard to see directly but becomes easy once you condition on which "case" occurred.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 2
cards.answer: law of total probability

cards.prompt: What does the law of total probability let you compute, and what must be true of the Bi for it to apply?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 2
cards.answer: It lets you compute the overall probability P(A) by weighting each conditional probability P(A|Bi) by how likely that case is, P(Bi), and summing over all cases; the Bi must partition the sample space — pairwise disjoint and collectively exhaustive — so every outcome falls into exactly one Bi.

cards.prompt: Independence is a separate idea from conditioning, and it is easy to blur the two. Events A and B are ___ when P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B) — equivalently, when P(A|B) = P(A): learning B occurred doesn't move A's probability at all. Mutual exclusivity is nearly the opposite: if A and B are mutually exclusive with both having positive probability, then learning B occurred tells you A definitely did not — maximally informative, not uninformative. Confusing "the events can't both happen" with "the events don't affect each other" is one of the most common early mistakes in probability.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 2
cards.answer: independent

cards.prompt: Which best describes the relationship between "independent" and "mutually exclusive," for two events A and B that each have positive probability?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 2

choices.text: They are close to opposites: independence means learning about one tells you nothing about the other, while mutual exclusivity means learning one occurred tells you the other definitely did not
They are the same property described in two different ways
Independent events are always mutually exclusive
Mutually exclusive events are always independent

cards.prompt: Explain, using the restricted-sample-space view of conditioning, why two events being independent in the full sample space gives no guarantee that they stay independent once you condition on some event C.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 2
cards.answer: Conditioning on C means the "universe" being reasoned about shrinks from the whole sample space down to just the outcomes in C, and the relative sizes (probabilities) of A and B's overlap can look completely different inside that smaller universe than they did in the full one. Independence in the full space is a statement about proportions in S; restricting to C can distort those proportions arbitrarily, so nothing about the unconditional relationship constrains the conditional one.

cards.prompt: A quantity is equally likely to fall anywhere in an interval [a, b], with no sub-region favored — which family, and what are E[X] and Var(X)?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 5, 7
cards.answer: Uniform(a, b); E[X] = (a+b)/2, Var(X) = (b-a)^2 / 12.

cards.prompt: The waiting time until the next event of a process running at constant rate lambda — which family, and what are E[X] and Var(X)?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 5, 7
cards.answer: Exponential(lambda); E[X] = 1/lambda, Var(X) = 1/lambda^2.

cards.prompt: Exponential has a defining, unusual property: however long you have already waited, the remaining wait looks exactly like a fresh draw from the same distribution — past waiting time carries no information about what's left. This is the ___ property, and among continuous distributions on [0, infinity), exponential is the *only* one that has it.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 5, 7
cards.answer: memoryless

cards.prompt: A lightbulb's remaining lifetime, given it has already survived 500 hours, has the exact same distribution as a brand-new bulb's lifetime. Which family must the lifetime follow?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 5, 7

choices.text: Exponential — the only continuous family on [0, infinity) with this no-aging property
Normal — normal lifetimes would imply the bulb gets predictably more or less likely to fail as it ages
Uniform — a uniform lifetime is bounded above, so remaining life shrinks deterministically as time passes
Gamma with shape > 1 — gamma lifetimes model wear that accumulates, the opposite of memorylessness

cards.prompt: A server receives requests as a Poisson process at rate lambda per second. What distribution describes the time gap between one request and the next, and why does that follow from the Poisson-process assumption rather than needing a separate derivation?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 5, 7
cards.answer: Exponential(lambda). The Poisson process assumption already says arrivals in disjoint time windows are independent and occur at a constant rate, and "no arrival yet in the next t seconds" is exactly the memoryless waiting-time question — so the inter-arrival gap inherits the exponential distribution directly from how the process was defined, rather than as a new fact needing its own proof.

cards.prompt: Every Normal(mu, sigma^2) can be rescaled into the single reference copy of the family, N(0, 1), by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation: Z = (X - mu) / sigma. This ___ is why one table of Z-values covers every normal distribution at once, regardless of its own particular mu and sigma.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 5, 7
cards.answer: standardization

cards.prompt: Given X ~ Normal(mu, sigma^2), what transformation produces a standard normal Z, and why is that transformation useful in practice?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 5, 7
cards.answer: Z = (X - mu) / sigma; it recenters X to mean 0 and rescales it to variance 1, so a single N(0, 1) table (or software routine) can answer probability questions for any normal distribution instead of needing one table per (mu, sigma) pair.

cards.prompt: A single yes/no trial with success probability p, where you care about the 0/1 outcome itself — which family, and what are E[X] and Var(X)?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 3-4
cards.answer: Bernoulli(p); E[X] = p, Var(X) = p(1 - p).

cards.prompt: You repeat that trial n independent times and count the total successes — which family, and what are E[X] and Var(X)?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 3-4
cards.answer: Binomial(n, p); E[X] = np, Var(X) = np(1 - p). It is literally a sum of n iid Bernoulli(p) trials, which is also the fastest way to derive its mean by linearity.

cards.prompt: You flip a p-coin until the first success and count the failures that preceded it — which family, and what are E[X] and Var(X)?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 3-4
cards.answer: Geometric(p); E[X] = (1-p)/p, Var(X) = (1-p)/p^2.

cards.prompt: Generalize by waiting for the rth success instead of the first, still counting failures along the way — which family, and what are E[X] and Var(X)?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 3-4
cards.answer: Negative Binomial(r, p); E[X] = r(1-p)/p, Var(X) = r(1-p)/p^2.

cards.prompt: A goalkeeper faces penalty kicks and saves each independently with probability p. Which family models the number of goals scored before her 4th save?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 3-4

choices.text: Negative binomial with r = 4 — counting failures (goals) before the 4th success (save)
Binomial(4, p) — that would fix the number of kicks, not the number of saves
Geometric(p) — that only counts failures before the *first* save
Poisson(4p) — there is no continuous rate here, just discrete trials

cards.prompt: You count events occurring at a constant average rate over a fixed interval, with no natural trial count — which family, and what are E[X] and Var(X)?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 3-4
cards.answer: Poisson(lambda); E[X] = lambda, Var(X) = lambda — the only common family whose mean and variance coincide.

cards.prompt: This same family also arises as a *limit* of the trial-based one above: hold the product n*p fixed at lambda while n grows large and p shrinks toward zero, and the binomial PMF converges term by term to the Poisson PMF. This is the ___, and it is the standard justification for using Poisson to model counts like typos or accident claims, where many opportunities exist but each is individually unlikely.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 3-4
cards.answer: law of rare events

cards.prompt: State the regime under which Binomial(n, p) is well approximated by Poisson(lambda).
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 3-4
cards.answer: n large, p small, with the product n*p held roughly fixed at lambda — many trials, each individually rare.

cards.prompt: A website gets 10,000 visitors a day, each independently completing a purchase with probability 0.0003. Which distribution is the standard approximation for the day's total purchases, and why?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 3-4

choices.text: Poisson(3) — n is large and p is tiny with n*p = 3 held moderate, the classic rare-events regime
Normal(3, 3) — a normal approximation is a separate large-sample tool, not this family's namesake limit
Geometric(0.0003) — that models waiting for one success, not counting successes in a day
Binomial(10000, 0.0003) exactly — correct in principle but exactly the thing the approximation exists to avoid computing

cards.prompt: You draw n objects without replacement from a finite population of w desired and b undesired items, and count the desired ones — which family, and how does it differ mechanically from binomial?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 3-4
cards.answer: Hypergeometric(w, b, n); it counts successes in n draws like binomial does, but the draws are dependent since sampling is without replacement, so each draw's odds shift based on what was already removed from the population.

cards.prompt: State the mean of Hypergeometric(w, b, n), and compare it to Binomial(n, p) with p = w/(w+b).
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 3-4
cards.answer: E[X] = n * w/(w+b) — identical in form to the binomial mean np with p = w/(w+b). The variance carries an extra finite-population correction factor (w+b-n)/(w+b-1), which shrinks toward 0 as n approaches the full population and equals 1 in the with-replacement limit, recovering the binomial variance exactly.

cards.prompt: A fair six-sided die is rolled. Which computation gives E[X] for the result X?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 4-5

choices.text: The most likely single outcome, since all six are equally likely
max(support(X)) - min(support(X)), divided by 2

cards.prompt: A fair six-sided die has E[X] = 3.5, a value the die can never actually land on. What does this reveal about E[X] in general, for any random variable?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 4-5
cards.answer: E[X] is a probability-weighted average over the support, not a prediction of a single trial's outcome, so there is no requirement that E[X] itself be one of the values the random variable can take. An expectation can fall anywhere between the extremes of the support, including at points the random variable never visits.

cards.prompt: Explain what LOTUS lets you skip when you want E[X^2] for a random variable X whose PMF you already know.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 4-5
cards.answer: Without LOTUS you would need to derive the PMF of the new random variable Y = X^2 — figuring out, for each possible value y, which x's square to it and summing their probabilities — and only then apply the definition of expectation to Y. LOTUS says you can instead plug g(x) = x^2 straight into sum_x g(x) f_X(x) using X's own PMF, skipping the intermediate distribution of Y entirely.

cards.prompt: A continuous random variable X has PDF f_X(x) = 2x on the interval [0,1]. Which expression, by LOTUS, computes E[X^2]?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 4-5

choices.text: int_0^1 x^2 * 2x dx
int_0^1 2x dx
sum_{x in [0,1]} x^2 * 2x
(int_0^1 x * 2x dx)^2

cards.prompt: What is E[c] when c is a constant — a "random variable" that always takes the same value with probability 1 — and why does the definition of expectation force that answer?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 4-5
cards.answer: E[c] = c. The definition of expectation is a probability-weighted average over the support, and a constant's support is the single point c with probability 1, so the weighted average collapses to exactly that one value with no averaging left to do.

cards.prompt: X and Y are two random variables with a complicated joint dependence — knowing X tells you a great deal about Y. What additional assumption is needed to conclude E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y]?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 4-5

choices.text: None — the identity holds regardless of any dependence between X and Y
X and Y must be independent
X and Y must have the same distribution
Cov(X, Y) must be computed and shown to be zero first

cards.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts the LOTUS approach to computing E[g(X)] with the naive approach?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 4-5

choices.text: LOTUS weights g(x) by X's own PMF or PDF directly; the naive approach first derives the distribution of Y = g(X) and then averages that
LOTUS first derives the distribution of Y = g(X); the naive approach skips straight to weighting g(x) by X's distribution
LOTUS only applies when g is linear; the naive approach is needed for any nonlinear g
The two approaches only differ for discrete random variables

cards.prompt: What is the marginal PMF f_X(x), computed from a joint PMF f_{X,Y}?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 3, 7, 9
cards.answer: Sum f_{X,Y}(x,y) over every value y in Y's support while holding x fixed — this "sums out" Y, leaving a function of x alone that is exactly X's own PMF.

cards.prompt: Given only the marginal distribution of X and the marginal distribution of Y, can you reconstruct the joint distribution f_{X,Y}(x,y)?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 3, 7, 9

choices.text: Not in general — the marginals discard all information about how X and Y relate to each other
Yes, always, by multiplying f_X(x) by f_Y(y)
Yes, but only by adding f_X(x) and f_Y(y)
Yes, but only for continuous random variables

cards.prompt: Random variables X and Y are ___ if knowing the value of one tells you nothing about the distribution of the other — formally, if their joint PMF (or PDF) factors as the product of the marginals for every x and y:
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 3, 7, 9
cards.answer: independent

cards.prompt: A joint PMF is given by f_{X,Y}(x,y) = c * x * y^2 over some range of x and y. Based on the factoring condition, are X and Y independent?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 3, 7, 9

choices.text: Yes — the formula factors into a function of x alone (x) times a function of y alone (y^2)
No — since both x and y appear in the same formula, they must be dependent
It cannot be determined without first computing the marginals
Only if the constant c happens to equal 1

cards.prompt: Two random variables X and Y are independent. What does that imply about the conditional distribution f_{X|Y}(x|y), and why does that match the informal idea of "independent"?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 3, 7, 9
cards.answer: f_{X|Y}(x|y) = f_X(x) for every y — conditioning on Y's value does not change X's distribution at all, because independence means f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_X(x) f_Y(y), and dividing that by f_Y(y) leaves just f_X(x). This matches the informal idea directly: learning what Y did gives you no new information about X.

cards.prompt: E[X|Y] is best described as which of the following?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 3, 7, 9

choices.text: A random variable — a function of Y, since its value depends on which outcome Y takes
A single fixed number, computed once from the joint distribution
Another name for E[X], unaffected by Y
The correlation between X and Y

cards.prompt: Suppose E[X|Y=1] = 3.5, E[X|Y=2] = 2, and P(Y=1) = P(Y=2) = 0.5. What does the law of total expectation give for E[X]?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 3, 7, 9
cards.answer: E[X] = E[E[X|Y]] = 3.5*0.5 + 2*0.5 = 2.75 — average the conditional expectations, each weighted by how likely its condition is.

cards.prompt: What is the key logical difference between the weak and the strong law of large numbers?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 10
cards.answer: The weak law only says that at each fixed large n, the probability the sample mean deviates from the true mean by more than any fixed tolerance shrinks to zero; the strong law says the entire sequence of sample means converges to the true mean with probability 1, a statement about the whole infinite trajectory, not just about each n considered separately.

cards.prompt: The quantity sigma / sqrt(n) — the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean itself, not of a single observation — is called the ___. It shrinks as sqrt(n) grows, which is why averaging more data narrows a confidence interval, but only at the square-root rate: quadrupling n only halves it.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 10
cards.answer: standard error

cards.prompt: The "sampling distribution of the sample mean" refers to which of these?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 10

choices.text: The distribution of Xbar_n itself, viewed as a random variable that varies from one sample of size n to the next
The distribution of a single observation X_i drawn from the population
The empirical histogram of one particular observed sample's values
The population's true underlying distribution

cards.prompt: Why does the standard error shrink at rate sqrt(n) rather than at rate n?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 10
cards.answer: Because Var(Xbar_n) = Var(X)/n, so the standard deviation of the sample mean is sigma/sqrt(n); halving the standard error therefore requires quadrupling the sample size, not just doubling it.

cards.prompt: Which of these is a correct statement of what the central limit theorem claims?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 10

choices.text: The distribution of the (rescaled) sample mean approaches a normal distribution as n grows, regardless of the shape of the original population distribution
Individual observations from a non-normal population become approximately normal once enough of them have been collected
Any distribution converges to the normal distribution as its parameters grow
The sample mean converges to a normal distribution only if the population distribution is already close to normal

cards.prompt: A colleague says "n = 30 is always enough for the CLT to kick in." Explain what is missing from that claim, using the idea of heavy tails.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 10
cards.answer: The CLT guarantees normality only in the limit as n goes to infinity and says nothing about the rate of convergence for any finite n; how large n needs to be depends on the shape of the underlying distribution. A distribution with heavy tails (large or infinite variance) can need a far larger sample size before the sample mean's distribution looks approximately normal, and if the variance is infinite the classical theorem does not apply at all — so a fixed rule like "n = 30" is not a universal guarantee, only a common rule of thumb for reasonably light-tailed populations.

cards.prompt: A function P from events to numbers is a legitimate probability only if it obeys three axioms: P(S) = 1 (something in the sample space happens), P(A) ≥ 0 for every event, and for any countable collection of ___ events, the probability of their union is the sum of their individual probabilities. Two events are called mutually exclusive precisely when they cannot both occur — their intersection is empty — which is the set-theoretic reading of "disjoint."
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 1
cards.answer: pairwise disjoint

cards.prompt: Which pair of events are mutually exclusive, given a single roll of a six-sided die?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 1

choices.text: "the roll is 2" and "the roll is 5"
"the roll is even" and "the roll is at least 4"
"the roll is prime" and "the roll is odd"
"the roll is at most 3" and "the roll is odd"

cards.prompt: When two events can overlap, adding their probabilities double-counts the overlap, so P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B). Extending this pattern to three or more events — add the singles, subtract the pairwise overlaps, add back the triple overlap, and so on with alternating sign — is the ___ formula.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 1
cards.answer: inclusion-exclusion

cards.prompt: Why is subtracting pairwise intersections not already the final answer once you go past two events?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 1
cards.answer: Subtracting every pairwise overlap removes the triple overlaps three times (once per pair that contains them) after having added them in three times (once per single event), so a region covered by three events ends up net-zero and has to be added back in; the alternating sum continues so that every region of the union is counted exactly once regardless of how many of the events contain it.

cards.prompt: The two counting tools that come up constantly: a ___ counts arrangements where order matters, and a combination counts selections where it doesn't. The number of ways to arrange all n distinct objects in a row is n!, and the number of ways to arrange k of them in order is n!/(n-k)!. Dropping the order — asking only which k objects are chosen, not in what sequence — divides that by k!, giving the binomial coefficient:
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 1
cards.answer: permutation

cards.prompt: Why does dividing the ordered-selection count by k! convert it into an unordered count?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 1
cards.answer: Every unordered selection of k objects corresponds to exactly k! different ordered selections (the k! ways to arrange those same k objects), so the ordered count treats each unordered outcome as k! duplicates; dividing by k! collapses each group of duplicates back down to the single unordered outcome it represents.

cards.prompt: A committee of 3 is chosen from 10 people, with no distinction between roles (no chair, secretary, etc.). Which expression counts the number of possible committees?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 1

choices.text: 10!/(10-3)! — the ordered-selection count
10^3 — choices made independently with repetition allowed
3! × C(10,3) — committees times an ordering of the members

cards.prompt: A byte is a string of 8 bits, each 0 or 1. Using the sample-space and equally-likely-outcomes framework of this note, explain how to compute the probability that a uniformly random byte has exactly 3 ones, without listing outcomes by hand.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 1
cards.answer: S is the set of all 2^8 bit strings of length 8, all equally likely, so |S| = 2^8. The event "exactly 3 ones" is the set of strings with exactly three 1-positions among the eight slots; choosing which 3 of the 8 positions hold a 1 is a combination, so |A| = C(8,3). The probability is C(8,3) / 2^8 — count the favorable outcomes, count the total, divide.

cards.prompt: The ___ of a random variable is the set of values it can actually take on — everything else has probability zero and can be ignored when describing its distribution.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 2-3
cards.answer: support

cards.prompt: For a continuous random variable X with PDF f_X, what does f_X(x) itself represent?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 2-3

choices.text: A density — it can exceed 1, and only becomes a probability once integrated over an interval
The probability that X equals exactly x
The probability that X is less than or equal to x
The fraction of all possible values of X that are less than x

cards.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a property every CDF F_X must satisfy?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 2-3

choices.text: F_X must be symmetric around its mean
F_X is nondecreasing as x increases
F_X(x) approaches 0 as x approaches negative infinity
F_X(x) approaches 1 as x approaches positive infinity

cards.prompt: For a continuous random variable, the PDF is the ___ of the CDF, and going the other way, the CDF is the PDF's running integral — the two functions determine each other completely.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 2-3
cards.answer: derivative

cards.prompt: A discrete random variable X has support {1, 2, 3} with f_X(1) = 0.2, f_X(2) = 0.5, f_X(3) = 0.3. What is F_X(2), and why is F_X(2) not simply equal to f_X(2)?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 2-3
cards.answer: F_X(2) = P(X <= 2) = f_X(1) + f_X(2) = 0.7. The CDF accumulates all probability at or below the point, while the PMF gives the probability of that one value in isolation; they only coincide at the smallest point in the support, where there is nothing smaller to accumulate.

cards.prompt: Y = g(X) is formed by applying a function g to a random variable X. In what sense is Y itself a genuine random variable, rather than merely a formula written in terms of X?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 2-3
cards.answer: X is already a function from the sample space to the reals, so composing it with g gives Y = g(X) as another function from that same sample space to the reals: for every outcome, first apply X to get a number, then apply g to that number. That composition is exactly what a random variable is, so Y inherits well-defined randomness from the same underlying experiment without needing a new probability model.

cards.prompt: A random variable's set of possible values is countably infinite, with gaps between consecutive values (like the nonnegative integers). Which kind of random variable must it be?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 2-3

choices.text: Discrete
Continuous
Neither discrete nor continuous
It could be either, depending only on its PDF

cards.prompt: If Y = 3X - 7, how does Var(Y) relate to Var(X)?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 4, 6

choices.text: Var(Y) = 9 * Var(X) — the shift by -7 does not matter, and the scale factor is squared
Var(Y) = 3 * Var(X) - 7
Var(Y) = 3 * Var(X)
Var(Y) = Var(X) - 7

cards.prompt: What is Cov(X,X), and how does it relate to Var(X)?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 4, 6
cards.answer: Cov(X,X) = E[(X - E[X])(X - E[X])] = E[(X - E[X])^2] = Var(X) — covariance of a random variable with itself is exactly its own variance, since the two factors in the definition become identical.

cards.prompt: Under what condition on X and Y does Var(X + Y) reduce to just Var(X) + Var(Y), with no extra term, and why does that condition make the cross term disappear?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 4, 6
cards.answer: When X and Y are independent (or, more precisely, whenever Cov(X,Y) = 0). Independence forces E[XY] = E[X]E[Y], which makes Cov(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y] equal to zero, so the 2*Cov(X,Y) term in Var(X+Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2*Cov(X,Y) vanishes and the sum's variance is just the sum of the individual variances.

cards.prompt: Two random variables X and Y are independent. Which of the following is guaranteed to hold?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 4, 6

choices.text: Both E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y] and Var(X+Y) = Var(X)+Var(Y)
Only Var(X+Y) = Var(X)+Var(Y); expectation of a sum needs independence too
Only E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y]; variance of a sum always needs a cross term
Neither — independence only guarantees Cov(X,Y) is small, not zero

cards.prompt: Which property does correlation Corr(X,Y) have that covariance Cov(X,Y) does not?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 4, 6

choices.text: It is unitless and always falls between -1 and 1, no matter the units of X and Y
It can only be zero when X and Y are independent
It ignores the sign of the relationship between X and Y
It is undefined whenever Var(X) is different from Var(Y)

cards.prompt: X and Y are called ___ when Cov(X,Y) = 0, equivalently Corr(X,Y) = 0.
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 4, 6
cards.answer: uncorrelated

cards.prompt: X is uniform on {-1, 0, 1} and Y = X^2. X and Y are perfectly dependent (Y is a deterministic function of X), yet Cov(X,Y) turns out to be exactly 0. What does this example demonstrate?
citations: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability 2e, Ch. 4, 6

choices.text: Uncorrelated does not imply independent — zero covariance only rules out a linear relationship
Independent does not imply uncorrelated
The formula for covariance is wrong for deterministic functions
X and Y must actually be independent, since Cov(X,Y) = 0

cards.prompt: TCP treats the network itself as a resource that must be shared without explicit coordination, so senders probe for available capacity and back off when they infer it has been exceeded, generally treating packet loss as a ___ signal.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.6-3.7
cards.answer: congestion

cards.prompt: AIMD (additive increase, multiplicative decrease) governs steady-state behavior: on each successful round trip the congestion window grows by roughly one segment, but on a detected loss the window is cut, typically ___. This sawtooth pattern keeps senders probing for more bandwidth without piling on indefinitely.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.6-3.7
cards.answer: in half

cards.prompt: During TCP slow start, how fast does the congestion window grow, and how does that compare to AIMD?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.6-3.7
cards.answer: The initial phase after a connection starts (or after a timeout), where the congestion window doubles every round trip until it reaches a threshold or a loss occurs, growing far faster than AIMD's linear increase.

cards.prompt: What triggers TCP's fast retransmit, and why does it beat waiting for the timer?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.6-3.7
cards.answer: A sender that receives three duplicate ACKs for the same segment infers that segment was lost and retransmits it immediately, without waiting for the retransmission timer to expire.

cards.prompt: Fast retransmit lets TCP recover from an isolated loss in roughly one round trip instead of waiting a full ___ interval, which is much longer than a typical RTT.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.6-3.7
cards.answer: timeout

cards.prompt: Why does TCP reduce its window more aggressively after a timeout than after fast retransmit (three duplicate ACKs)?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.6-3.7
cards.answer: A timeout suggests a more severe congestion event with no ACKs getting through at all, so TCP resets the window to its minimum and re-enters slow start, whereas duplicate ACKs mean segments are still arriving and only one was lost, so TCP can halve the window and continue.

cards.prompt: CUBIC, used by default in Linux, grows its window as a cubic function of time since the last loss rather than AIMD's linear growth, letting it reach a link's available capacity faster on high-bandwidth, high-delay paths than ___-style AIMD does.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.6-3.7
cards.answer: Reno

cards.prompt: A TCP sender's window is 20 segments when it experiences a timeout. What does it do?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.6-3.7

choices.text: Resets the window to 1 segment and re-enters slow start
Halves the window to 10 and continues in congestion avoidance
Leaves the window unchanged and retransmits the lost segment
Doubles the window to probe for more bandwidth

cards.prompt: Explain what "congestion avoidance" means as a TCP Reno phase, and how it differs in growth rate from slow start.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.6-3.7

cards.prompt: Transmission delay is the time to push all of a packet's bits onto the link, equal to packet length divided by ___. Propagation delay is the time for a bit to travel the physical link, equal to link length divided by the propagation speed of the medium.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 1.4
cards.answer: link bandwidth

cards.prompt: What is queuing delay, and what determines how long a packet waits in it?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 1.4
cards.answer: The time a packet waits in a router's output buffer before it can be transmitted, and it depends on how many other packets are already queued ahead of it.

cards.prompt: Traffic intensity is defined as the ratio of the average bit arrival rate to the link's transmission rate. As traffic intensity approaches ___, average queuing delay grows without bound for bursty arrivals, and a full buffer starts dropping packets.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 1.4

cards.prompt: Why can two routers with the same average load see very different queuing delay?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 1.4
cards.answer: Delay depends on the burstiness of arrivals, not just the average rate; bursty traffic causes queues to build even when the long-run average utilization is well below 1.

cards.prompt: End-to-end throughput between a sender and receiver is limited by the ___ — the link along the path with the smallest available capacity — regardless of how fast the other links are.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 1.4
cards.answer: bottleneck link

cards.prompt: A path has links of capacity 10 Mbps, 100 Mbps, and 1 Gbps in series. What is the maximum achievable end-to-end throughput?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 1.4

choices.text: 10 Mbps
100 Mbps
1 Gbps
The average of the three, about 370 Mbps

cards.prompt: Explain why queuing delay, unlike transmission and propagation delay, cannot be computed from static link properties alone.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 1.4

cards.prompt: The hierarchy has three main levels: ___ servers at the top, which point to top-level domain (TLD) servers (`.com`, `.org`, country codes), which point to authoritative servers that hold the actual records for a specific domain.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 2.4
RFC 1035
cards.answer: root

cards.prompt: In an iterative DNS query, what does the queried server return instead of the final answer, and who has to follow up?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 2.4
RFC 1035
cards.answer: A DNS server responds with the address of the next server to ask, rather than the final answer, leaving the requester to follow the chain itself.

cards.prompt: In a recursive DNS query, who does the work of contacting further servers, and what does the original requester get back?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 2.4
RFC 1035
cards.answer: A DNS server takes on the work of contacting other servers on the requester's behalf and returns only the final answer.

cards.prompt: A local DNS resolver typically issues ___ queries to itself on behalf of the client, while it issues iterative queries when walking down the root-to-authoritative chain.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 2.4
RFC 1035
cards.answer: recursive

cards.prompt: A local DNS resolver typically issues recursive queries to itself on behalf of the client, while it issues ___ queries when walking down the root-to-authoritative chain.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 2.4
RFC 1035
cards.answer: iterative

cards.prompt: Why does a DNS record carry a TTL, and what happens when it expires?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 2.4
RFC 1035
cards.answer: The TTL tells resolvers how long they may cache the record before it must be discarded and re-fetched, letting operators trade off staleness against reducing repeated lookups at the authoritative server.

cards.prompt: A resolver's cache holds an `A` record with TTL 300 seconds, cached 400 seconds ago. What should the resolver do on the next lookup?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 2.4
RFC 1035

choices.text: Discard the cached entry and query again, since the TTL has expired
Serve the cached entry, since DNS records never truly expire
Serve the cached entry but flag it as insecure
Contact the root servers directly, bypassing the authoritative server

cards.prompt: Explain why caching DNS results at local resolvers is important for the scalability of the whole DNS system.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 2.4
RFC 1035

cards.prompt: What are the two phases HTTP caching splits into, and what question does each answer?
citations: RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching)
RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: The freshness phase asks whether a stored response is still within its lifetime and can be served with zero network trips. Once that lifetime expires the response is stale, and the validation phase takes over, asking the origin server whether the stale copy still matches reality before reusing or replacing it.

cards.prompt: A response is served with `Cache-Control: no-cache`. What must a cache do before it can reuse a stored copy of that response for a later request?
citations: RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching)
RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)

choices.text: Revalidate with the origin server first — no-cache does not forbid storing the response, only reusing it without asking
Nothing — the response must never be reused at all
Discard it immediately, since no-cache forbids storage
Reuse it freely without contacting the origin, since only a separate directive requires validation

cards.prompt: Storage and reuse are two different permissions, and the directive that actually withholds the first one is spelled differently. The ___ directive is the one that forbids a cache from keeping any copy of the response at all, in any form, for any later use.
citations: RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching)
RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: no-store

cards.prompt: `Cache-Control` also separates *who* a response is fresh for. A response marked ___ is meant for a single end user's own cache (a browser), not for a cache shared across many users; a `public` response may be stored by anyone, including a shared cache sitting between the origin and every client it serves. A CDN that ignored the distinction and stored the wrong one would end up serving one user's personalized page to every other visitor.
citations: RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching)
RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: private

cards.prompt: If a response carries both `max-age=60` and `s-maxage=600`, what freshness lifetime applies in a private browser cache versus a shared cache like a CDN?
citations: RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching)
RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: A private cache without special support for s-maxage just uses max-age, so it treats the response as fresh for 60 seconds. A shared cache uses s-maxage instead, which exists specifically to override max-age for shared caches, so it treats the same response as fresh for 600 seconds.

cards.prompt: A response marked ___ tells a cache the underlying resource will never change for the rest of its freshness lifetime, so even an explicit user reload should skip revalidation entirely rather than checking just in case.
citations: RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching)
RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: immutable

cards.prompt: What does Cache-Control: must-revalidate change about how a cache is allowed to handle a stale response, compared to ordinary staleness handling?
citations: RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching)
RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: Ordinarily a cache is permitted to serve a known-stale response anyway if it can't reach the origin, for example during a network outage. must-revalidate removes that fallback: the cache must fail the request rather than serve stale content without successfully validating it first.

cards.prompt: Once a response goes stale, validation needs something to compare against — a **validator**. HTTP defines two independent kinds. What are the two kinds of validators HTTP caching uses to check whether a stale response has actually changed, and what does each compare?
citations: RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching)
RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: An ETag is an opaque token — often a content hash — representing the exact representation, compared for equality between what the cache has and what the origin currently serves. Last-Modified is a timestamp of when the resource last changed, compared by date. A cache sends whichever validator it has back to the origin (as If-None-Match or a conditional date header) and gets a 304 back if nothing has changed.

cards.prompt: ETags come in two comparison strengths. A weak validator is prefixed with ___ and only claims the representation is semantically equivalent, not byte-for-byte identical — so it's good enough to skip re-sending a page whose content is unchanged in meaning, but it cannot be trusted for something like a range request that needs exact identity between the ranges being stitched together.
citations: RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching)
RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: W/

cards.prompt: Why does an incorrect Vary header on a response stored in a shared cache risk poisoning that cache for other users?
citations: RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching)
RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: Vary lists which request headers split a single URL into separate cached variants — Accept-Language and Accept-Encoding are common examples. If a response's Vary header omits a request header that actually changes the response body, the shared cache stores just one variant under that URL and may later serve it to a different user whose request differed exactly on the omitted header — handing them the wrong language or an encoding their client can't decode.

cards.prompt: Waiting out the validation round-trip is itself a latency cost, which is what the newest directive addresses. The ___ directive lets a cache serve its stale copy to the user immediately while it revalidates with the origin in the background, trading a small window of possible staleness for making that request's latency disappear entirely — the served copy just might be a few seconds out of date until the background check completes.
citations: RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching)
RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: stale-while-revalidate

cards.prompt: Why can a slow response on a persistent HTTP/1.1 connection delay a request that was sent after it, even though the connection has spare capacity?
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
Grigorik, High Performance Browser Networking
cards.answer: HTTP/1.1 allows only one request in flight per connection at a time, so a later request cannot even be sent — let alone answered — until the response to the request ahead of it completes. The delay comes from the protocol's request/response ordering rule, not from any shortage of network bandwidth.

cards.prompt: What does HTTP pipelining allow a client to do that plain persistent HTTP/1.1 does not?
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
Grigorik, High Performance Browser Networking
cards.answer: Send several requests over one connection before any of their responses have arrived, instead of sending each request only after the previous response has fully returned.

cards.prompt: HTTP pipelining lets a client send several requests without waiting for each response in between. Explain why this still does not prevent one slow request from delaying requests that were queued behind it.
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
Grigorik, High Performance Browser Networking

cards.prompt: Beyond the in-order response requirement, why did major browsers never enable HTTP pipelining by default?
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
Grigorik, High Performance Browser Networking

choices.text: Deployed intermediaries such as proxies handled pipelined requests unreliably, causing silent corruption
Pipelining was never actually included in the HTTP/1.1 specification
Pipelining required a new TCP option unsupported by most operating systems
Pipelining only worked over encrypted connections, which were rare at the time

cards.prompt: With pipelining a practical dead end, browsers worked around application-layer head-of-line blocking a different way: instead of one connection to a server, open several. The de facto convention that emerged was roughly ___ parallel connections per origin (host plus scheme plus port).
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
Grigorik, High Performance Browser Networking
cards.answer: six

cards.prompt: What are the two per-connection costs a browser accepts by opening roughly six parallel connections to one origin instead of reusing a single connection?
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
Grigorik, High Performance Browser Networking
cards.answer: Each additional connection needs its own setup handshake before it can carry data, and each maintains its own separate congestion window that starts small and ramps up independently, rather than sharing one already-warmed connection's capacity.

cards.prompt: Domain sharding serves a site's resources from several different subdomains instead of one hostname. Explain, in terms of how browsers apply the parallel-connection limit, why this gets a page more simultaneous connections than staying on a single hostname would.
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
Grigorik, High Performance Browser Networking

cards.prompt: Why could aggressive domain sharding end up slowing a page down rather than speeding it up, given what each extra shard costs?
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
Grigorik, High Performance Browser Networking
cards.answer: Each additional shard is a new hostname needing its own DNS resolution and its own set of TCP connections, each with a handshake and a cold congestion window; past a certain shard count that per-connection overhead outweighs the benefit of the added parallelism.

cards.prompt: What is "proactive negotiation," and which three request headers commonly drive it?
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: Proactive negotiation is the client telling the server upfront, before any response is sent, which representations it's willing to accept — via the Accept header for media types, Accept-Encoding for compression schemes, and Accept-Language for languages. The server picks the best match from those preferences and returns that one representation directly, rather than making the client choose among several offered alternatives afterward.

cards.prompt: A response arrives with `Content-Encoding: gzip`. What must the recipient do to read the actual resource?
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)

choices.text: Decompress it — Content-Encoding is an end-to-end property of the representation itself, and reversing it is required to recover the resource
Nothing — Content-Encoding is metadata for intermediate caches only, not the final recipient
Strip it at the first hop, since it behaves like Transfer-Encoding
Nothing — encodings named in this header are undone automatically below the application layer

cards.prompt: Why is Transfer-Encoding a hop-by-hop concern while Content-Encoding is end-to-end?
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: Transfer-Encoding describes how a message is packaged for one specific connection between adjacent nodes — for example, breaking the body into chunks for this hop — and any intermediary is free to add, remove, or change it. Content-Encoding describes a property of the representation itself, applied by the origin and left untouched by every intermediary, so it arrives at the final recipient exactly as sent and that recipient is the one who must decode it.

cards.prompt: The hop-by-hop case that matters most in practice is one specific framing scheme. ___ transfer encoding lets a server start sending a response body before it knows the total length in advance, splitting the body into a series of length-prefixed pieces and signaling the end with a final zero-length one — useful for streamed or dynamically generated content where buffering the whole thing first isn't practical.
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: Chunked

cards.prompt: Why can a response not declare both a Content-Length and chunked Transfer-Encoding?
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: Content-Length commits to the exact total body size upfront, which requires already knowing the full length before sending the first byte. Chunked encoding exists precisely to handle the opposite case, where that length isn't known in advance, so a recipient is told where the body ends by the framing itself instead. The two are alternative ways of answering the same question — where does the body stop — and only one can apply at a time.

cards.prompt: Content-Encoding is where actual body compression lives, and the choice of scheme is a real tradeoff rather than a solved question. What's the practical tradeoff between choosing gzip versus brotli to compress a response body?
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: Brotli generally compresses text more tightly than gzip, partly thanks to a static dictionary tuned for web content, but costs more CPU time to compress at high quality settings. gzip compresses faster and is supported by a wider range of older clients, making it the safer universal default even where brotli would save more bytes.

cards.prompt: Why did headers become a disproportionately large share of HTTP/2 traffic once bodies were already compressed and connections were reused for many requests?
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
RFC 9204 (QPACK)
cards.answer: Because headers are large and highly repetitive across the requests sharing a connection, yet — before HPACK — every request sent them again in full; with body compression already shrinking the response side, the uncompressed, repeated header block became the dominant remaining overhead.

cards.prompt: A ___ ships with the specification itself: a fixed list of common header fields and common values (`:method: GET`, common `content-type` values, and so on) that every HPACK implementation already knows, so referencing one costs only a small index rather than any text at all.
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
RFC 9204 (QPACK)
cards.answer: static table

cards.prompt: A ___ is built up *during* the connection: the first time a header not already in the static table appears, the endpoint adds it to a table private to that connection. Later requests on the same connection can then reference that entry by index instead of resending its text.
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
RFC 9204 (QPACK)
cards.answer: dynamic table

cards.prompt: For a header that has no table entry at all — a fresh cookie value, a freshly generated request ID — HPACK falls back to sending it as a literal, but even that literal is not sent as raw bytes. It is passed through a ___ tuned to the byte-frequency statistics of real HTTP header text, so the literal itself comes out smaller than its plain-text form.
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
RFC 9204 (QPACK)
cards.answer: Huffman code

cards.prompt: What are HPACK's three space-saving mechanisms, and which of them applies to a header value seen for the first time on a connection?
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
RFC 9204 (QPACK)
cards.answer: A static table of common fields shared by all implementations, a per-connection dynamic table built up as new headers appear, and Huffman coding of literal values; a first-time value has no table entry yet, so it is sent as a Huffman-coded literal.

cards.prompt: Explain why a header repeated on request 50 of a long-lived HTTP/2 connection is cheap under HPACK even though it was expensive on request 1.
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
RFC 9204 (QPACK)
cards.answer: Request 1 has no table entry for that header, so it goes out as a Huffman-coded literal. Once sent, the encoder adds it to the connection's dynamic table. Every later request that repeats it can reference that dynamic-table entry by a small index instead of resending any text, so the cost drops from the literal's size to a few bits regardless of how long the header actually is.

cards.prompt: Why is HPACK a purpose-built indexing scheme rather than a thin wrapper around a generic compressor like gzip?
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
RFC 9204 (QPACK)
cards.answer: Because a generic compressor builds a shared dictionary from everything it compresses, and compressing attacker-influenced data together with a secret lets the compressed size leak information about the secret; HPACK's explicit static/dynamic table and literal-encoding rules avoid that shared, uncontrolled compression context.

cards.prompt: ___ is the response to exactly that mismatch. It keeps HPACK's core idea — static table, dynamic table, Huffman-coded literals — but decouples dynamic-table updates from the request streams that use them, carrying them on their own dedicated stream and having each reference name the specific table state it depended on. That lets a decoder process a request referencing the table without having to wait for every earlier update to arrive in a fixed sequence first.
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
RFC 9204 (QPACK)
cards.answer: QPACK

cards.prompt: Why couldn't HTTP/2's HPACK be reused unchanged for HTTP/3, given that QPACK keeps the same static table, dynamic table, and Huffman-coding ideas?
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
RFC 9204 (QPACK)
cards.answer: HPACK's dynamic table only stays synchronized if table-update instructions are delivered in the exact order they were sent, which HTTP/2 could guarantee because it multiplexed everything onto one ordered stream. HTTP/3's streams are delivered independently of one another, so that strict-order guarantee no longer holds, and QPACK exists to decouple table updates from request streams so the encoding survives that.

cards.prompt: What is the smallest unit of communication in HTTP/2's binary framing layer, and what does each one carry to identify where it belongs?
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
Grigorik, High Performance Browser Networking
cards.answer: A frame — a binary structure carrying a type, a length, and a stream identifier that says which logical stream the frame's contents belong to.

cards.prompt: What makes an HTTP/2 stream "independent," as distinct from just being a labeled group of frames?
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
Grigorik, High Performance Browser Networking
cards.answer: Each stream carries its own request and response and progresses without waiting on any other stream on the same connection, so work on one stream is not gated by the state of another — the streams share a connection but not each other's pace.

cards.prompt: A single TCP connection carries many streams at once — this is ___. Unlike HTTP/1.1's six separate connections standing in for parallelism, HTTP/2 gets genuine concurrency from one connection, because the streams sharing it are a construct of the protocol itself rather than of the transport.
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
Grigorik, High Performance Browser Networking
cards.answer: multiplexing

cards.prompt: How does frame interleaving on a single HTTP/2 connection prevent one slow response from delaying an unrelated request, given that HTTP/1.1 could not avoid exactly that?
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
Grigorik, High Performance Browser Networking
cards.answer: Frames from many streams share the same connection but are tagged with a stream identifier and can be sent interleaved; a stream still generating its response simply contributes no frames for a moment while other streams' frames continue to flow, so a slow response no longer occupies the whole connection the way a slow HTTP/1.1 response did.

cards.prompt: Why does HTTP/2 assign odd stream identifiers to client-initiated streams and even ones to server-initiated streams, instead of both sides drawing from one shared counter?
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
Grigorik, High Performance Browser Networking
cards.answer: Splitting the numbering space this way lets client and server each open new streams independently, without asking the other side which numbers are already taken — a shared counter would need coordination between the two ends to avoid collisions.

cards.prompt: HTTP/2 flow control operates at which level(s)?
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
Grigorik, High Performance Browser Networking

choices.text: Per individual stream and per connection as a whole
Per connection only, with no per-stream limit
Per individual stream only, with no connection-wide limit
Per TCP segment

cards.prompt: HTTP/2 added a stream prioritization scheme so clients could hint which responses mattered most. Why did this feature largely underdeliver in practice, despite being part of the standard?
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
Grigorik, High Performance Browser Networking

cards.prompt: Why do the six-connections-per-origin convention and domain sharding both stop making sense once a browser is talking HTTP/2 to a server?
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
Grigorik, High Performance Browser Networking
cards.answer: Both existed to work around HTTP/1.1 allowing only one request in flight per connection, by giving the browser more connections to spread requests across. HTTP/2 removes that limit directly — one connection carries many interleaved streams — so opening extra connections or extra subdomains no longer buys any additional parallelism, only added setup overhead.

cards.prompt: HTTP is a request-response protocol where a client sends a request and a server returns a response, with the server retaining no memory of past requests by default — HTTP is a ___ protocol.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 2.2
RFC 9110
cards.answer: stateless

cards.prompt: Under non-persistent HTTP, how many objects share each TCP connection, and what does that cost per object?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 2.2
RFC 9110
cards.answer: Each object is fetched over its own new TCP connection, which is opened, used once, and closed, adding a full connection setup delay per object.

cards.prompt: Under persistent HTTP, how many objects can share one TCP connection, and what overhead does that avoid?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 2.2
RFC 9110
cards.answer: Multiple requests and responses can be sent over the same open TCP connection, avoiding repeated handshake overhead for objects on the same server.

cards.prompt: The `GET` method requests a resource, `POST` submits data to be processed (often creating or modifying state), and `PUT` replaces a resource at a given URL. A status code in the ___ range indicates success, while a 4xx code means the problem was with the client's request rather than the server.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 2.2
RFC 9110
cards.answer: 2xx

cards.prompt: The `GET` method requests a resource, `POST` submits data to be processed (often creating or modifying state), and `PUT` replaces a resource at a given URL. A status code in the 2xx range indicates success, while a ___ code means the problem was with the client's request rather than the server.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 2.2
RFC 9110
cards.answer: 4xx

cards.prompt: How does a server use a cookie to recognize a returning client?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 2.2
RFC 9110
cards.answer: The server sets a unique identifier in a Set-Cookie response header; the browser stores it and automatically resends it in the Cookie header on later requests to that domain, letting the server look up state associated with that identifier.

cards.prompt: The `Cache-Control` and `If-Modified-Since` headers let a client avoid re-downloading unchanged content: a conditional GET asks the server to send the object only if it has changed since a given time, and the server replies ___ if it has not.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 2.2
RFC 9110
cards.answer: 304 Not Modified

cards.prompt: Which HTTP status code tells a browser that a cached copy of a resource is still valid?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 2.2
RFC 9110

choices.text: 304 Not Modified
204 No Content
404 Not Found
200 OK

cards.prompt: Explain why persistent HTTP connections reduce page load latency compared to non-persistent connections, especially for pages with many small objects.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 2.2
RFC 9110

cards.prompt: Which three parts make up an HTTP message, and which one is optional?
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: A start line, header fields, and an optional body — the body is the only one that may be absent (for example, on many GET requests or a 204 response).

cards.prompt: Why does upgrading a connection from HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2 change nothing about what a client's GET request means or how a server is expected to handle it?
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: Because GET's meaning is defined at the semantics layer, which RFC 9110 specifies independently of any version's wire format; HTTP/2 changes only how the request is framed and transmitted, not what the method, headers, or status codes signify.

cards.prompt: RFC 9110 separates HTTP semantics from HTTP syntax. Explain what each term covers, and why that separation lets the same request meaning survive a move from HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2 even though the two versions encode messages completely differently on the wire.
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: Semantics is the meaning layer: what a method, header, or status code signifies — "create this resource," "the request was unauthorized," and so on. Syntax is the encoding layer: how a message expressing that meaning is actually serialized onto the connection, whether as newline-delimited text (HTTP/1.1) or as binary frames (HTTP/2, /3). Because a client and server only need to agree on semantics to understand each other, a version change can swap out the entire wire format without altering what any request or response means.

cards.prompt: A method is called ___ when it is not expected to produce any state-changing effect on the server.
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: safe

cards.prompt: Which of these methods is defined as "safe" — meaning a compliant server is not expected to produce any state-changing effect from it?
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)

choices.text: GET
POST
PUT
DELETE

cards.prompt: A method is called ___ when sending the identical request multiple times produces the same effect on server state as sending it once.
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: idempotent

cards.prompt: What is the actual definition of an idempotent method, as opposed to the common misreading of the term?
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: An idempotent method is one where issuing the identical request N times leaves the server in the same state as issuing it once — it is a guarantee about the resulting state, not about the response body or status code being identical on each call.

cards.prompt: Which single statement correctly places POST, PUT, and DELETE on the safe/idempotent axes?
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)

choices.text: POST is neither safe nor idempotent; PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe
POST and PUT are both idempotent and safe; DELETE is neither
All three are idempotent since they are standard HTTP methods
PUT is safe because it uses a fixed target URL

cards.prompt: Why is it safe for an HTTP client to automatically retry a request that timed out if the method was PUT or DELETE, but not if the method was a plain POST?
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: PUT and DELETE are idempotent, so repeating the exact same request changes server state no further than the first attempt did, even if the client can't confirm the first attempt succeeded. POST carries no such guarantee — the resource's handling might create a new effect (like a duplicate order) on every call, so an automatic retry risks applying the request's effect twice.

cards.prompt: Name a method that is both safe and idempotent, one that is idempotent but not safe, and one that is neither safe nor idempotent. For the idempotent-but-not-safe one, explain what "idempotent" guarantees about repeating it, given that it does modify server state.
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)

cards.prompt: QUIC runs on top of ___ rather than replacing TCP in place.
citations: RFC 9000 (QUIC)
RFC 9114 (HTTP/3)
cards.answer: UDP

cards.prompt: TCP's behavior is implemented inside operating system kernels, and the middleboxes sitting on paths across the internet — firewalls, NATs, load balancers — have been built and tuned against decades of that exact behavior. A protocol that tried to ship as "an improved TCP" would get rewritten, dropped, or mishandled by equipment that assumes TCP looks a certain way. That fossilization of assumed behavior is called protocol ___, and it is what made incrementally evolving TCP itself impractical at internet scale.
citations: RFC 9000 (QUIC)
RFC 9114 (HTTP/3)
cards.answer: ossification

cards.prompt: What made UDP a workable foundation for a new transport, when a modified TCP was not?
citations: RFC 9000 (QUIC)
RFC 9114 (HTTP/3)
