cards.answer: UDP carries almost no behavior for middleboxes to have ossified around, and because TCP lives in the OS kernel while UDP just carries arbitrary payloads, QUIC's own logic can run entirely in userspace — shipping and evolving with an application's own release cycle instead of waiting on kernel and network-equipment upgrades everywhere.

cards.prompt: How does QUIC avoid the transport-layer head-of-line blocking that persists under HTTP/2 running over TCP?
citations: RFC 9000 (QUIC)
RFC 9114 (HTTP/3)
cards.answer: QUIC makes streams a transport-level primitive with independent delivery, so a packet loss only stalls the one stream whose data it carried; data for every other stream can still be delivered to and read by the application immediately, unlike a single TCP byte stream where any loss blocks everything queued behind it.

cards.prompt: Because identity no longer depends on the network path, a client can change networks entirely — moving from Wi-Fi to a cellular radio, for instance — in the middle of a connection, and the same session keeps running without being torn down and rebuilt. This capability is called ___.
citations: RFC 9000 (QUIC)
RFC 9114 (HTTP/3)
cards.answer: connection migration

cards.prompt: A phone switches from Wi-Fi to cellular mid-download, changing its IP address and port entirely. What happens to its QUIC connection?
citations: RFC 9000 (QUIC)
RFC 9114 (HTTP/3)

choices.text: It survives, because QUIC identifies the connection by a connection ID rather than by IP and port
It is dropped, since QUIC connections are still tied to the four-tuple exactly like TCP
It survives, but only after the application performs a fresh TLS handshake
It survives only if the client stays on the same subnet

cards.prompt: Explain why integrating the TLS 1.3 handshake into QUIC's own connection handshake, instead of running a transport handshake and then a cryptographic handshake on top of it in sequence, lets a QUIC connection typically become usable in fewer round trips than TCP plus TLS 1.3.
citations: RFC 9000 (QUIC)
RFC 9114 (HTTP/3)

cards.prompt: What does HTTP/3 change relative to earlier HTTP versions, and what does it deliberately leave untouched?
citations: RFC 9000 (QUIC)
RFC 9114 (HTTP/3)
cards.answer: HTTP/3 leaves HTTP's request-response semantics, methods, and status codes unchanged; what it changes is the transport underneath, mapping those semantics onto QUIC streams instead of a TCP connection, which is where HTTP/3 inherits QUIC's independent per-stream delivery and connection migration.

cards.prompt: Why does HTTP/2 server push frequently waste bandwidth rather than simply providing no benefit?
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
RFC 8297 (Early Hints)
cards.answer: The server cannot see what the client already has cached, so it may push a resource the client already holds a valid copy of; that push still consumes bandwidth and server-push connection capacity, actively costing more than doing nothing.

cards.prompt: ___ is the mechanism that replaced push's proactive delivery with a much smaller commitment: an interim response, sent before the final response is ready, that lists resources the client will probably need — via ordinary `Link` headers — so the client can start fetching them itself while the server is still preparing the main response. The server still guesses what will be needed, but the guess only costs a small header list; the client decides whether to act on it, checking its own cache before fetching anything, which is exactly the check server push could never make.
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
RFC 8297 (Early Hints)
cards.answer: 103 Early Hints

cards.prompt: How does 103 Early Hints avoid the core problem that undermined HTTP/2 server push?
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
RFC 8297 (Early Hints)

choices.text: It tells the client what it might need and lets the client decide whether to fetch it, so the client's own cache check still applies
It pushes the resources directly but only over a separate low-priority stream
It requires the client to advertise its full cache contents to the server first
It compresses the pushed resources so wasted pushes cost less bandwidth

cards.prompt: A related, unglamorous optimization is ___: when a client already holds an open, suitable connection to a server (matching scheme and a certificate valid for the new host), it can reuse that connection for requests to a different hostname instead of opening a new one, provided the existing connection's negotiated identity actually covers that hostname. This cuts the handshake cost of serving resources split across host names on the same underlying server or CDN edge, independent of anything push or hints do.
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
RFC 8297 (Early Hints)
cards.answer: connection coalescing

cards.prompt: Server push and Early Hints are both about *what* gets sent and when requests are avoided. Neither touches a much more basic limitation: HTTP/2 multiplexes many logical streams onto one TCP connection, but ___. TCP guarantees only one thing about delivery — bytes arrive at the application in the exact order they were sent — and it enforces that guarantee by holding back everything after a gap until a retransmission fills it, whatever that later data belongs to.
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
RFC 8297 (Early Hints)
cards.answer: TCP itself has no concept of streams

cards.prompt: On a connection with significant packet loss, how can HTTP/2's single multiplexed connection compare to HTTP/1.1's convention of six independent connections per host?
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
RFC 8297 (Early Hints)

choices.text: HTTP/2 can perform worse, because a lost segment on the one connection stalls all multiplexed streams, whereas a loss on one of six independent HTTP/1.1 connections only stalls the requests on that one connection
HTTP/2 always performs better, because multiplexing means loss on one stream is fully isolated from the others
They perform identically, since both are built on TCP and inherit the same retransmission behavior per connection
HTTP/2 performs worse only because it disables retransmission to preserve stream ordering

cards.prompt: Explain, from TCP's in-order delivery guarantee alone, why HTTP/2 multiplexing many streams onto one connection does not remove head-of-line blocking the way it appears to at the HTTP layer.
citations: RFC 9113 (HTTP/2)
RFC 8297 (Early Hints)
cards.answer: TCP's guarantee is about bytes, not about the HTTP-layer streams multiplexed inside them: it will not deliver any byte to the application until every byte before it in the sequence has arrived. A lost segment creates a gap, and everything sent after that gap — regardless of which HTTP/2 stream it belongs to — sits in the TCP receive buffer undelivered until retransmission closes the gap. The multiplexing exists only above TCP; TCP's delivery order still applies to the whole connection as one sequence.

cards.prompt: Which two of the four redirect codes guarantee that the client will reuse the original request method and body, rather than potentially switching to GET?
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: 307 Temporary Redirect and 308 Permanent Redirect. 301 and 302 predate that guarantee and historically left method-switching behavior up to the client.

cards.prompt: If a resource has permanently moved and the client must keep using its original method on the follow-up request, which single status code fits both conditions?
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: 308 Permanent Redirect — permanent like 301, but with 307/308's guarantee that the method and body are preserved rather than possibly downgraded to GET.

cards.prompt: A server returns 403 for a request that already carried a valid, correctly-formatted API key. Does supplying a different, also-valid key for the same account have any chance of succeeding?
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: No — 403 means the server already identified the requester and is denying access to that identity's account regardless of which valid credential represented it; only a genuinely different identity, or a permission change on the server side, could change the outcome.

cards.prompt: `404 Not Found` says nothing more than "no resource is currently found at this URL" — the server is not committing to any claim about whether it ever existed or might reappear. ___ Gone is a deliberate, stronger statement: the resource used to exist at this URL and has been intentionally and permanently removed, with no forwarding address.
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)

cards.prompt: Why might a server deliberately choose to return 410 Gone instead of 404 Not Found for a resource it just deleted?
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: 410 communicates that the removal is intentional and permanent, discouraging clients and crawlers from retrying or re-indexing the URL, whereas 404 leaves that question open and could be read as "not found right now, maybe try later."

cards.prompt: A client submits a well-formed JSON body to create a user, but the "email" field fails a validation rule the server enforces. Which status code fits best?
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)

choices.text: 422 Unprocessable Content
409 Conflict
400 Bad Request due to malformed syntax
401 Unauthorized

cards.prompt: `429 Too Many Requests` tells a client it has been rate-limited. It is commonly paired with a `___` header giving either a number of seconds or an HTTP date after which the client may try again. A well-behaved client reads that header and waits the indicated time rather than retrying immediately or backing off with an arbitrary guess.
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: Retry-After

cards.prompt: A reverse proxy in front of an application server can return 502, 503, or 504 for requests it can't fulfill. Describe the distinct failure story each code tells, focusing on what the proxy did or didn't receive from upstream in each case.
citations: RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)
cards.answer: 502 Bad Gateway: the proxy got a response from upstream, but it was malformed or invalid, so the proxy can't relay it. 503 Service Unavailable: the proxy or server is currently unable to handle requests at all, typically overload or maintenance, independent of any specific upstream call. 504 Gateway Timeout: the proxy sent the request upstream and simply never got a response back before its timeout elapsed.

cards.prompt: The way there is the ___ handshake: a client sends an ordinary HTTP request asking the server to switch the protocol running on this same TCP connection, and if the server agrees, both sides stop speaking HTTP on it and start speaking a different, bidirectional protocol instead.
citations: RFC 6455 (WebSocket)
cards.answer: Upgrade

cards.prompt: How does the server prove it understood the request, given the client's Sec-WebSocket-Key?
citations: RFC 6455 (WebSocket)
cards.answer: It concatenates the client's key with a fixed, spec-defined GUID, takes the SHA-1 hash of that concatenation, base64-encodes the result, and returns it in a Sec-WebSocket-Accept header — a value only a server implementing the WebSocket handshake would compute correctly.

cards.prompt: A client sends `Upgrade: websocket` and `Connection: Upgrade` headers along with a Sec-WebSocket-Key. Which response tells it the switch succeeded?
citations: RFC 6455 (WebSocket)

choices.text: 101 Switching Protocols, with a matching Sec-WebSocket-Accept header
200 OK, with a Upgrade-Confirmed header
204 No Content
302 Found, redirecting to a `ws://` URL

cards.prompt: The server signals success with a ___ status, the one status code whose entire job is to say the protocol on this connection is about to change.
citations: RFC 6455 (WebSocket)

cards.prompt: After the 101 response, is the traffic on that connection still HTTP?
citations: RFC 6455 (WebSocket)
cards.answer: No — the connection has switched entirely to WebSocket framing; there are no more HTTP requests or responses on it, only WebSocket frames sent by either side until the connection closes.

cards.prompt: Not every "server needs to push updates" problem calls for a full duplex protocol, though. ___ give a server a plain-HTTP, one-way channel to the client, with reconnection handled automatically by the browser's own EventSource API — no separate handshake, no client-to-server frames, and no custom reconnect logic to write.
citations: RFC 6455 (WebSocket)
cards.answer: Server-Sent Events

cards.prompt: An app needs a one-way stream of live updates from server to client, delivered over plain HTTP, with reconnection handled automatically by the browser. What fits without the overhead of a full-duplex protocol?
citations: RFC 6455 (WebSocket)

choices.text: Server-Sent Events
WebSockets
Long polling, reissued manually on every disconnect
Short polling on a fixed interval

cards.prompt: What connects HTTP/2 to the Upgrade mechanism this note describes?
citations: RFC 6455 (WebSocket)
cards.answer: Nothing directly — HTTP/2 does not use the HTTP/1.1 Upgrade header to negotiate anything about itself, so a WebSocket connection cannot reuse this same 101 handshake on top of an HTTP/2 connection; running WebSockets over HTTP/2 instead needed a separate mechanism, an extended form of the CONNECT method defined for that purpose.

cards.prompt: An access network is the link that physically connects an end system to the first router on its path, sometimes called the ___. Common examples include DSL, cable, fiber-to-the-home, and cellular.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 1
cards.answer: edge router

cards.prompt: In circuit switching, for how long is a connection's link capacity reserved?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 1
cards.answer: A network reserves a fixed slice of link capacity (a circuit) for the entire duration of a connection, whether or not data is being sent.

cards.prompt: In packet switching, how do packets share a link's bandwidth, and how is each one forwarded?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 1
cards.answer: Data is split into packets that share link bandwidth on demand, each queued and forwarded independently based on store-and-forward transmission.

cards.prompt: Packet switching is more efficient for bursty traffic than circuit switching because unused capacity during silent periods can ___ instead of sitting idle.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 1
cards.answer: be given to other flows

cards.prompt: Why can packet-switched networks experience congestion that circuit-switched networks cannot?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 1

choices.text: Packets from many flows statistically share link capacity, so aggregate demand can exceed it
Packets are always larger than the reserved circuit capacity
Circuit switching uses more bandwidth per connection
Packet switching requires a dedicated end-to-end path

cards.prompt: What is a tier-1 ISP?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 1

choices.text: A network that peers with other tier-1 networks to form the global backbone, with no ISP above it
The ISP that directly serves residential customers
A regional network that only connects to one upstream provider
A content delivery network embedded inside access networks

cards.prompt: Describe the store-and-forward transmission behavior of a packet switch and why it adds delay proportional to packet size.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 1

cards.prompt: The IPv4 header carries, among other fields, a version number, a header length, a total length, a time-to-live (TTL) that is decremented at every router hop, a protocol field identifying the transport-layer payload, and 32-bit source and destination addresses. When TTL reaches ___, a router discards the packet, which is what makes traceroute-style tools possible.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 4
RFC 791
RFC 2131

cards.prompt: Fragmentation happens when a packet is larger than the maximum transmission unit (MTU) of an outgoing link; the router splits it into smaller fragments, each with the same identification field so the destination can reassemble them, and an offset field recording each fragment's position. The default Ethernet MTU is ___.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 4
RFC 791
RFC 2131
cards.answer: 1500 bytes

cards.prompt: Subnetting divides an IP address into a network portion and a host portion using a mask; ___ notation (e.g. `/24`) expresses how many leading bits belong to the network portion, letting routers aggregate many addresses under one routing table entry.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 4
RFC 791
RFC 2131
cards.answer: CIDR

cards.prompt: What does a NAT router rewrite in outgoing packets, and how does it route replies back?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 4
RFC 791
RFC 2131
cards.answer: A NAT-enabled router rewrites the source IP and port of outgoing packets from a private address to its own public address and a chosen port, keeping a translation table so replies can be routed back to the correct internal host.

cards.prompt: Why can NAT make it difficult for two hosts behind separate NATs to establish a direct peer-to-peer connection?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 4
RFC 791
RFC 2131
cards.answer: Neither host has a public address that the other can dial directly; a connection has to be initiated from inside each NAT (or use techniques like hole punching or a relay) because an unsolicited inbound packet has no translation table entry to match against.

cards.prompt: DHCP lets a host joining a network automatically obtain an IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS server, through a four-message exchange commonly remembered as ___: discover, offer, request, and acknowledge.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 4
RFC 791
RFC 2131
cards.answer: DORA

cards.prompt: A router receives an IPv4 packet with TTL = 1. After decrementing it, what does the router do?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 4
RFC 791
RFC 2131

choices.text: Drops the packet, since TTL reached 0, and typically sends an ICMP time-exceeded message
Forwards the packet normally and resets TTL to 255
Fragments the packet to extend its lifetime
Sends the packet back to its source unmodified

cards.prompt: Explain why NAT breaks the original end-to-end connectivity model of IP, where any two hosts could address each other directly.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 4
RFC 791
RFC 2131

cards.prompt: Pipelining improves on stop-and-wait by letting the sender have multiple unacknowledged packets in flight at once, bounded by a ___. The two classic pipelined protocols differ in how they recover from loss.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.4
cards.answer: window size

cards.prompt: In Go-Back-N, what does the sender retransmit once it detects a lost segment?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.4
cards.answer: On detecting a lost or out-of-order segment (via a timeout or an out-of-order ACK), the sender retransmits that segment and every segment sent after it, even ones the receiver already got correctly.

cards.prompt: In selective repeat, what's retransmitted after a loss, and how are out-of-order segments handled?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.4
cards.answer: Both sender and receiver maintain a window and buffer out-of-order segments; only the specific lost segment is retransmitted, and the receiver individually acknowledges each correctly received segment.

cards.prompt: Go-Back-N needs a smaller receiver buffer than selective repeat because the receiver ___ any out-of-order segment instead of buffering it, simplifying the receiver at the cost of wasted retransmissions.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.4
cards.answer: discards

cards.prompt: Sequence numbers must be large enough that the sender's window cannot wrap around and reuse a number still in flight; if it did, the receiver could not tell a genuinely new packet from a ___ of an old one.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.4
cards.answer: retransmission

cards.prompt: Under Go-Back-N, a receiver gets segments 0, 1, 3, 4 (segment 2 is lost). What does the receiver do with segments 3 and 4?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.4

choices.text: Discards them, since they arrived out of order, and re-ACKs segment 1
Buffers them and waits for segment 2 to arrive before delivering any
Delivers them to the application immediately, out of order
Sends a NAK for segment 2 and buffers 3 and 4 for later delivery

cards.prompt: Explain the main tradeoff between Go-Back-N and selective repeat in terms of receiver complexity versus retransmission efficiency.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.4

cards.prompt: In link-state routing, what does each router learn from flooding, and how does it use that to compute routes?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 5-6
cards.answer: Every router floods information about its directly connected links to all other routers in the network, so each router independently builds a complete map of the topology and computes shortest paths itself, typically with Dijkstra's algorithm.

cards.prompt: In distance-vector routing, what does a router know, and how does it update its distances?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 5-6
cards.answer: Each router only knows the distance to each destination as reported by its immediate neighbors, and iteratively recomputes its own distances by combining a neighbor's reported distance with the cost to reach that neighbor, using a form of the Bellman-Ford algorithm.

cards.prompt: A well-known problem with naive distance-vector routing is ___: when a link fails, routers can keep telling each other stale, ever-increasing distances to a now-unreachable destination before the bad route is finally purged.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 5-6
cards.answer: count-to-infinity

cards.prompt: Within a single administrative domain (an autonomous system), OSPF is the common ___ intra-domain protocol. Between autonomous systems, BGP is used instead — it is a path-vector protocol that lets each AS apply its own routing policy, not just minimize hop count or cost.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 5-6
cards.answer: link-state

cards.prompt: Why does BGP use policy rather than shortest-path selection between autonomous systems?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 5-6
cards.answer: Different autonomous systems are independent businesses with their own commercial relationships (customer, provider, peer), so route selection has to respect contracts and business interests, not just technical distance, which shortest-path metrics alone cannot express.

cards.prompt: At the link layer, Ethernet frames are addressed using ___ MAC addresses that are (in principle) globally unique and burned into the network interface, unlike IP addresses which change with location in the network.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 5-6
cards.answer: 48-bit

cards.prompt: A switch is a link-layer device that is ___: it builds its forwarding table by observing the source MAC address and incoming port of each frame it sees, rather than requiring manual configuration or running a routing protocol.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 5-6
cards.answer: self-learning

cards.prompt: How does ARP discover the MAC address that corresponds to an IP address on the local network?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 5-6
cards.answer: A host broadcasts a request asking "who has this IP address" on the local network, and the host owning that IP replies directly with its MAC address, which the requester then caches for future frames to that IP.

cards.prompt: How does a router fundamentally differ from a switch in how it forwards traffic?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 5-6

choices.text: A router forwards based on IP addresses and participates in routing protocols across networks, while a switch forwards based on MAC addresses within a single local network
A router only works with wireless links, while a switch only works with wired links
A switch can connect different IP subnets, while a router cannot
A router requires no configuration, while a switch must be manually configured

cards.prompt: Explain why link-state routing is generally more resistant to the count-to-infinity problem than distance-vector routing.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 5-6

cards.prompt: Connection teardown is a ___ exchange, because each direction is closed independently with its own FIN and ACK.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.5
RFC 9293
cards.answer: four-way

cards.prompt: The side that closes first enters ___ and waits 2·MSL before releasing the socket.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.5
RFC 9293
cards.answer: TIME_WAIT

cards.prompt: The side that closes first enters TIME_WAIT and waits ___ before releasing the socket.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.5
RFC 9293
cards.answer: 2·MSL

cards.prompt: What does the TIME_WAIT state protect against?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.5
RFC 9293
cards.answer: Delayed duplicate segments from the old connection being delivered to a new connection reusing the same four-tuple, and the loss of the final ACK.

cards.prompt: TCP's retransmission timeout is derived from a smoothed RTT estimate plus four times the RTT ___.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.5
RFC 9293
cards.answer: deviation

cards.prompt: A TCP receiver advertises a window of 0. What does the sender do?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.5
RFC 9293

choices.text: Sends periodic window-probe segments until the window reopens
Retransmits the last segment until acknowledged
Closes the connection after the retransmission timeout
Switches to slow start and continues sending

cards.prompt: Which field makes a TCP connection uniquely identifiable on a host?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.5
RFC 9293

choices.text: The four-tuple of source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port
The destination port alone
The initial sequence number
The socket file descriptor

cards.prompt: Explain why TCP's head-of-line blocking hurts a multiplexed protocol like HTTP/2, and how QUIC avoids it.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.5
RFC 9293

cards.prompt: On the sending side, what does multiplexing do with data from multiple sockets before handing it to the network layer?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.1-3.3
RFC 768
cards.answer: The sending-side task of gathering data from multiple sockets, wrapping each chunk with header information, and passing the resulting segments down to the network layer.

cards.prompt: On the receiving side, how does demultiplexing decide which socket gets an arriving segment's data?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.1-3.3
RFC 768
cards.answer: The receiving-side task of using header fields to deliver each arriving segment's data to the correct socket.

cards.prompt: A UDP segment carries very little header overhead: just source port, destination port, length, and checksum, each occupying ___. This compactness is part of why UDP is favored for latency-sensitive applications like streaming and DNS.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.1-3.3
RFC 768
cards.answer: 16 bits

cards.prompt: Unlike TCP, UDP provides no connection setup, no reliability guarantees, and no congestion control — it simply hands datagrams to the network layer and lets the application deal with loss or reordering ___.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.1-3.3
RFC 768
cards.answer: itself

cards.prompt: The UDP checksum is computed over the segment (header and data) plus a pseudo-header containing source and destination IP addresses; if the computed value does not match, the receiver ___ the segment.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.1-3.3
RFC 768
cards.answer: discards

cards.prompt: Why might a real-time voice application prefer UDP over TCP?
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.1-3.3
RFC 768

choices.text: TCP's retransmission and reordering can add delay that is worse for real-time audio than simply dropping a late packet
UDP guarantees in-order delivery, which voice requires
UDP has a larger header, giving more room for timestamps
TCP cannot be used for audio data at all

cards.prompt: Explain how a socket's (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port) tuple is used differently by UDP demultiplexing versus TCP demultiplexing.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking 8e, Ch. 3.1-3.3
RFC 768

cards.prompt: An ___ happens when a sequence of memory accesses that was intended to be treated as one indivisible unit is instead interrupted by another thread partway through, because no lock (or the wrong lock) protects the whole sequence.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 32 (Concurrency Bugs)
cards.answer: atomicity violation

cards.prompt: Why does checking a pointer for NULL, then using it separately, risk an atomicity violation?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 32 (Concurrency Bugs)
cards.answer: Another thread can run between the check and the use and change or clear the pointer, so the use no longer sees the value the check verified — the check and use needed to be one atomic, lock-protected unit but were not.

cards.prompt: An ___ happens when code assumes a particular happens before relationship between two pieces of code in different threads — for example, that some setup thread always initializes a value before a second thread reads it — but nothing actually enforces that ordering, so the second thread can run first.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 32 (Concurrency Bugs)
cards.answer: order violation

cards.prompt: Why can't an unsynchronized boolean flag reliably make thread B wait for thread A to finish?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 32 (Concurrency Bugs)
cards.answer: An unsynchronized flag read/write is itself subject to reordering and to the reader simply checking before the writer runs, so nothing guarantees B observes the flag's final value at the right time; a condition variable or similarly synchronized primitive is needed to make the ordering itself an enforced fact, not an assumption.

cards.prompt: Which fix distinguishes an order violation from an atomicity violation?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 32 (Concurrency Bugs)
cards.answer: An atomicity violation is fixed by making a sequence of accesses exclusive (a lock); an order violation is fixed by making one thread's action wait for another thread's prior action (a condition variable or ordering semaphore) — exclusion alone does not force a particular order between two threads.

cards.prompt: A thread checks `if (ptr != NULL)` and then dereferences `ptr` two lines later, with no lock held across both steps, while another thread can set `ptr = NULL`. What category of bug is this?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 32 (Concurrency Bugs)

choices.text: Atomicity violation
Order violation
Deadlock
Starvation

cards.prompt: Explain why simply adding one lock around each individual access (the check, and separately the use) does NOT fix the atomicity-violation example above, even though each access is now individually protected.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 32 (Concurrency Bugs)

cards.prompt: Why does even a small serial (locked) fraction cap a program's speedup as cores are added?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 29 (Lock-based Concurrent Data Structures)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 28 (Locks)
cards.answer: The serial fraction cannot be parallelized regardless of core count, so as cores increase, the parallel portion's time shrinks toward zero while the fixed serial portion's time stays constant, and total runtime approaches a floor set entirely by that serial fraction — this is the intuition behind Amdahl's Law.

cards.prompt: ___ is what happens when multiple threads frequently try to acquire the same lock at the same time; heavy contention means most of the waiting threads' time goes to blocking or spinning rather than useful work, and adding threads under high contention for one lock can make things worse instead of better.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 29 (Lock-based Concurrent Data Structures)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 28 (Locks)
cards.answer: Lock contention

cards.prompt: Why doesn't finer-grained locking (many small locks instead of one big one) come for free?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 29 (Lock-based Concurrent Data Structures)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 28 (Locks)
cards.answer: Each additional lock adds its own acquire/release overhead on every operation, and correctness gets harder to reason about (e.g. avoiding deadlock across multiple locks now matters), so finer-grained locking is a deliberate trade of extra per-operation cost and complexity for reduced contention — worthwhile only when contention was actually the bottleneck.

cards.prompt: Why can more threads hurt throughput against one already-saturated shared resource, like a disk?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 29 (Lock-based Concurrent Data Structures)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 28 (Locks)
cards.answer: When the resource itself, not the CPU-side critical section, is the bottleneck, extra threads just add queuing and coordination overhead in front of a resource that cannot serve requests any faster, so throughput plateaus or falls while latency for each request climbs.

cards.prompt: A program spends 20% of its total work in an unavoidable serial critical section and 80% in perfectly parallelizable work. What best describes its scalability?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 29 (Lock-based Concurrent Data Structures)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 28 (Locks)

choices.text: Speedup is bounded well below the number of cores added, because the 20% serial portion cannot shrink
Speedup scales linearly with the number of cores with no ceiling
The program cannot run correctly with more than one thread
Adding cores always reduces the serial portion's absolute time as well

cards.prompt: Explain why measuring lock contention (not just correctness) matters when choosing between a single coarse lock and a finer-grained locking scheme, and what evidence would tell you the coarse lock is actually the bottleneck.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 29 (Lock-based Concurrent Data Structures)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 28 (Locks)

cards.prompt: `pthread_cond_wait(cond, mutex)` requires the caller to already hold `mutex`. Its critical behavior: it ___ releases the mutex and puts the calling thread to sleep, so no other thread can slip in and change the shared state in the gap between "release the lock" and "start sleeping." When the thread is later woken, `wait` re-acquires the mutex before returning, so the caller resumes still holding the lock it started with.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 30 (Condition Variables)
cards.answer: atomically

cards.prompt: Why must wait() release the mutex and sleep as one atomic step, not two separate calls?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 30 (Condition Variables)
cards.answer: If a thread unlocked and then slept as two separate steps, another thread could run in the gap between them, change the shared state, and call signal before the first thread was actually asleep to receive it — the wakeup would be lost and the sleeping thread could wait forever.

cards.prompt: Every wait must be guarded by a ___ loop re-checking the condition, never a bare `if`, because a thread that wakes from wait is not guaranteed the condition it cared about still holds: another thread may have run first (Mesa-style semantics let that happen) and already consumed whatever changed, or the platform may deliver spurious wakeups.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 30 (Condition Variables)
cards.answer: while

cards.prompt: Why guard every condition-variable wait with `while`, never a bare `if`?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 30 (Condition Variables)
cards.answer: Because between a thread being woken and actually running, some other thread can grab the lock first and re-invalidate the condition (or the wakeup can be spurious), so the condition must be re-tested after wait returns, not just once before sleeping.

cards.prompt: What real problem does a condition variable solve that a lock by itself cannot?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 30 (Condition Variables)
cards.answer: A lock only guarantees exclusive access to a critical section; a condition variable additionally lets a thread sleep, without wasting CPU, until some other thread's action makes a specific state true, then be woken to recheck it.

cards.prompt: Thread A calls `pthread_cond_wait(&cv, &m)` while holding `m`. What happens to `m` for the duration that A is actually asleep?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 30 (Condition Variables)

choices.text: `m` is unlocked, so other threads may acquire it and change shared state
`m` stays locked by A until A is woken and wait() returns
`m` is destroyed and must be re-initialized before use
`m` is transferred to whichever thread calls signal() next

cards.prompt: Explain, in terms of the mutex, exactly what makes `pthread_cond_wait` different from simply calling `pthread_mutex_unlock` followed by some separate sleep call — why does the atomicity of "release and sleep" matter for correctness?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 30 (Condition Variables)

cards.prompt: Four conditions are ___ for deadlock: mutual exclusion (a resource can be held by only one thread at a time), hold-and-wait (a thread holds one resource while waiting for another), no preemption (a resource cannot be forcibly taken from the thread holding it), and circular wait (a cycle of threads, each waiting on a resource the next one in the cycle holds).
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 32 (Concurrency Bugs)
cards.answer: jointly necessary

cards.prompt: Why is it wrong to say any single one of the four conditions "causes" deadlock on its own?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 32 (Concurrency Bugs)
cards.answer: The four conditions are jointly necessary, not individually sufficient — deadlock requires all four to hold at once, so a system with mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, and no preemption but no circular dependency chain among the specific threads involved will still not deadlock; breaking just one of the four is enough to rule deadlock out.

cards.prompt: Prevention attacks one condition so it can never arise. Hold-and-wait is broken by requiring a thread to acquire all the locks it will ever need in one atomic step up front, before doing any work — simple, but it sacrifices concurrency since it demands knowing all needs in advance and locking early. Circular wait is broken by imposing a total, agreed-on ___ across the whole program: if every thread that needs locks A and B always acquires A before B, the opposite-order interleaving above becomes impossible.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 32 (Concurrency Bugs)
cards.answer: lock ordering

cards.prompt: Why does a program-wide total lock ordering rule out circular wait specifically?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 32 (Concurrency Bugs)
cards.answer: If every thread acquires locks in the same fixed order, no thread can be holding a later lock in that order while waiting on an earlier one, which is exactly what a cycle in the wait-for graph would require; without a cycle, circular wait cannot occur.

cards.prompt: Deadlock ___ takes a different approach from prevention: rather than making deadlock structurally impossible, it uses global knowledge of which resources each thread might ever need (as in the banker's algorithm) to refuse any individual resource request that would move the system into a state from which deadlock becomes possible, even if that request would not deadlock immediately.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 32 (Concurrency Bugs)
cards.answer: avoidance

cards.prompt: How does deadlock avoidance differ from deadlock prevention in what it actually guarantees?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 32 (Concurrency Bugs)
cards.answer: Prevention removes one of the four necessary conditions so deadlock cannot structurally occur, using only local rules (like a fixed lock order); avoidance instead requires advance, global knowledge of every thread's maximum resource needs and dynamically refuses requests that would enter an unsafe state, even without a specific cycle yet existing.

cards.prompt: A system has mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, and circular wait present among its threads, but resources CAN be forcibly preempted from a holding thread when needed. Does deadlock occur?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 32 (Concurrency Bugs)

choices.text: No — breaking the no-preemption condition alone is enough to prevent deadlock, even with the other three present
Yes — three of the four conditions being present is sufficient
Yes, but only if more than two threads are involved
It depends on the scheduler's time-slice length

cards.prompt: Explain why requiring every thread to acquire all its locks atomically up front (breaking hold-and-wait) is correct but often impractical compared to a total lock-ordering rule (breaking circular wait).
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 32 (Concurrency Bugs)

cards.prompt: Thread-based concurrency hands each unit of work its own thread and relies on the scheduler and locks to keep things correct, but that comes with real costs: thread creation and context-switch overhead, and the constant risk of races and deadlock whenever threads share state. Event-based concurrency is a different model built around a single thread running an ___: wait for an event, handle it to completion, then wait for the next one.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 33 (Event-based Concurrency)
cards.answer: event loop

cards.prompt: Why does a single-threaded event loop avoid races over shared state without locks?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 33 (Event-based Concurrency)
cards.answer: Only one event handler executes at any instant and each one runs uninterrupted to completion before the loop dispatches the next, so no two handlers ever interleave their accesses to shared state — mutual exclusion falls out of the model rather than needing explicit locks.

cards.prompt: What is the central risk of using a blocking system call inside an event handler?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 33 (Event-based Concurrency)
cards.answer: Because only one thread runs the loop, a handler that blocks (on disk I/O, a slow lock, or any blocking call) stalls the entire loop — no other event, however ready, can be handled until that call returns, defeating the model's whole purpose.

cards.prompt: To avoid that trap, event-based systems push I/O through ___ variants of system calls, which return immediately with an error code (rather than blocking) if the operation is not ready yet, so the loop can move on and retry later instead of stalling.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 33 (Event-based Concurrency)
cards.answer: non-blocking

cards.prompt: Why is blocking disk I/O more troublesome for an event loop than blocking network I/O?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 33 (Event-based Concurrency)
cards.answer: Most operating systems lack a general non-blocking interface for disk I/O the way they have one for sockets, so a handler that needs to read from disk has few good options besides blocking the whole loop or offloading the work to a helper thread, which reintroduces some of the concurrency concerns event-based design was meant to avoid.

cards.prompt: Why does an event-based server typically avoid ordinary blocking `read()` calls inside its handlers?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 33 (Event-based Concurrency)

choices.text: A blocking call stalls the single event loop thread, delaying every other pending event
Blocking calls are not allowed by the C standard library
Blocking calls always corrupt shared state without a lock
`select()` cannot be used at all once any blocking call exists in the program

cards.prompt: Explain what problem manual state management (turning "the rest of this handler" into an explicit continuation) is solving in event-based code, and why a thread-based program does not need it.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 33 (Event-based Concurrency)

cards.prompt: Why can more threads on a coarsely-locked shared counter fail to raise throughput?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 29 (Lock-based Concurrent Data Structures)
cards.answer: Every increment must pass through the same single lock, so beyond a small number of threads the added threads mostly wait for the lock rather than doing useful work, and the extra contention and context-switching overhead can make total throughput worse, not better.

cards.prompt: A linked list can do better than one lock for the whole list by using ___: a thread holds the lock on a node only long enough to grab the lock on the next node before releasing the first, letting different threads work on different parts of the list at once.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 29 (Lock-based Concurrent Data Structures)
cards.answer: hand-over-hand locking

cards.prompt: Why does hand-over-hand list locking trade more overhead for real parallelism?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 29 (Lock-based Concurrent Data Structures)
cards.answer: Every step down the list now costs an extra lock acquire and release (more overhead than one list-wide lock), but because no single lock covers the whole structure, threads operating on distant parts of the list can genuinely run in parallel instead of queuing behind one another.

cards.prompt: Why lock a concurrent hash table per bucket instead of with one table-wide lock?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 29 (Lock-based Concurrent Data Structures)
cards.answer: Operations that hash to different buckets touch entirely disjoint state, so per-bucket locks let those operations run fully in parallel, while a single table-wide lock would serialize every operation regardless of which bucket it targets.

cards.prompt: A concurrent linked list uses one lock for the entire list. What is the main downside compared to hand-over-hand locking, assuming both are implemented correctly?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 29 (Lock-based Concurrent Data Structures)

choices.text: Every operation serializes behind the single lock, even ones touching disjoint parts of the list
The single-lock version is not correct under concurrent access
The single-lock version requires more lock acquire/release calls per traversal
Hand-over-hand locking eliminates the need for locks entirely

cards.prompt: Explain the general strategy behind making a data structure "more concurrent" once a single coarse lock becomes a bottleneck: what is being traded for what, and why finer-grained locking is not free.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 29 (Lock-based Concurrent Data Structures)

cards.prompt: Why does disabling interrupts fail as a general lock on a multicore machine?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 28 (Locks)
cards.answer: Disabling interrupts only stops the scheduler on the one CPU that executed the instruction; it has no effect on other cores, which can still enter the same critical section concurrently.

cards.prompt: A hardware ___ instruction reads a memory location's old value and unconditionally writes a new value into it, both as one indivisible step the CPU guarantees cannot be interrupted or split between threads.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 28 (Locks)
cards.answer: test-and-set

cards.prompt: Why must test-and-set be one hardware-atomic instruction, not a separate load then store?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 28 (Locks)
cards.answer: A plain load-then-store has a gap between reading the flag and writing it, during which another thread can also read the still-unset flag, so both threads believe they got the lock; hardware performs the check-and-set as one step precisely to close that gap.

cards.prompt: A ___ hands out an ever-increasing ticket number via fetch-and-add on arrival, and a separate "now serving" counter advances by one on every release; a thread spins until its own ticket matches the counter.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 28 (Locks)
cards.answer: ticket lock

cards.prompt: Why does a ticket lock guarantee no starvation, unlike a plain test-and-set spin lock?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 28 (Locks)
cards.answer: Because tickets are handed out in arrival order and the lock is granted strictly in that order, every waiting thread is guaranteed to be served eventually; a test-and-set lock lets any spinning thread win the race on release, so an unlucky thread can in principle be skipped indefinitely.

cards.prompt: A test-and-set spin lock and a ticket lock both provide mutual exclusion correctly. What does the ticket lock add that the plain test-and-set lock does not guarantee?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 28 (Locks)

choices.text: FIFO fairness: threads acquire the lock in the order they arrived
Atomicity of the critical section's own instructions
The ability to work correctly on a single CPU
Zero CPU cost while a thread waits for the lock

cards.prompt: Explain what "spinning" costs on a single-CPU system specifically, and why an OS that puts a waiting thread to sleep instead (rather than spinning) can do better once more than a couple of threads contend for the same lock.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 28 (Locks)

cards.prompt: Used as a ___, a semaphore is initialized to 1: the first `sem_wait()` decrements it to 0 and proceeds, a second thread's `sem_wait()` decrements it to -1 and blocks, and `sem_post()` on release brings it back to 0, waking the waiter. This is exactly binary mutual-exclusion behavior, just expressed as a counting primitive.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 31 (Semaphores)
cards.answer: lock

cards.prompt: Why does starting a semaphore at 1 make wait/post behave like a lock's acquire/release?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 31 (Semaphores)
cards.answer: With an initial value of 1, exactly one thread's wait() can decrement it to 0 and proceed; any other thread's wait() drives the value negative and blocks, so only one thread is ever "inside," which is precisely mutual exclusion.

cards.prompt: Used as an ___, a semaphore is initialized to 0: a thread that must wait for some event calls `sem_wait()` and blocks immediately (since the value starts at 0 or below), while the thread that produces the event calls `sem_post()` when it happens. Whichever order the two threads actually run in, the semaphore itself records whether the event has already occurred.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 31 (Semaphores)
cards.answer: ordering primitive

cards.prompt: Why start an ordering semaphore at 0 rather than 1, when signaling one event?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 31 (Semaphores)
cards.answer: Starting at 0 means a waiter that arrives before the event blocks immediately, and a poster that arrives first leaves the semaphore at a positive count so a later waiter proceeds without blocking — either arrival order is handled correctly, which is what "ordering" rather than "exclusion" requires.

cards.prompt: Why must a producer wait on the empty-slots semaphore before waiting on the mutex, not after?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 31 (Semaphores)
cards.answer: Waiting on mutex first while empty is 0 would hold the buffer's lock while blocked, so a consumer could never acquire mutex to remove an item and free a slot — the two threads would deadlock waiting on each other.

cards.prompt: A semaphore used purely as a mutual-exclusion lock is initialized to what value?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 31 (Semaphores)

choices.text: The number of threads that will contend for it

cards.prompt: Explain why a semaphore, unlike a condition variable, does not lose a signal that happens before anyone is waiting — and why that matters for the producer/consumer pattern specifically.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 31 (Semaphores)

cards.prompt: Why is the order in which a preemptive scheduler runs two threads unpredictable?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 26 (Concurrency and Threads)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 27 (Thread API)
cards.answer: The scheduler (or a second CPU core) can switch between threads at almost any instruction boundary, so nothing guarantees that a thread's next line of code runs before another thread gets a turn once more than one thread is active.

cards.prompt: A ___ exists whenever a program's result depends on the timing or interleaving of multiple threads, rather than on the program's logic alone.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 26 (Concurrency and Threads)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 27 (Thread API)
cards.answer: race condition

cards.prompt: The instructions that touch the shared resource — here, the three instructions around `counter` — form a ___: code that must not run in more than one thread at a time if the result is to stay correct.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 26 (Concurrency and Threads)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 27 (Thread API)
cards.answer: critical section

cards.prompt: What single property must a critical section guarantee to be safe under concurrent execution?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 26 (Concurrency and Threads)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 27 (Thread API)
cards.answer: Mutual exclusion — at most one thread executes the section at a time, so its reads and writes to the shared resource can never interleave with another thread's.

cards.prompt: Besides waiting for a thread to finish, what else can `pthread_join()` give the caller?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 26 (Concurrency and Threads)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 27 (Thread API)
cards.answer: The finished thread's return value, passed back through an output parameter the caller supplies.

cards.prompt: Two threads each run unsynchronized `counter++` once on a shared counter starting at 0. What are the possible final values?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 26 (Concurrency and Threads)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 27 (Thread API)

choices.text: 1 or 2, depending on how the three underlying instructions interleave
Always 2, because both increments are eventually applied in full
Always 1, because the second thread's write is always discarded
0, because the compiler serializes access to shared globals automatically

cards.prompt: Explain why running the exact same multi-threaded program twice can produce two different, each individually plausible, outputs, and why that makes concurrency bugs hard to reproduce and debug.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 26 (Concurrency and Threads)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 27 (Thread API)

cards.prompt: A crash between a file system's related writes (an inode update, a bitmap update, a data block write) can leave the disk in an ___ state, since only some of those writes may have actually completed before the crash.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 42 (Crash Consistency: FSCK and Journaling)
cards.answer: inconsistent

cards.prompt: One recovery strategy is ___: after a crash, scan every inode, bitmap, and directory on the whole disk and reconcile any inconsistencies found, using redundancy already present in the structures (like link counts) to guess the right fix.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 42 (Crash Consistency: FSCK and Journaling)
cards.answer: fsck

cards.prompt: Why does fsck not scale as disks grow into the terabyte range?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 42 (Crash Consistency: FSCK and Journaling)
cards.answer: Its recovery time is proportional to total disk size and inode count, regardless of how few writes were actually in flight at the moment of the crash, so a crash right after mount can trigger a scan lasting minutes to hours on a large disk.

cards.prompt: Explain why write-ahead journaling writes and commits a transaction to the journal BEFORE applying any of its changes to the file system's actual home locations, rather than the other way around.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 42 (Crash Consistency: FSCK and Journaling)

cards.prompt: Once a journaled transaction's changes are safely applied to their home locations, the file system performs a ___ and can then reclaim that transaction's journal space for future use.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 42 (Crash Consistency: FSCK and Journaling)
cards.answer: checkpoint

cards.prompt: After a crash, how does a journaling file system know which journal transactions to replay?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 42 (Crash Consistency: FSCK and Journaling)
cards.answer: Only transactions with a complete commit record are replayed; a transaction interrupted before its commit record was fully written is discarded, since it was never guaranteed durable in the first place.

cards.prompt: Journaling comes in two common flavors. ___ writes both a block's content and its metadata to the journal before writing them again to their home locations, doubling I/O for every changed block but protecting file content itself against a crash. Metadata-only journaling logs only metadata, writing data blocks directly to their home locations once, before the commit record — much cheaper, at the cost of a smaller window where a crash can leave stale (but not corrupt) data behind a valid pointer.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 42 (Crash Consistency: FSCK and Journaling)
cards.answer: Data journaling

cards.prompt: Journaling comes in two common flavors. Data journaling writes both a block's content and its metadata to the journal before writing them again to their home locations, doubling I/O for every changed block but protecting file content itself against a crash. ___ logs only metadata, writing data blocks directly to their home locations once, before the commit record — much cheaper, at the cost of a smaller window where a crash can leave stale (but not corrupt) data behind a valid pointer.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 42 (Crash Consistency: FSCK and Journaling)
cards.answer: Metadata-only journaling

cards.prompt: Why does data journaling write more total I/O than metadata-only journaling?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 42 (Crash Consistency: FSCK and Journaling)
cards.answer: Data journaling logs both file content and metadata to the journal, then writes both again to their home locations, doubling writes for every changed data block, while ordered journaling logs only metadata and lets data blocks be written once, directly, before the commit record.

cards.prompt: A file system uses metadata-only (ordered) journaling instead of full data journaling. What does it give up in exchange for less journal I/O?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 42 (Crash Consistency: FSCK and Journaling)

choices.text: A guarantee that a file's actual data content survives a crash unchanged, since only metadata is journaled
The ability to recover the directory structure at all after a crash
Any consistency guarantee whatsoever
The use of a journal — ordered journaling does not use one

cards.prompt: A ___ is a small value computed from a block's data so that a later mismatch between the stored value and a freshly recomputed one reveals the data changed, without needing to keep a full second copy of the block just to compare against.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 45 (Data Integrity and Protection)
cards.answer: checksum

cards.prompt: Why is silent (undetected) disk corruption more dangerous than a disk simply failing to respond?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 45 (Data Integrity and Protection)
cards.answer: A failed or unresponsive disk clearly signals a problem the OS can react to, while silent corruption returns data that reads back as valid but is actually wrong, so nothing above notices until, if ever, something explicitly checks it against a checksum or a redundant copy.

cards.prompt: A checksum alone can only ___ corruption, not repair it — recovering the correct bytes requires redundancy, such as a mirrored copy or a parity block, that a checksum by itself does not provide.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 45 (Data Integrity and Protection)
cards.answer: detect

cards.prompt: Why can't a mismatched checksum tell you what the correct original data was?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 45 (Data Integrity and Protection)
cards.answer: A checksum is a small, lossy summary derived from a whole block, so many different corrupted contents could still be consistent with observing a mismatch; it can only flag that something disagrees, not reconstruct the block it was originally computed from.

cards.prompt: Explain why a RAID array with parity can use a checksum mismatch to actually repair a corrupted block, not merely detect that it's wrong.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 45 (Data Integrity and Protection)

cards.prompt: ___ periodically reads every block on disk and checks its checksum, catching latent corruption early — before, say, a second disk fails during a RAID rebuild that depends on the surviving data actually being intact.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 45 (Data Integrity and Protection)
cards.answer: Scrubbing

cards.prompt: Why do systems scrub disks proactively instead of only checking checksums when data is read?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 45 (Data Integrity and Protection)
cards.answer: Some blocks may go unread for a long time, letting corruption sit undetected; if a later failure elsewhere (like another disk in a RAID array) depends on that stale block being intact, discovering the corruption only then is too late, so scrubbing surfaces it earlier while redundancy still exists to fix it.

cards.prompt: A RAID-5 array detects a checksum mismatch on one block during a read. What can it do that a single disk with only a checksum cannot?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 45 (Data Integrity and Protection)

choices.text: Reconstruct the correct data from parity and the other surviving disks in the stripe
Recompute the correct bytes directly from the mismatched checksum value alone
Nothing differently — checksums provide the same guarantee everywhere
Automatically know which bit flipped without consulting any redundant data

cards.prompt: FFS divides the disk into ___, each with its own inodes, bitmaps, and data blocks, instead of relying on one disk-wide inode table far away from the data it describes.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 41 (Locality and The Fast File System)
cards.answer: cylinder groups

cards.prompt: Why does keeping a file's inode and data blocks in the same cylinder group improve performance?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 41 (Locality and The Fast File System)
cards.answer: Reading a file means reading its inode and then its data blocks in short order; keeping both nearby means the disk head barely has to seek between the two, unlike a layout where the inode region sits physically far from the data region.

cards.prompt: FFS also places a new file's data, where possible, in the ___ as its parent directory, on the heuristic that files created together in one directory are often accessed together later too.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 41 (Locality and The Fast File System)
cards.answer: same cylinder group

cards.prompt: What tradeoff does FFS accept by keeping a large file confined to one cylinder group?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 41 (Locality and The Fast File System)
cards.answer: A very large file would eventually fill its group and force later allocations elsewhere regardless, so FFS spreads a big file's later chunks into new groups once one fills up, trading perfect locality for balanced use of space across the whole disk.

cards.prompt: Why does FFS deliberately leave a fraction of the disk unallocated?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 41 (Locality and The Fast File System)
cards.answer: FFS reserves roughly 10% of total space as headroom; letting a disk fill completely forces the allocator to scatter later writes across whatever scraps of free space remain, which destroys the very locality FFS is designed to preserve and degrades performance sharply as free space grows scarce.

cards.prompt: A workload creates thousands of small files, all inside one directory. What does FFS's placement policy do to help?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 41 (Locality and The Fast File System)

choices.text: Cluster those files' inodes and data in the same cylinder group as the directory, reducing seeks between them
Spread the files evenly across every cylinder group to balance disk wear
Keep all small files in RAM permanently instead of writing them to disk
Merge the small files into one large file transparently

cards.prompt: Explain why the original UNIX file system's placement policy caused fragmentation and heavy seeking over time, even though nothing about its individual allocation decisions was obviously wrong in isolation.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 41 (Locality and The Fast File System)

cards.prompt: The ___ is the first structure read when a file system is mounted; it holds file-system-wide metadata such as block size, total inode and block counts, and pointers to where the other regions begin.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 40 (File System Implementation)
cards.answer: superblock

cards.prompt: A ___ marks each inode or data block as free or in-use with a single bit, letting the allocator find free space by scanning for a 0 bit rather than maintaining a separate free list.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 40 (File System Implementation)
cards.answer: bitmap

cards.prompt: Why do inodes use indirect pointers instead of one flat block-pointer list?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 40 (File System Implementation)
cards.answer: A fixed-size inode can't hold enough direct pointers for large files, so an indirect pointer (a pointer to a block full of further pointers) adds one level of indirection, and a double-indirect pointer adds another; small files stay cheap with only direct pointers and one I/O, while large files reach far more blocks through progressively deeper indirection.

cards.prompt: Why do most inodes reserve room for several direct pointers before any indirect pointer?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 40 (File System Implementation)
cards.answer: Most files are small, so a handful of direct pointers lets small files' data be reached with zero extra indirection I/O; the indirect pointers only get consulted once a file's size outgrows that direct capacity.

cards.prompt: Why does opening a deeply nested path like /a/b/c.txt require several separate disk reads?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 40 (File System Implementation)
cards.answer: Each path component's directory must be read in turn to find the next component's inode number, so the OS walks the tree one directory-read (and inode-read) at a time rather than jumping straight to the final file.

cards.prompt: A file system needs to allocate a new data block for a growing file. What must it check first?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 40 (File System Implementation)

choices.text: The data bitmap, to find a block currently marked free
The superblock's block-size field, since block size changes on each allocation
The file's directory entry, since directories track free space
Nothing — the OS always appends at the next unused disk address

cards.prompt: Explain why reading even a single, small file can require multiple distinct disk I/Os, even though the file's own data fits in one block.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 40 (File System Implementation)

cards.prompt: A file descriptor returned by ___ is just a small integer index into a per-process table pointing at an open-file entry — it is not the file's contents, and two descriptors can point at independent positions within the same underlying file.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 39 (Files and Directories)
cards.answer: open()

cards.prompt: Why doesn't write() guarantee data has reached disk when it returns?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 39 (Files and Directories)
cards.answer: The OS typically buffers writes in memory (the page cache) and flushes them to disk later for performance, so a successful write() only guarantees the data is queued; fsync() (or similar) is needed to force it to durable storage before the call returns.

cards.prompt: A directory is not a special data structure at the file-system level — it is just a file whose contents are a list of ___ pairs, which is why directory operations (create, rename, list) are really just reads and writes of an ordinary file's data.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 39 (Files and Directories)
cards.answer: (name, inode number)

cards.prompt: What actually gets removed when unlink() is called on a file with one remaining hard link?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 39 (Files and Directories)
cards.answer: Its directory entry is removed, and because the inode's link count then drops to zero, the inode and its data blocks are freed; if other hard links still point at the same inode, the data survives untouched.

cards.prompt: A file has two hard links, `a` and `b`, both pointing at the same inode. `a` is deleted. What happens to the file's data?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 39 (Files and Directories)

choices.text: It remains fully accessible through `b`, since the inode's link count is still above zero
It's deleted immediately, since deleting any link deletes the underlying data
It becomes read-only until `b` is also deleted
A private copy is silently made for `b`

cards.prompt: Why can a symbolic link "dangle" in a way a hard link cannot?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 39 (Files and Directories)
cards.answer: A symlink stores a path string that is resolved fresh at access time, so if the target is deleted the symlink is left pointing at a name that no longer resolves; a hard link instead is another direct reference to the same inode, so it cannot outlive the data it names.

cards.prompt: Explain why a hard link and "the file it links to" are not actually distinguishable at the file-system level — why there is no original versus copy once both links exist.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 39 (Files and Directories)

cards.prompt: Flash memory can be read and written at ___ granularity but can only be erased at the larger block granularity (each such unit holds many pages), so overwriting even one of them in place would require first erasing — and therefore rewriting — the whole surrounding region.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 44 (Flash-based SSDs)
cards.answer: page

cards.prompt: Flash memory can be read and written at page granularity but can only be erased at the larger ___ granularity (each such unit holds many pages), so overwriting even one of them in place would require first erasing — and therefore rewriting — the whole surrounding region.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 44 (Flash-based SSDs)
cards.answer: block

cards.prompt: Why does an SSD write updates to a fresh page instead of overwriting in place?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 44 (Flash-based SSDs)
cards.answer: Overwriting in place would force erasing the whole containing block first, a comparatively slow operation, so instead the drive writes the new version to an already-erased page elsewhere and remaps the logical address to it, deferring the erase until garbage collection reclaims the old block later.

cards.prompt: The ___ maps the logical block addresses the OS uses to physical flash locations, hiding erase-before-write and block-level erase granularity from the file system entirely — to the OS, the SSD still looks like an ordinary block device.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 44 (Flash-based SSDs)
cards.answer: FTL

cards.prompt: Why does an SSD need internal garbage collection, like LFS's cleaner?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 44 (Flash-based SSDs)
cards.answer: The FTL's out-of-place writes leave old page versions behind as garbage inside blocks, just as LFS's segments do, so the FTL needs its own background process to reclaim blocks by copying any still-live pages forward before erasing them.

cards.prompt: Explain why wear levelling is necessary, given that each flash block can survive only a limited number of program/erase cycles before it becomes unreliable.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 44 (Flash-based SSDs)

cards.prompt: Without ___, an FTL that kept reusing the same handful of free blocks would wear those specific blocks out to failure long before the rest of the drive's capacity was ever touched, even though plenty of usable life remained elsewhere on the drive.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 44 (Flash-based SSDs)
cards.answer: wear levelling

cards.prompt: What does "write amplification" mean for an SSD?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 44 (Flash-based SSDs)
cards.answer: The ratio of physical flash writes actually performed to the logical writes the host requested; garbage collection copying live pages out of a block, plus erasing the whole block to reclaim only a fraction of dead pages in it, both add physical writes beyond what the host asked for.

cards.prompt: An OS issues one small logical write to an SSD. Why might the SSD perform noticeably more physical write and erase work than that single logical write implies?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 44 (Flash-based SSDs)

choices.text: Garbage collection may copy live pages out of the target block and erase the whole block before it can be reused, amplifying one logical write into several physical operations
SSDs always write every logical write to every block for redundancy
The FTL requires the OS to explicitly request a separate erase command for every write
Flash pages are always physically larger than the write, wasting the unused remainder

cards.prompt: A single disk access has three components: ___ (move the arm to the target track), rotational latency (wait for the target sector to spin under the head), and transfer time (actually read or write once positioned). Seek and rotation are pure overhead paid before any useful data moves.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 37 (Hard Disk Drives)
cards.answer: seek time

cards.prompt: Why is sequential access on a disk far faster than random access to the same amount of data?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 37 (Hard Disk Drives)
cards.answer: Sequential access pays one seek and one rotational wait, then streams many contiguous sectors in a row; random access pays a fresh seek and rotational wait for nearly every block, and those mechanical delays dwarf the time actually spent transferring data.

cards.prompt: The ___ scheduler always services the pending request closest to the disk head's current position. It minimizes seek distance greedily, but a steady stream of nearby requests can keep pushing a distant request to the back indefinitely.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 37 (Hard Disk Drives)
cards.answer: SSTF

cards.prompt: How does the elevator (SCAN) algorithm avoid the starvation SSTF can cause?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 37 (Hard Disk Drives)
cards.answer: It sweeps the head in one direction, servicing every request in its path in position order, then reverses at the far end and sweeps back, so any single request's maximum wait is bounded by one sweep instead of being pushed back indefinitely by closer arrivals.

cards.prompt: Why might a disk report a write done before data reaches the platter?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 37 (Hard Disk Drives)
cards.answer: A disk with an on-board write-back cache can acknowledge a write as soon as it lands in that volatile buffer, trading a small window of vulnerability (power loss before the buffer flushes) for lower perceived write latency.

cards.prompt: A workload issues many small requests to scattered locations, arriving continuously. Compared with pure SSTF, what does SCAN most directly improve?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 37 (Hard Disk Drives)

choices.text: Bounded worst-case wait for far-away requests, since the sweep must eventually reach them
Total seek distance, which SCAN always makes smaller than SSTF
Rotational latency, which SCAN eliminates entirely
Transfer time per request, which SCAN halves on average

cards.prompt: Explain why disk scheduling can change total service time even though the same requests eventually get serviced and the same data is read or written either way.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 37 (Hard Disk Drives)

cards.prompt: The simplest way to drive a device is ___: repeatedly read the status register in a loop until it reports the device is ready. That's simple but wastes CPU cycles spinning while a slow device does its work.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 36 (I/O Devices)
cards.answer: polling

cards.prompt: Why do fast devices sometimes perform better with polling than with interrupts?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 36 (I/O Devices)
cards.answer: An interrupt costs a context switch and trap-handling overhead; if a device usually finishes before that overhead would even be paid, briefly polling is cheaper than triggering, delivering, and dispatching an interrupt for a result that was already ready by the time it arrived.

cards.prompt: On completion, a slower device instead raises ___, a hardware signal that traps the CPU into a pre-registered handler, letting the CPU run other work while waiting rather than spinning on a status register.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 36 (I/O Devices)
cards.answer: an interrupt

cards.prompt: Why do high-throughput devices batch interrupts instead of firing one each?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 36 (I/O Devices)
cards.answer: Interrupt handling carries a fixed per-interrupt cost (trap, register save, handler dispatch), so coalescing many completed operations into one interrupt amortizes that fixed cost across all of them, at the price of delaying notification for whichever operation finished first.

cards.prompt: Without ___, the CPU itself must copy every byte of a large transfer between a device and memory through the data register, one word at a time — wasteful for anything beyond a few bytes.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 36 (I/O Devices)
cards.answer: DMA

cards.prompt: What does a DMA controller let the CPU skip during a large data transfer?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 36 (I/O Devices)
cards.answer: The OS hands the DMA controller a source, destination, and length, and the controller moves the data between device and memory on its own, interrupting the CPU only once when the whole transfer completes rather than once per word copied.

cards.prompt: A disk request takes 5ms to complete, and handling an interrupt costs about 2 microseconds of overhead. Which approach best uses the CPU while waiting?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 36 (I/O Devices)

choices.text: Interrupt-driven waiting, so the CPU can run other work during the 5ms
Busy-wait polling, since 5ms is a short amount of time
DMA instead of interrupts, since DMA replaces interrupt-driven waiting entirely
Disabling the device driver until the device signals readiness on its own
