cards.prompt: Explain why polling and interrupts are not mutually exclusive strategies, and why a driver might deliberately poll for a short window before arming an interrupt instead of committing to one approach.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 36 (I/O Devices)

cards.prompt: LFS buffers writes in memory and flushes them together as one large ___ write, turning many small, scattered updates into a single efficient streaming write to the next free region of disk.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 43 (Log-structured File Systems)
cards.answer: sequential

cards.prompt: Why can't LFS simply update an inode in place, the way FFS does?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 43 (Log-structured File Systems)
cards.answer: Updating in place would mean seeking back to that inode's old, fixed disk location on every write, reintroducing exactly the random-access cost LFS exists to avoid; instead LFS writes the updated inode to whatever the next free spot in the current write happens to be.

cards.prompt: Because inodes move on every update, LFS adds an ___ translating inode numbers to their current on-disk location — itself written to the log rather than kept at one fixed spot.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 43 (Log-structured File Systems)
cards.answer: inode map (imap)

cards.prompt: Why must even the imap itself avoid a single fixed disk location?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 43 (Log-structured File Systems)
cards.answer: A fixed imap location would need an in-place update on every write, the exact random-access cost LFS was built to eliminate; so LFS logs imap updates too, and keeps only a small, fixed checkpoint region to bootstrap finding the current imap after a restart.

cards.prompt: Explain why old versions of overwritten blocks are left behind as "dead" data in earlier parts of the log, rather than being erased immediately at the moment a newer version is written.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 43 (Log-structured File Systems)

cards.prompt: A background ___ process identifies segments holding mostly dead blocks, copies their few remaining live blocks forward into a fresh segment, and frees the old segment for reuse.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 43 (Log-structured File Systems)
cards.answer: cleaner

cards.prompt: Why does cleaning cost more as a segment's fraction of live data increases?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 43 (Log-structured File Systems)
cards.answer: A mostly-dead segment yields a lot of reclaimed space for very little copying, but a mostly-live segment forces the cleaner to read and rewrite almost as much data as it frees, so cleaning nearly-full segments has poor amortized efficiency compared to cleaning mostly-empty ones.

cards.prompt: LFS just finished writing several updated blocks. Where does it place a data block belonging to a file whose inode lives at a completely different disk location?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 43 (Log-structured File Systems)

choices.text: Wherever the current write's next free slot is — LFS never seeks back to a fixed home location for an update
At the exact same offset the block held before, overwriting it in place
In a fixed region reserved per file, adjacent to nothing else
Immediately next to the inode, regardless of where the current log write is

cards.prompt: ___ stripes data across disks with no redundancy at all: it gains capacity and parallel performance, but tolerates zero disk failures — losing any one drive loses data, since no other disk holds a copy or a way to reconstruct it.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 38 (RAID)
cards.answer: RAID-0

cards.prompt: Why does RAID-1 (mirroring) cost the most usable capacity among common RAID levels?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 38 (RAID)
cards.answer: Every block is written twice, to two separate disks, so exactly half of the raw capacity across the array is ever usable no matter how many mirrored pairs are added.

cards.prompt: ___ dedicates one disk entirely to parity, computed across the corresponding blocks on the other disks. Because every write must also update that one parity disk, it becomes a bottleneck whenever writes happen concurrently, even though the data disks themselves could be written in parallel.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 38 (RAID)
cards.answer: RAID-4

cards.prompt: How does RAID-5 fix RAID-4's parity-disk bottleneck without adding disks?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 38 (RAID)
cards.answer: RAID-5 rotates which physical disk holds parity from one stripe to the next instead of dedicating a single disk to it, so parity writes are spread across every drive and no one disk absorbs the write load of the whole array.

cards.prompt: RAID-5 tolerates exactly ___ disk failure per stripe: losing a second disk before the array finishes rebuilding from the first loses data, because a stripe's parity can only reconstruct a single missing block, not two.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 38 (RAID)
cards.answer: one

cards.prompt: What does RAID-6 add over RAID-5, and what does that buy?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 38 (RAID)
cards.answer: A second, independently computed parity block per stripe, so the array can reconstruct data even when any two disks fail at the same time, not just one.

cards.prompt: A RAID-5 array has one failed disk and is mid-rebuild when a second disk fails before the rebuild finishes. What happens?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 38 (RAID)

choices.text: Data is lost — RAID-5's single parity block can only recover from one failure per stripe
The array keeps running normally using the remaining parity
RAID-5 automatically reconfigures itself into RAID-6 to absorb the second failure
Only the blocks written during the rebuild window are lost; the rest survive

cards.prompt: Explain the "small write problem" in parity-based RAID (RAID-4 and RAID-5): why updating a single data block requires more disk I/O than simply writing that one block would on its own.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 38 (RAID)

cards.prompt: Why can't the OS fix a process's address space at one physical location forever?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 13 (Address Spaces)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 14 (Interlude: Memory API)
cards.answer: Multiple processes are being run and swapped in and out of physical memory over time, and each one thinks it owns address zero, so the OS needs the freedom to place (and later move) a process's data anywhere in physical RAM without the process's own code having to change.

cards.prompt: Conventionally, the heap is drawn growing ___ from just above the code and static data, while the stack grows upward from the top of the address space — leaving unused space between them that either region can claim as it grows, without a fixed boundary between them.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 13 (Address Spaces)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 14 (Interlude: Memory API)
cards.answer: downward

cards.prompt: Conventionally, the heap is drawn growing downward from just above the code and static data, while the stack grows ___ from the top of the address space — leaving unused space between them that either region can claim as it grows, without a fixed boundary between them.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 13 (Address Spaces)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 14 (Interlude: Memory API)
cards.answer: upward

cards.prompt: Why does free() need no size argument even though malloc() does?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 13 (Address Spaces)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 14 (Interlude: Memory API)
cards.answer: The allocator stores each block's size as metadata alongside the block itself (commonly just before the returned pointer), so free() can look up how much to reclaim from that bookkeeping rather than requiring the caller to remember and pass it back.

cards.prompt: A program calls `free(p)` and then, later in the same function, reads through `p` again without reallocating it. What kind of bug is this?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 13 (Address Spaces)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 14 (Interlude: Memory API)

choices.text: A memory leak
A dangling pointer (use-after-free)
A double allocation
A stack overflow

cards.prompt: Explain why a long-running server process is far more vulnerable to slow memory leaks than a short command-line utility that runs once and exits, even though both have the same kind of bug in their code.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 13 (Address Spaces)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 14 (Interlude: Memory API)

cards.prompt: The simplest scheme is dynamic relocation using a pair of hardware registers: the CPU has a ___ register holding where this process's memory starts in physical RAM, and a bounds register holding the size of that region. A virtual address is translated by adding that starting offset, and the hardware checks the address against the size limit first to catch out-of-range accesses.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 15 (Address Translation)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 16 (Segmentation)
cards.answer: base

cards.prompt: The simplest scheme is dynamic relocation using a pair of hardware registers: the CPU has a base register holding where this process's memory starts in physical RAM, and a ___ register holding the size of that region. A virtual address is translated by adding that starting offset, and the hardware checks the address against the size limit first to catch out-of-range accesses.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 15 (Address Translation)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 16 (Segmentation)
cards.answer: bounds

cards.prompt: Why is a bounds check needed even though the base register already relocates addresses?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 15 (Address Translation)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 16 (Segmentation)
cards.answer: Without a bounds check, a process could generate a virtual address larger than its own address space and, after the base is added, land inside another process's memory or unallocated physical memory — the bounds check is what turns relocation into isolation.

cards.prompt: How does segmentation avoid wasting the gap between a small heap and the stack?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 15 (Address Translation)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 16 (Segmentation)
cards.answer: Because the stack is its own segment with its own base and bounds, the OS only needs to allocate physical memory for the segments actually in use and their current sizes, not for a single contiguous span that has to cover the gap between an unrelated heap and stack.

cards.prompt: A system uses segmentation with separate code, heap, and stack segments. What new fragmentation problem does this introduce that plain base-and-bounds did not have?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 15 (Address Translation)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 16 (Segmentation)

choices.text: Internal fragmentation within a single segment
External fragmentation across free chunks of physical memory
Fragmentation of the CPU's register file
Fragmentation only affects the code segment

cards.prompt: Explain why a bounds violation should trap into the OS rather than the hardware simply refusing the access silently — what does the OS need to do with that information?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 15 (Address Translation)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 16 (Segmentation)

cards.prompt: Free-space allocators commonly track free chunks with a ___, a linked structure threaded through the free chunks themselves — each free chunk's header doubles as a list node, which is why free chunks need to be at least large enough to hold that header.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 17 (Free-Space Management)
cards.answer: free list

cards.prompt: Why does best fit, despite its name, often perform worse in practice than it sounds like it should?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 17 (Free-Space Management)
cards.answer: Best fit tends to leave behind many tiny, barely-usable leftover slivers (the chunk chosen is only just big enough, so the remainder after splitting is often too small to satisfy future requests), and a full linear scan of the free list to find the best chunk is also slow.

cards.prompt: What operation reverses splitting, and why does an allocator need to perform it?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 17 (Free-Space Management)
cards.answer: Coalescing merges two adjacent free chunks back into one larger free chunk when a block is freed and it happens to sit next to another already-free block; without coalescing, a system could accumulate many small, adjacent free fragments that could have combined into a block big enough for a large future request.

cards.prompt: Fragmentation itself comes in two distinct flavors worth keeping apart. ___ fragmentation is space wasted inside an allocated chunk because it is bigger than what was requested (as buddy allocation's rounding causes), while external fragmentation is space wasted between allocated chunks, scattered across many free fragments none of which individually fits the next request.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 17 (Free-Space Management)
cards.answer: Internal

cards.prompt: An allocator uses buddy allocation. A caller requests 12KB from a system where blocks are always powers of two. What is the main cost of this scheme?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 17 (Free-Space Management)

choices.text: External fragmentation from scattered chunk sizes
Internal fragmentation from rounding requests up to the next power of two
O(n) search time through the whole free list
Inability to ever coalesce freed memory

cards.prompt: Explain why external fragmentation cannot be fully solved just by choosing a cleverer placement strategy (best fit, worst fit, first fit) among fixed free chunks, and what compaction would have to do instead.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 17 (Free-Space Management)

cards.prompt: The hardware provides two privilege levels. In ___, code cannot directly issue privileged instructions (like ones that touch disk or reconfigure the MMU) — attempting one causes the hardware to trap into the OS instead. In kernel mode, the OS itself runs with full access to the hardware. A process's normal code always runs at that lower privilege level.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 6 (Limited Direct Execution)
cards.answer: user mode

cards.prompt: The hardware provides two privilege levels. In user mode, code cannot directly issue privileged instructions (like ones that touch disk or reconfigure the MMU) — attempting one causes the hardware to trap into the OS instead. In ___, the OS itself runs with full access to the hardware. A process's normal code always runs at that lower privilege level.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 6 (Limited Direct Execution)
cards.answer: kernel mode

cards.prompt: How does a user-mode process ask the OS to perform a privileged operation, such as reading a file?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 6 (Limited Direct Execution)
cards.answer: It executes a system call, a special trap instruction; the trap saves the caller's register state and jumps to a fixed, OS-defined entry point in kernel mode, so the process cannot jump into arbitrary kernel code, only through the sanctioned entry.

cards.prompt: Why must only the OS be allowed to configure the trap table, and never a user process?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 6 (Limited Direct Execution)
cards.answer: If a user process could set the trap handler address, it could point a system call trap at its own code and have that code run with full kernel privilege, defeating the entire protection scheme.

cards.prompt: A single trap into the kernel isn't enough to keep control forever, though — a process could simply never make a system call and monopolize the CPU. The classic fix is a ___: hardware raises an interrupt at a fixed interval regardless of what the process is doing, forcing a trap back into the OS, which can then decide whether to keep running this process or switch to another. This is what makes preemptive scheduling possible without cooperation from the program being interrupted.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 6 (Limited Direct Execution)
cards.answer: timer interrupt

cards.prompt: A process is running an infinite loop with no system calls and no I/O. What lets the OS regain control of the CPU?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 6 (Limited Direct Execution)

choices.text: The process's next system call
The scheduler polling the process's state
A periodic timer interrupt forcing a trap into the OS
The compiler inserting yield calls automatically

cards.prompt: Why does "return-from-trap" not necessarily resume the same process that trapped into the kernel?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 6 (Limited Direct Execution)
cards.answer: Between the trap and the return, the OS's scheduler is free to swap in a different process's saved register state, so the trap and the eventual return-from-trap can belong to two different processes even though they are the same hardware instruction pair.

cards.prompt: Explain why direct execution alone (running a program straight on the CPU with no traps or timer interrupts) is unsafe for a multiprogrammed OS, even though it is the fastest possible way to run code.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 6 (Limited Direct Execution)

cards.prompt: The base rules: a higher-priority queue always runs before a lower one, and jobs on the same queue share the CPU in round robin. To decide how priority changes over time, MLFQ tracks a job's ___: the amount of CPU time it may use at its current priority level before being demoted one queue.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 8 (Multi-Level Feedback Queue)
cards.answer: allotment

cards.prompt: Why does a job entering the system start at the highest-priority queue rather than the lowest?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 8 (Multi-Level Feedback Queue)
cards.answer: The scheduler has no information yet about whether the job is short and interactive or long and CPU-bound, so it optimistically assumes short/interactive first; a truly short job finishes quickly from there, while a long job reveals itself by using up its allotment and sinking down.

cards.prompt: How can a process game a naive MLFQ that resets allotment on voluntary yield?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 8 (Multi-Level Feedback Queue)
cards.answer: The process can issue a near-instant I/O request just before its allotment runs out, over and over, so it never gets demoted despite consuming nearly all of the CPU's time — it "relinquishes" just often enough to stay parked at the top queue.

cards.prompt: What mechanism keeps a long-running, low-priority MLFQ job from starving?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 8 (Multi-Level Feedback Queue)
cards.answer: A periodic priority boost: after a fixed time period S, every job in the system — regardless of current queue — is moved back to the topmost queue, giving starved long-running jobs a fresh chance to run again.

cards.prompt: The priority-boost interval S is set far too long for the workload. What is the most likely symptom?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 8 (Multi-Level Feedback Queue)

choices.text: Long-running jobs starve for extended stretches before being boosted
Short jobs never get to run at all
The scheduler degenerates into pure FIFO immediately
Context-switch overhead disappears entirely

cards.prompt: Explain why MLFQ counts as "learning from history to predict the future," and describe one way that strategy can backfire if a job's behavior changes partway through its life.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 8 (Multi-Level Feedback Queue)

cards.prompt: Why do multi-level page tables use less memory than a single-level table?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 20 (Paging: Smaller Tables)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 21 (Beyond Physical Memory: Mechanisms)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 22 (Beyond Physical Memory: Policies)
cards.answer: An entire region of the address space that is unused doesn't need its second-level page table allocated at all — the page directory entry for that region can simply be marked invalid, so memory is only spent on page-table chunks that actually cover pages the process is using.

cards.prompt: Swapping extends virtual memory beyond what physical RAM can hold, by using disk (or, in modern systems, flash) as a backing store for pages that don't currently fit in RAM. The OS designates a region of the disk as ___, and a page not currently resident in physical memory is instead written out there.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 20 (Paging: Smaller Tables)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 21 (Beyond Physical Memory: Mechanisms)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 22 (Beyond Physical Memory: Policies)
cards.answer: swap space

cards.prompt: What happens on a page fault for a valid page currently swapped out to disk?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 20 (Paging: Smaller Tables)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 21 (Beyond Physical Memory: Mechanisms)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 22 (Beyond Physical Memory: Policies)
cards.answer: The OS's page-fault handler reads the page's location from the PTE, finds (or evicts something to make) a free physical frame, reads the page's contents in from disk into that frame, updates the PTE to point at the new frame and mark it present, and then retries the faulting instruction.

cards.prompt: Why do real systems use the clock algorithm instead of exact LRU?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 20 (Paging: Smaller Tables)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 21 (Beyond Physical Memory: Mechanisms)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 22 (Beyond Physical Memory: Policies)
cards.answer: Exact LRU would require updating bookkeeping on every memory reference, which is far too costly to do at hardware speed; the clock algorithm instead relies on a cheap hardware-set "use" bit per page and periodic sweeps, trading precision for something actually affordable to run.

cards.prompt: Physical memory is nearly full and every running process's active pages together exceed it. What is this condition called?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 20 (Paging: Smaller Tables)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 21 (Beyond Physical Memory: Mechanisms)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 22 (Beyond Physical Memory: Policies)

choices.text: Internal fragmentation
A TLB miss storm
Thrashing
Priority inversion

cards.prompt: Explain why the optimal page-replacement policy (evict what's used furthest in the future) is useful even though no real OS can implement it directly.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 20 (Paging: Smaller Tables)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 21 (Beyond Physical Memory: Mechanisms)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 22 (Beyond Physical Memory: Policies)

cards.prompt: A virtual address is split into a ___ (VPN), which selects an entry in the process's page table, and a page offset, which is left unchanged by translation because it just locates a byte within the page — only the page number needs to be translated, not the offset.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 18 (Paging: Introduction)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 19 (Paging: Faster Translations (TLBs))
cards.answer: virtual page number

cards.prompt: Why does a page table need a valid bit, given sparse address spaces?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 18 (Paging: Introduction)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 19 (Paging: Faster Translations (TLBs))
cards.answer: Most address spaces are sparse (a small amount of used memory in a huge virtual range), so allocating a PTE only marks pages actually in use as valid; an access to an unmapped page's still-present-but-invalid PTE traps to the OS instead of silently succeeding against garbage.

cards.prompt: What hardware structure avoids a full page-table walk on every memory access?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 18 (Paging: Introduction)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 19 (Paging: Faster Translations (TLBs))
cards.answer: The TLB (translation lookaside buffer), a small hardware cache of recently used virtual-to-physical page translations sitting inside (or next to) the CPU; a TLB hit supplies the frame number in one cycle, skipping the memory access to the page table entirely.

cards.prompt: Who refills a TLB entry after a miss on a software-managed TLB, and how?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 18 (Paging: Introduction)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 19 (Paging: Faster Translations (TLBs))
cards.answer: The OS does: the hardware traps into a miss handler, which walks the OS's own page-table structure and installs the new translation using privileged instructions, then the faulting instruction is retried.

cards.prompt: Why does switching between processes risk invalidating the TLB's cached entries?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 18 (Paging: Introduction)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 19 (Paging: Faster Translations (TLBs))
cards.answer: TLB entries map virtual addresses to physical frames for one specific address space, so after a context switch the previous process's cached translations are meaningless (or, worse, wrong) for the new process's virtual addresses, unless the TLB tags entries with a process/address-space id to keep multiple processes' translations valid at once.

cards.prompt: A process has excellent temporal locality but the TLB is very small relative to its working set. What is the most likely consequence?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 18 (Paging: Introduction)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 19 (Paging: Faster Translations (TLBs))

choices.text: Frequent TLB misses forcing repeated page-table walks
The page table itself becomes unnecessary
Internal fragmentation increases sharply
The valid bit is checked less often

cards.prompt: Explain why fixed-size pages eliminate external fragmentation compared to segmentation, and what kind of fragmentation paging can still leave behind.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 18 (Paging: Introduction)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 19 (Paging: Faster Translations (TLBs))

cards.prompt: The OS tracks a process's status internally, typically as one of three states: it is ___ when its instructions are actually executing on a CPU, ready when it could run but the OS has chosen another process instead, and blocked when it cannot run until some event (such as an I/O completion) occurs, even if a CPU is free.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 4 (Processes)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 5 (Process API)
cards.answer: running

cards.prompt: The OS tracks a process's status internally, typically as one of three states: it is running when its instructions are actually executing on a CPU, ___ when it could run but the OS has chosen another process instead, and blocked when it cannot run until some event (such as an I/O completion) occurs, even if a CPU is free.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 4 (Processes)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 5 (Process API)
cards.answer: ready

cards.prompt: The OS tracks a process's status internally, typically as one of three states: it is running when its instructions are actually executing on a CPU, ready when it could run but the OS has chosen another process instead, and ___ when it cannot run until some event (such as an I/O completion) occurs, even if a CPU is free.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 4 (Processes)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 5 (Process API)
cards.answer: blocked

cards.prompt: Why can't a blocked process simply be given the CPU when it becomes the highest-priority job?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 4 (Processes)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 5 (Process API)
cards.answer: A blocked process is waiting on an event outside the CPU's control (e.g., a disk read); running it would not make progress, so the OS leaves it off the ready pool until the event fires and moves it to ready.

cards.prompt: Why does fork() return a different value in the parent than in the child?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 4 (Processes)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 5 (Process API)
cards.answer: fork() returns the child's process ID to the parent and 0 to the child, so the same post-fork code can branch on the return value to run different logic in each process even though both start from the identical point in the program.

cards.prompt: Why split process creation into fork() then exec() instead of one spawn call?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 4 (Processes)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 5 (Process API)
cards.answer: Splitting them lets the shell run code between the fork and the exec, in the child only — for example redirecting a file descriptor or setting up a pipe — before the child's image is replaced by the target program, which a single combined call could not support.

cards.prompt: A parent calls `wait()` right after `fork()`. What is the parent waiting for?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 4 (Processes)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 5 (Process API)

choices.text: The child to call exec()
The child to terminate, so the parent can reap its exit status
The scheduler to grant the parent another time slice
The child to release its file descriptors

cards.prompt: Explain why an OS needs `wait()` at all — what would go wrong for the parent, or for the system's process table, if a parent never collected a terminated child's exit status?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 4 (Processes)
Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 5 (Process API)

cards.prompt: Lottery scheduling implements this with randomness. Each job holds some number of ___, and on every scheduling decision the scheduler draws a random winning ticket and runs whichever job holds it — a job with twice as many as another wins (and thus runs) about twice as often, in expectation, over many draws.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 9 (Scheduling: Proportional Share)
cards.answer: tickets

cards.prompt: Why is lottery scheduling only probabilistically fair over short intervals?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 9 (Scheduling: Proportional Share)
cards.answer: Because the winner is chosen by drawing a random ticket each time, short runs can deviate from the target ratio purely by chance (e.g., a low-ticket job could win several draws in a row); the guarantee only holds as a long-run average, by the law of large numbers.

cards.prompt: Which job does stride scheduling pick to run next?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 9 (Scheduling: Proportional Share)
cards.answer: The scheduler always picks whichever runnable job currently has the lowest accumulated pass value, then adds that job's stride to its pass value — since a high-ticket job's stride is small, its pass value climbs slowly, so it gets picked more often.

cards.prompt: Linux's CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler) takes a related but distinct approach: instead of tickets, it tracks each runnable process's ___, virtual runtime, which increases as the process consumes CPU time, and always runs whichever runnable process currently has the lowest such value — approximating an ideal where every process's virtual runtime advances at the same rate.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 9 (Scheduling: Proportional Share)
cards.answer: vruntime

cards.prompt: How does CFS use "nice" values to give some processes a larger share of the CPU than others?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 9 (Scheduling: Proportional Share)
cards.answer: A process's nice value sets a weight that scales how fast its vruntime accumulates per unit of real CPU time — a higher-priority (lower nice) process's vruntime grows more slowly for the same work, so it appears to have run "less" and gets picked again sooner.

cards.prompt: Two jobs run under lottery scheduling: A has 100 tickets, B has 300 tickets (400 total). What is B's expected long-run share of the CPU?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 9 (Scheduling: Proportional Share)

choices.text: 100%, since it holds the most tickets

cards.prompt: Explain why stride scheduling can reproduce lottery scheduling's target ratios with far less short-term variance, given that both are driven by the same underlying ticket counts.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 9 (Scheduling: Proportional Share)

cards.prompt: Why can a scheduler that is excellent for turnaround time be terrible for response time?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 7 (Scheduling: Introduction)
cards.answer: Optimizing turnaround favors running whichever job finishes soonest to completion without interruption, but that can force an interactive job to wait behind a long job's entire run before it is ever touched, producing a long response time even though total turnaround looks good on average.

cards.prompt: What is the "convoy effect" in FIFO scheduling?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 7 (Scheduling: Introduction)
cards.answer: A short, quick job gets queued behind a long-running job that arrived slightly earlier, so many short jobs collectively wait on one long one, inflating average turnaround time well beyond what the jobs' own lengths would justify.

cards.prompt: STCF optimizes for turnaround time but is bad for ___ under a steady stream of arrivals, because it always favors whichever job has the least remaining time — so a job still waiting for its first turn can keep getting bumped by newer, shorter jobs indefinitely, and can starve outright, even while STCF's average turnaround time looks excellent.
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 7 (Scheduling: Introduction)
cards.answer: response time

cards.prompt: Why does an overly short RR time slice hurt performance despite better response time?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 7 (Scheduling: Introduction)
cards.answer: A very short time slice means the fixed cost of a context switch (saving and restoring register state, flushing caches/TLB entries) happens far more often relative to useful work done, so switching overhead starts to dominate and total throughput drops.

cards.prompt: Jobs A (100ms), B (10ms), C (10ms) all arrive at time 0 and run under FIFO in that order. Which policy would give B and C the best average turnaround time here?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 7 (Scheduling: Introduction)

choices.text: FIFO, unchanged
SJF, running B and C before A
Round robin with a 50ms time slice
Running A first always minimizes turnaround for all three

cards.prompt: Explain why no single scheduling policy can simultaneously minimize average turnaround time and minimize average response time for a mixed workload of long and short jobs — what is the fundamental tension?
citations: Arpaci-Dusseau, OSTEP, Ch. 7 (Scheduling: Introduction)

cards.prompt: A rigid body has zero net external torque about its center of mass but a nonzero net external force acting on it. What can you conclude?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 11

choices.text: Its angular momentum about the center of mass is conserved, but its linear momentum is not — the two conservation laws have independent hypotheses (net torque vs. net force)
Neither angular nor linear momentum is conserved, since a net force must produce a net torque
Both are conserved, since the body is rigid
This situation is physically impossible

cards.prompt: Why is it possible for a system to have zero net external torque about some axis while still having a nonzero net external force acting on it?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 11
cards.answer: Torque depends on both the force and the lever arm — where the force is applied relative to the axis, through $rF\sin(\theta)$. A force whose line of action passes through the axis (zero lever arm, or $\theta = 0$) contributes zero torque about that axis regardless of its magnitude, yet it still contributes fully to the net force and would still change linear momentum. The two conservation laws are governed by genuinely different quantities.

cards.prompt: The **spinning skater** pulling their arms in is the canonical demonstration, and the mechanism is precise, not just qualitative: pulling the arms inward decreases the ___, and since no external torque acts (ignoring the small friction at the skate blades), $L = I\omega$ must stay constant, so $\omega$ has to increase to compensate.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 11
cards.answer: moment of inertia

cards.prompt: A skater spinning with arms outstretched pulls them in. Using $L = I\omega$, explain why the skater's angular velocity increases, and then explain what happens to the skater's rotational kinetic energy — and where that energy comes from or goes.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 11
cards.answer: Pulling the arms in decreases I (mass moves closer to the rotation axis). With no external torque, L = I*omega is constant, so a smaller I forces a larger omega. Rotational kinetic energy, (1/2)*I*omega^2, is not conserved here — it actually *increases*, because omega grows faster (as 1/I) than I shrinks. That extra energy isn't free: it comes from the mechanical work the skater's muscles do pulling the arms inward against the outward (centrifugal, in the rotating frame) tendency of the arms to stay out — angular momentum conservation says nothing about energy, only about L itself.

cards.prompt: Does an isolated system's angular momentum being conserved imply its rotational kinetic energy is also conserved?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 11
cards.answer: No. Angular momentum conservation follows from zero net external torque; kinetic energy is a completely separate bookkeeping that changes whenever any work is done, including internal work like a skater's muscles pulling their arms inward. The skater's KE_rot visibly increases even while L stays exactly fixed, showing the two are governed by unrelated conditions.

cards.prompt: Angular momentum is a vector, $L = I\omega$ pointing along the rotation axis by the right-hand rule, and this vector nature is why a rapidly spinning object — a bicycle wheel, a gyroscope — resists having its rotation axis reoriented: changing $L$'s *direction* requires a torque just as changing its magnitude does, via $\tau_{net} = dL/dt$ read as a vector equation. Apply a torque perpendicular to a spinning wheel's $L$ (trying to tip its axis over) and instead of tipping the way you pushed, the axis slowly sweeps sideways instead — a phenomenon called ___ — because $dL/dt$ points in the direction of the applied torque, not in the direction you tried to rotate the wheel.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 11
cards.answer: precession

cards.prompt: You try to tip over the axis of a fast-spinning gyroscope by pushing straight down on one end of its axle. What actually happens?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 11

choices.text: The axle sweeps sideways (precesses) instead of tipping down, because dL/dt points along the applied torque's direction, which is sideways, not along the push
The axle tips down exactly as pushed, since torque directly rotates the object about the torque's axis of application
Nothing happens, since a spinning gyroscope is immune to external torques
The gyroscope stops spinning

cards.prompt: Why does a planet speed up as it approaches the sun in its elliptical orbit, in terms of angular momentum?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 11
cards.answer: Gravity is a central force, always directed along the line to the sun, so it produces zero torque about the sun and the planet's angular momentum $L = r \times p$ about the sun is conserved throughout the orbit. As the planet's distance $r$ from the sun decreases near perihelion, conserving $L = mrv_{perp}$ requires the tangential speed to increase to compensate — the same $I\omega$ trade-off as the spinning skater, with $r$ playing the role of the lever arm.

cards.prompt: A car moves around a circular track at constant speed. Explain why it has a nonzero acceleration despite the speed never changing, and give the two equivalent formulas for the magnitude of that acceleration.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 6
cards.answer: Acceleration measures the rate of change of velocity, a vector, and velocity changes whenever direction changes — even at constant speed, the car's direction is changing continuously as it goes around the curve, so it has nonzero acceleration. That acceleration points toward the circle's center, with magnitude $a_c = v^2/r = \omega^2 r$.

cards.prompt: This is the note's central point: **centripetal force is not a fifth fundamental force.** It is simply the name given to whatever net force happens to point toward the center and produce that inward acceleration — which in real situations is supplied by tension, gravity, friction, or a normal force, depending on the setup. There is nothing pulling "outward" on the orbiting object itself; the outward pull you feel in a turning car is ___, an artifact of analyzing motion from inside the rotating, non-inertial frame, and it vanishes entirely once you switch to an inertial frame outside the car.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 6
cards.answer: fictitious

cards.prompt: A ball on a string is swung in a horizontal circle. What force supplies the centripetal force that keeps it moving in a circle?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 6

choices.text: The tension in the string, directed toward the center — there is no separate "centripetal force" beyond whichever real force points inward
A distinct centripetal force generated by the circular motion itself, in addition to the string's tension
The centrifugal force pushing the ball outward, balanced against tension
Gravity, since it is the only force acting on the ball besides tension

cards.prompt: Why is calling something "the centripetal force" different from naming a force like gravity or tension — what category of thing is it?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 6
cards.answer: It's a role, not a distinct type of force with its own source. "Centripetal" describes the direction and effect of whatever net real force (tension, gravity, friction, a normal force, or some combination) happens to be pointing toward the center of the circular path; it never appears as an extra term added on top of the real forces already in a free-body diagram.

cards.prompt: Two identical curves have the same radius: curve A is flat, curve B is banked and icy (essentially zero friction). At the banked curve's design speed, what supplies the centripetal force in each case?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 6

choices.text: Curve A: static friction alone. Curve B: a component of the normal force alone, requiring no friction at the design speed
Both rely entirely on friction, since only friction can point toward the center of a curve
Curve A: normal force. Curve B: friction, since banking removes the normal force's horizontal component
Neither needs any force, because uniform circular motion requires zero net force

cards.prompt: Why does $v_{min} = \sqrt{gr}$ represent the *minimum* speed at the top of a vertical loop rather than some other special value?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 6
cards.answer: Below that speed, gravity alone would be more than what's needed to supply the centripetal force at that radius, which is impossible for the track to compensate for (a track can only push, via normal force, never pull) — so the object would fall away from the circular path. At $v_{min}$, gravity exactly supplies the required centripetal force with the normal force at zero; at any higher speed, the track adds a positive normal force on top of gravity to supply the extra centripetal force needed.

cards.prompt: Why must the centripetal and tangential components of acceleration be treated as perpendicular contributions rather than added as scalars, for an object speeding up while moving along a circular path?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 6
cards.answer: Because they change different, independent aspects of the velocity vector — centripetal acceleration is always perpendicular to velocity and changes only its direction, while tangential acceleration is parallel to velocity and changes only its magnitude (speed). Since they point in perpendicular directions, the total acceleration is their vector sum, not a simple scalar sum of magnitudes.

cards.prompt: A ball of putty is thrown at a wall and sticks — a perfectly inelastic collision. Which quantity, if any, is conserved during the impact?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 9

choices.text: Momentum of the ball-wall(-Earth) system, but not kinetic energy
Kinetic energy, but not momentum
Both momentum and kinetic energy
Neither — "inelastic" means nothing is conserved

cards.prompt: A **perfectly inelastic** collision is the opposite extreme: the bodies ___ and move off with one common velocity afterward.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 9
cards.answer: stick together

cards.prompt: Why is a perfectly inelastic collision, where the bodies stick together, the case of *maximum* kinetic energy loss rather than some intermediate case?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 9
cards.answer: Momentum conservation fixes the total momentum after the collision, but not how it's divided between the bodies. Sticking together removes every degree of freedom in the final velocities except the one shared value momentum conservation forces on them, leaving the least kinetic energy any momentum-conserving outcome can have; any relative motion left over after the collision only adds kinetic energy on top of that minimum.

cards.prompt: The **equal-mass** elastic case is worth memorizing on its own, because its result is so clean: when $m_1 = m_2$, solving the pair above gives $v_1' = v_2$ and $v_2' = v_1$ — the two bodies simply ___.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 9
cards.answer: exchange velocities

cards.prompt: Derive, or at least justify without re-deriving the algebra, why two equal-mass bodies in a one-dimensional elastic collision exchange velocities rather than ending up with some other pair of final speeds.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 9
cards.answer: With $m_1 = m_2 = m$, the momentum equation becomes $v_1 + v_2 = v_1' + v_2'$ and the kinetic energy equation becomes $v_1^2 + v_2^2 = v_1'^2 + v_2'^2$. The pair $v_1' = v_2, v_2' = v_1$ satisfies both trivially (it just swaps the two terms in each sum), and because two equations in two unknowns pin down the solution (excluding the trivial no-collision case $v_1'=v_1, v_2'=v_2$), that swap is the unique physical outcome.

cards.prompt: What does a measured coefficient of restitution of $e = 0.6$ tell you about a collision, and what would $e = 0$ and $e = 1$ each mean physically?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 9
cards.answer: $e = 0.6$ means the bodies separate afterward at 60% of the relative speed they approached with — some kinetic energy was lost, but they did not stick. $e = 1$ means they separate at the same relative speed they approached with (no kinetic energy lost — elastic). $e = 0$ means the relative speed afterward is zero — the bodies move off together, which is the perfectly inelastic case.

cards.prompt: A dropped ball bounces back to exactly the height it was dropped from, over and over. What does this imply about its coefficient of restitution with the floor, and about the collision type?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 9

choices.text: e = 1 — no kinetic energy is lost on each bounce, so the collision is (effectively) elastic
e = 0 — the ball is undergoing a perfectly inelastic collision each bounce
e = 1 — but this says nothing about whether energy is conserved
The coefficient of restitution cannot be determined from bounce height alone

cards.prompt: If a car crash's crumpling is measured to dissipate 40,000 J as heat, sound, and permanent deformation, has the collision violated conservation of energy?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 9
cards.answer: No. Conservation of energy always holds; what is not conserved in an inelastic collision is specifically kinetic energy. The 40,000 J did not vanish — it converted into other forms (deformation, heat, sound), so the total energy of the system, counting those forms, is exactly what it was before the crash.

cards.prompt: State the mechanical energy conservation law together with the condition under which it holds.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 8
cards.answer: KE + PE = constant, but only when no non-conservative force does work on the system. In general, KE_f + PE_f = KE_i + PE_i + W_nc, where W_nc is the work done by non-conservative forces.

cards.prompt: A block slides down a ramp with friction. Which statement about its mechanical energy is correct?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 8

choices.text: Mechanical energy is not conserved — friction does negative work, so KE + PE decreases
Mechanical energy is conserved, since gravity is still conservative
Mechanical energy is conserved as long as PE is measured from the bottom of the ramp
Mechanical energy increases, since the block speeds up

cards.prompt: When can KE + PE = constant be applied to a system, and what condition invalidates it?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 8
cards.answer: It applies exactly when no non-conservative force does work on the system over the interval considered — commonly true for gravity and springs alone. It is invalidated the moment friction, air drag, or an applied external force does nonzero work, since that work adds or removes energy from the KE + PE total rather than merely converting between its two forms.

cards.prompt: A ball rolls down each of three differently shaped frictionless ramps, all starting at the same height and ending at the same lower height. How do their speeds at the bottom compare?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 8
cards.answer: They are all equal. Mechanical energy conservation only relates the initial and final heights (through PE = m*g*h), never the shape of the path between them, so any frictionless track connecting the same two heights produces the same final speed.

cards.prompt: Friction does not destroy energy — that would violate a far broader conservation law than the mechanical one. What friction does is convert mechanical energy into ___ energy (and sometimes sound), which is exactly why the general form above needs a $W_{nc}$ term rather than energy simply vanishing: the "lost" mechanical energy is accounted for, just not as $KE + PE$ anymore.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 8
cards.answer: thermal

cards.prompt: Two motors each lift an identical 1000 kg load to the same height, doing the same total work. Motor A finishes in 5 seconds; Motor B takes 50 seconds. What can you conclude?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 8

choices.text: Motor A delivers ten times the power of Motor B, even though both do the same total work
Motor A does ten times more work than Motor B
The two motors are equivalent, since power is just another name for work
Motor B is more efficient, since it uses energy more slowly

cards.prompt: What distinguishes "how much energy a task requires" from "how much power a task requires"?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 8
cards.answer: Energy (or total work) is fixed by the task itself — the mass moved and the height or distance involved — regardless of how quickly it happens. Power is the rate at which that fixed amount of energy is delivered, so the same task can be done by a low-power source taking a long time or a high-power source taking a short time, with the energy requirement unchanged either way.

cards.prompt: A 10 kg crate sits at rest on a floor with mu_s = 0.5. A person pushes horizontally with 20 N and the crate does not move. What is the magnitude of the static friction force on the crate?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 6

choices.text: 20 N — static friction matches the applied force exactly, up to its maximum, so with the crate not accelerating it must equal the push
mu_s*N = 0.5 * (10*9.8) ≈ 49 N, since static friction is always at its maximum value
0 N, since the crate isn't moving so no friction acts
It cannot be determined without knowing the crate's speed

cards.prompt: Why is $f_s = \mu_s N$ the wrong general formula for static friction, even though it correctly gives the maximum static friction available?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 6
cards.answer: Because static friction is a self-adjusting response that takes on whatever value, between zero and mu_s*N, is needed to prevent relative sliding — mu_s*N is only reached at the threshold of slipping. Below that threshold, the actual static friction equals whatever other force it must balance, which can be any value up to that maximum, not the maximum itself.

cards.prompt: Given that mu_k is typically less than mu_s for a given pair of surfaces, what does that predict about the force needed to start a stationary object sliding versus the force needed to keep it sliding at constant velocity once moving?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 6
cards.answer: More force is needed to start the object moving (overcoming the higher maximum static friction, mu_s*N) than to keep it sliding at constant velocity afterward (overcoming the smaller kinetic friction, mu_k*N). Once past the initial threshold, the required force drops.

cards.prompt: Explain what makes the friction model's independence from contact area surprising, and state one condition under which the model is known to break down.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 6
cards.answer: It's surprising because a naive expectation is that more contact area means more friction (more surface "gripping"), the way it would for an adhesive. Instead, over a wide range of ordinary conditions, doubling the contact area while keeping normal force fixed leaves friction essentially unchanged — a smaller area presses harder per unit area, compensating. The model breaks down at extremes: very high contact pressure, very high sliding speed, or surfaces that deform or heat significantly under sliding.

cards.prompt: Derive the condition for the angle at which a block on an incline is on the verge of sliding, starting from the down-slope and perpendicular components of gravity.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 6
cards.answer: Gravity resolves into m*g*sin(theta) along the incline and m*g*cos(theta) into the incline, so N = m*g*cos(theta). The block is on the verge of slipping when the down-slope component equals the maximum static friction: m*g*sin(theta) = mu_s*N = mu_s*m*g*cos(theta). Mass cancels, leaving tan(theta) = mu_s — the tipping angle depends only on the coefficient of static friction, not on the block's mass.

cards.prompt: Tension is the pulling force a stretched string, rope, or cable exerts along its length. The standard simplifying idealization is a **massless** string: since $F_{net} = ma$ with $m = 0$ forces the net force on any segment of the string to be zero, tension must be the ___ throughout its length (through an ideal, frictionless pulley too), which is what lets you treat the string as a single connector transmitting one force rather than solving for its internal distribution.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 6
cards.answer: same

cards.prompt: What physical assumption makes tension uniform throughout a massless, frictionless string or rope?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 6
cards.answer: With zero mass, F_net = m*a forces the net force on every segment of the string to be exactly zero, since any nonzero net force on a massless segment would produce infinite acceleration. That requires the tension pulling on each end of every segment to be equal in magnitude, which propagates the same tension value along the whole string.

cards.prompt: A car's acceleration increases steadily from 0 to 4 m/s^2 over 10 seconds (it is not constant). What happens if you use $v = v_0 + at$ with $a$ set to the average acceleration to find the final velocity?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 2

choices.text: It gives the wrong answer — the equation assumes constant acceleration throughout, and no single "effective" value of $a$ reproduces the true final velocity from a changing one in general
It gives the exact right answer, since averaging the acceleration always compensates for it changing
The equation still applies unchanged, because $v = v_0 + at$ never assumed anything about acceleration in the first place
It works as long as you also average the initial velocity

cards.prompt: Write the four constant-acceleration kinematic equations, and state the variable each one omits.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 2
cards.answer: v = v0 + a*t (omits x - x0) x - x0 = v0*t + (1/2)*a*t^2 (omits v) v^2 = v0^2 + 2*a*(x - x0) (omits t) x - x0 = (1/2)*(v0 + v)*t (omits a)

cards.prompt: Why does knowing which variable an equation omits matter for solving a kinematics problem, rather than just picking any of the four and solving algebraically?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 2
cards.answer: Because the four equations are not independent alternatives to plug numbers into at random — each is missing exactly one of the five quantities (x - x0, v0, v, a, t). If a problem never states or asks for one of those five, the equation that omits it is the one solvable directly from the given data, without first solving for an unneeded intermediate quantity.

cards.prompt: Position, velocity and acceleration are all vectors, and in more than one dimension each component evolves independently under its own acceleration. This is exactly what makes projectile motion tractable: horizontal velocity stays ___ (no horizontal acceleration, ignoring air resistance), while gravity alone governs the vertical component, at $-9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 2
cards.answer: constant

cards.prompt: What lets you analyze horizontal and vertical motion in a projectile separately, using the same time variable t, instead of solving one coupled two-dimensional problem?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 2
cards.answer: Acceleration in one perpendicular direction has no effect on velocity or position in the other. Horizontal and vertical motion are governed by independent equations of the same t, which is why a projectile's horizontal velocity component never changes while its vertical component follows ordinary free-fall kinematics.

cards.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up, and you choose upward as positive. What sign is its acceleration while in flight (ignoring air resistance)?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 2

choices.text: Negative throughout the flight — gravity points downward, opposite the chosen positive direction, regardless of whether the ball is rising or falling
Positive while rising, negative while falling
Negative while rising, positive while falling
Zero at the instant it reverses direction, otherwise negative

cards.prompt: Average velocity over an interval is displacement divided by elapsed time; instantaneous velocity is the derivative of position at one instant. The two are ___ only when acceleration is zero over that interval — otherwise the object's speed is changing throughout, so the average necessarily differs from the value at any single instant.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 2
cards.answer: equal

cards.prompt: Why do average velocity and instantaneous velocity coincide for an object moving at constant velocity, but generally differ for one under constant nonzero acceleration?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 2
cards.answer: With zero acceleration, velocity never changes, so its value at every instant equals the constant value that also equals displacement over time. With nonzero acceleration, velocity is different at every instant during the interval, so the single average value (displacement over elapsed time) cannot equal all of those changing instantaneous values — it can coincide with at most one moment.

cards.prompt: $F = ma$ is the special case of this law that holds only under the hypothesis of ___ — differentiate $p = mv$ with constant $m$ and the mass falls out of the derivative, leaving $F = m(dv/dt) = ma$. The general form is what you need whenever mass changes during the motion, such as a rocket burning fuel or a raindrop accreting water as it falls.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 9
cards.answer: constant mass

cards.prompt: Why does $F_{net} = dp/dt$ reduce to $F = ma$ for a rocket only before it starts burning fuel, and not during the burn?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 9
cards.answer: During the burn, mass is changing with time, so $dp/dt = d(mv)/dt$ expands by the product rule into $m(dv/dt) + v(dm/dt)$ — a second term that vanishes only when $dm/dt = 0$. $F = ma$ silently drops that term, so applying it to a rocket mid-burn omits the thrust contribution from expelled mass and gets the dynamics wrong.

cards.prompt: A car crashes into a rigid wall versus into a crumple-zone barrier that brings it to rest over a longer distance and time, losing the same amount of momentum either way. Explain, from the impulse-momentum theorem, why the occupant experiences a smaller peak force in the second case.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 9
cards.answer: Both cases deliver the same impulse $J = \Delta p$, since the car loses the same momentum either way. $J = F \Delta t$, so for fixed $J$, force and time are inversely related: stretching the stopping time over the crumple zone's longer deceleration means a smaller average force is needed to produce that same $\Delta p$. The rigid wall delivers the same momentum change almost instantly, forcing $F$ to be much larger.

cards.prompt: Two skaters push off each other on frictionless ice. Why is the total momentum of the two-skater system conserved during the push?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 9

choices.text: The push is an internal force pair; by Newton's third law the two forces are equal and opposite, so they cancel in the system's total momentum, and there is no net external horizontal force
Because each skater's individual momentum is conserved separately
Because the push forces are too small to matter
Because kinetic energy is conserved in the push, and momentum follows from that

cards.prompt: Why is momentum conserved in essentially every collision, while kinetic energy is conserved only in special ones?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 9
cards.answer: Momentum conservation follows just from Newton's third law canceling internal forces in the total, given no net external force — true regardless of how the bodies interact. Kinetic energy conservation additionally requires the internal forces to do zero net work on the system, which fails whenever a collision deforms, heats, or otherwise dissipates energy internally; that is a much more restrictive condition.

cards.prompt: Momentum's directionality matters in practice: it is a ___, so two equal-mass bodies moving toward each other at the same speed have equal and opposite momenta that sum to zero, even though neither one's speed is zero. Treating momentum as if it were speed — summing magnitudes instead of components — is a common setup error in collision problems.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 9
cards.answer: vector

cards.prompt: In a real car crash, why is treating "momentum before" and "momentum after" as conserved a good approximation, even though the road exerts friction (an external force) on the cars throughout?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 9
cards.answer: Conservation strictly requires zero net external force, but the collision itself happens over a very short time compared to the impulse the collision forces deliver. Friction from the road acts the whole time but is comparatively small, so the external impulse it contributes over the brief collision window is negligible next to the internal collision forces — momentum is conserved to good approximation during the collision itself, even though it is not conserved over the whole longer process of skidding to a stop afterward.

cards.prompt: A garden hose sprays water at constant mass flow rate and constant speed against a wall, where it stops. Which form of Newton's second law correctly gives the force the water exerts on the wall?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 9

choices.text: F_net = dp/dt, evaluated using the rate at which momentum arrives, since the mass of water interacting with the wall is continuously changing, not fixed
F = m*a, treating the total mass of water sprayed as a single accelerating object
Neither applies, because the water's speed never changes
F = m*a, using the wall's own mass

cards.prompt: Why is the first law not just the special case of $F_{net} = ma$ with $F_{net} = 0$?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 5-6
cards.answer: Because the second law is only true in an inertial frame, and something has to say which frames those are. The first law does that job: it declares that a frame where a force-free object moves at constant velocity is inertial. Read as a special case of the second law it is redundant, but read as a definition it is what licenses applying the second law at all — in a braking car or on a rotating platform, objects accelerate with no real force acting, and $F_{net} = ma$ simply does not hold there.

cards.prompt: A box sits on a table under gravity, a normal force, and someone pushing sideways with friction resisting the push. To find the box's acceleration correctly, $F_{net}$ in $F_{net} = ma$ should be taken as:
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 5-6

choices.text: The vector sum of gravity, the normal force, the push, and friction, all acting on the box
Only the push, since that is the force causing the motion
The push minus friction only, ignoring gravity and the normal force since they are vertical
Whichever single force has the largest magnitude

cards.prompt: A book rests on a table, in equilibrium. Its weight (gravity) and the table's normal force on it are equal and opposite. Are these two forces a Newton's-third-law action-reaction pair?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 5-6

choices.text: No — both forces act on the same body (the book); a third-law pair always consists of forces on two different bodies
Yes — they're equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, which is exactly what a third-law pair requires
Yes, but only because the book is in equilibrium
No, because gravity and normal force are different types of force, and third-law pairs must be the same type

cards.prompt: State the four steps of drawing a free-body diagram for a single body, and explain why restricting the diagram to forces acting on only that one body is what makes the technique work on complicated systems.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 5-6
cards.answer: 1. Isolate one body. 2. Draw only the external forces acting on that body (never forces it exerts elsewhere, never a reaction-pair force acting on a different object). 3. Choose axes. 4. Resolve each force into components along those axes and sum them. Restricting the diagram to one body's own forces turns a system of interacting objects into a single vector equation, F_net = m*a, for that body alone — the interactions with other bodies are already captured as individual forces in the diagram, so nothing about the rest of the system needs to be tracked simultaneously.

cards.prompt: An object's weight in newtons on Earth is $mg$ with $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$. What happens to its weight, and what happens to its mass, if the same object is moved to the Moon (g ≈ 1.6 m/s^2)?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 5-6
cards.answer: Its weight decreases, since W = m*g and g is smaller — the object weighs roughly a sixth as much. Its mass is unchanged, because mass is an intrinsic property of the object (its amount of matter and its inertia), not a force, and does not depend on the local gravitational field.

cards.prompt: Why is it wrong to assume the normal force on a person standing in an accelerating elevator always equals m*g?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 5-6
cards.answer: Because normal force is not a fundamental force with a fixed formula — it is whatever value the surface must supply to prevent penetration, determined by applying F_net = m*a to the person. When the elevator accelerates, the net force on the person is nonzero, so the normal force must differ from m*g by exactly m*a to produce that acceleration; N = m*g only holds in the special case of zero vertical acceleration.

cards.prompt: What property of a force is *equivalent* to it being conservative, and therefore to a potential energy being definable for it at all?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 8

choices.text: The work it does around any closed path is zero
It always points toward a single fixed center
It never does negative work
Its magnitude never depends on position

cards.prompt: Why does path-independence of work matter enough to be the defining property of a conservative force, rather than just an incidental fact about gravity and springs?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 8
cards.answer: Because it is exactly what allows "potential energy at a point" to be well-defined. If work depended on the path taken to reach a point, the energy assigned to that point would depend on history rather than position, so no single-valued function of position could represent it. Path-independence is what lets the force's work be captured entirely by a function U(position).

cards.prompt: Write the standard forms of gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface and elastic potential energy of an ideal spring, and give the units.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 8
cards.answer: PE_grav = m*g*h and PE_spring = (1/2)*k*x^2, both in joules (J). h is height above a chosen reference, and x is the spring's displacement from its unstretched length.

cards.prompt: Nothing in physics tells you where to put $h = 0$, and nothing needs to — only ___ in potential energy between two configurations produce a force or do work; the reference point is a free choice that cancels out of every physical prediction. This is exactly why a negative potential energy (an object below your chosen $h = 0$) is not a sign of an error: it just means that position sits below the arbitrary reference, not below some absolute floor of energy.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 8
cards.answer: changes

cards.prompt: A satellite orbit calculation defines gravitational potential energy as zero at infinite separation, making PE negative everywhere a bound orbit exists. What does that negative value indicate?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 8
cards.answer: Nothing physically alarming — it only reflects the chosen reference point (zero at infinite separation), which puts every bound configuration, being closer than infinite separation, below that reference. Only differences in PE between two configurations are physical; the value at any single point depends entirely on where the zero was placed.

cards.prompt: State the relation between a conservative force and its potential energy function in one dimension, and explain what the sign means physically.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 8
cards.answer: F = -dU/dx. The negative sign means the force points in the direction of decreasing potential energy — toward lower U, not higher — so an object under a conservative force alone always accelerates "downhill" in its potential energy.

cards.prompt: An object slides from point A to point B twice: once along a short straight path, once along a long looping path, both on a floor with kinetic friction. How does the work done by friction compare?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 8

choices.text: It is different (more negative) on the longer path, because friction's work depends on path length, not just the endpoints
It is identical on both paths, because friction always does the same total work between two fixed endpoints
It is zero on both paths, since friction is a contact force
It is positive on the longer path and negative on the shorter one

cards.prompt: The $\sin(\theta)$ factor is the whole content of the ___ idea.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 10-11
cards.answer: lever arm

cards.prompt: You push on a door with the same force magnitude in two ways: (A) at the doorknob, perpendicular to the door's face, and (B) at the same spot but pushing straight toward the hinge (along the door's plane toward the axis). Which produces more torque about the hinge?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 10-11

choices.text: (A) — the force is perpendicular to r, giving sin(theta) = 1 and the full r*F as torque; (B) is directed along r, giving sin(theta) = 0 and zero torque
(B) — pushing toward the hinge concentrates force closer to the axis
Both produce equal torque, since the force magnitude and application point are the same
Neither produces torque unless the door is already moving

cards.prompt: Why does pushing on a door exactly at the hinge produce no rotation, regardless of how much force is applied?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 10-11
cards.answer: Torque's magnitude is r*F*sin(theta); at the hinge, the distance r from the axis to the point of application is essentially zero, so the torque r*F*sin(theta) is zero regardless of F. There is no lever arm for the force to act through.

cards.prompt: A solid disc and a ring have the same mass and the same outer radius. Why does the ring have a larger moment of inertia about the central axis?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 10-11

choices.text: All of the ring's mass sits at the maximum radius, while the disc's mass is spread from the center outward — since I weights mass by r^2, concentrating mass farther from the axis increases I even with equal total mass
The ring has more mass than the disc
Moment of inertia only depends on total mass, so they must be equal, and the premise is wrong
The ring rotates faster, which increases its moment of inertia

cards.prompt: Explain, from the definition $I = \int r^2\, dm$, why a thin rod's moment of inertia about an axis through one end is larger than about an axis through its center — without looking up the standard-forms table.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 10-11
cards.answer: Every mass element's distance to the axis matters through $r^2$. Measuring from the center, distances range symmetrically from 0 up to $L/2$ on both sides. Measuring from one end, every element is farther from that axis — distances now range from 0 to the full $L$ — so every $r^2$ term is larger, and the integral comes out bigger (in fact $\tfrac{1}{3}ML^2$ versus $\tfrac{1}{12}ML^2$, a factor of 4).

cards.prompt: State the parallel axis theorem and identify what each symbol requires (in particular, what I_cm must be measured about).
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 10-11
cards.answer: I = I_cm + M*d^2, where I_cm is the moment of inertia about an axis through the body's center of mass, d is the perpendicular distance from that center-of-mass axis to the new (parallel) axis, and M is the total mass. I_cm specifically must be about the center of mass — the theorem does not let you shift between two arbitrary parallel axes directly; one of them has to be the center-of-mass axis.

cards.prompt: The case where a round body rolls along a surface with no skidding is called ___, and it is the case worth having a name for because its kinetic energy has two independent pieces.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 10-11
cards.answer: rolling without slipping

cards.prompt: Why do a hoop and a solid disc of equal mass and radius, released from rest at the top of the same ramp, arrive at the bottom at different times despite losing the same gravitational potential energy?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 10-11
cards.answer: Rolling without slipping splits the released energy between translational and rotational kinetic energy. The hoop's larger moment of inertia (I = M*R^2 versus the disc's (1/2)*M*R^2) means a larger share of the available energy must go into spinning it up for a given rolling speed, leaving less for translation — so the hoop reaches a lower v_cm and arrives later than the disc, even though both started with identical energy.

cards.prompt: A block slides across a rough horizontal floor. Which force acting on it does zero work as it slides?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 7

choices.text: The normal force, because it is always perpendicular to the block's displacement
Friction, because it always opposes the motion
Gravity, because the block is on a horizontal surface
The applied force pushing the block forward

cards.prompt: Why does a force perpendicular to an object's displacement do zero work on it, regardless of how large that force is?
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 7
cards.answer: Work depends on the component of force along the direction of motion, $F\cos(\theta)$. A perpendicular force has $\theta = 90$ degrees, so $\cos(\theta) = 0$ no matter how large the force's magnitude is — it can change the object's direction (as centripetal force does) without ever adding or removing energy.

cards.prompt: Work is a ___, not a vector, and unlike distance or speed it can be negative: a force with a component opposite the displacement does negative work. Kinetic friction is the standard case — it always points opposite the direction of sliding, so it always removes energy from whatever is moving, never adds it.
citations: Halliday, Resnick & Walker, Fundamentals of Physics 10e, Ch. 7
cards.answer: scalar
